lessons.title: JavaScript Basics: Variables, Data Types and Operators
lessons.metaTitle: JavaScript Variables, Types and Operators
lessons.description: Start JavaScript from zero: let and const, strings, numbers, booleans, null and undefined, operators, strict equality, truthy and falsy values.

content.text: Node.js and Express are written in JavaScript, so this is where the course really begins. If you have never programmed, do not worry. We will move slowly, run every example, and explain each word the first time it appears. JavaScript is the language of the web: it started in browsers to make pages interactive, and Node.js lets the same language run on a server. Learn it once and you can build the front end and the back end of an app.

A program is a list of instructions for a computer. Most instructions work with **data**, so the first thing to learn is how to store data and what kinds of data exist. Think of a variable as a labelled box. The label is the name, and the box holds a value. When you need the value, you use the label.
Variables: let and const

You make a variable with `const` or `let`. Use `const` when the value will not be given a new value, and `let` when it will. Start with `const` for everything, and change to `let` only when you need to. There is also an old keyword, `var`, that you will see in old code. Avoid it, because it behaves in surprising ways. A variable name must start with a letter, an underscore or a dollar sign, cannot contain spaces, and is case sensitive: `price` and `Price` are different names. By habit, programmers write names in camelCase, such as `totalPrice`.
The basic data types

items: **String:** text, written in quotes, such as `'Node.js'`.
**Number:** whole and decimal numbers. JavaScript uses one type for both, so `10` and `10.5` are both numbers.
**Boolean:** only `true` or `false`. Booleans answer yes-or-no questions.
**null:** a value that means *empty on purpose*, like an empty box that you labelled yourself.
**undefined:** the value that a variable has before you give it one. It means *nothing was set yet*.
**BigInt:** whole numbers too large for a normal number. You rarely need it.
**Objects and arrays:** collections of values. Later lessons cover them.
Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Save the code below as `basics.js` and run it with `node basics.js`.

content.text: node basics.js

Node.js 125 499.5 true null undefined
string number boolean object undefined bigint
10 4 21 3.5 1 32
53 2
true false
false
true
[
  false, false, false,
  false, false, true,
  true,  true,  true
]
Guest 
undefined
Node.js has 125 students

Read the output line by line. The second line shows the result of `typeof`, an operator that tells you the type of a value. Notice that `typeof null` says `object`. That is an old mistake in the language that cannot be fixed without breaking old websites, so just remember it.
Operators

Operators are small symbols that do work. The arithmetic operators are `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%` (the remainder after division) and `**` (power). In the output, `7 % 2` is 1 because 7 divided by 2 leaves a remainder of 1. The line `'5' + 3` gives `53`, because when one side of `+` is text, JavaScript joins the two as text. But `'5' - 3` gives `2`, because `-` only works with numbers, so it turns the text into a number first. This kind of automatic conversion is called **type coercion**, and it is the cause of many beginner bugs. The best protection is to convert values on purpose, with `Number('5')`, and to use strict equality.

There are two ways to compare for equality. `==` is *loose*: it converts the types first, so `5 == '5'` is true. `===` is *strict*: it also compares the types, so `5 === '5'` is false. Always use `===` and `!==`. You will almost never need the loose version. Another famous surprise appears in the output too: `0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3` is `false`, because computers store many decimal fractions only approximately. That is why, in the payment lessons of this course, money is stored as whole numbers of cents.
Truthy and falsy

When you put any value in a condition, JavaScript treats it as true or false. The values that count as false are called **falsy**: `false`, `0`, the empty string `''`, `null`, `undefined` and `NaN` (short for *not a number*). Everything else is **truthy**, including the text `'hello'`, the number 42, and even an empty array `[]` or an empty object `{}`. The output above shows exactly which values are false, in the same order as the list.
Safe defaults: ||, ?? and ?.

Backend code constantly deals with missing values, such as a query string that was not sent. The `||` operator gives a default when the left side is falsy, so an empty text becomes `'Guest'`. The newer `??` operator gives a default only when the left side is `null` or `undefined`, so an empty text stays empty. Choose `??` when `0` or an empty string are valid values. The `?.` operator, called *optional chaining*, reads a property only if the thing before it exists. In the example, `user.profile?.city` gives `undefined` instead of crashing, while `user.profile.city` would throw an error because `profile` is `null`.

Finally, **template strings** use backticks and `${}` to place values inside text: `` `${course} has ${students} students` ``. They are the clean way to build messages, URLs and log lines, so you will use them everywhere.

The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.
Common mistakes

items: Using `=` when you mean `===`. A single `=` stores a value, and three compare.
Forgetting that `+` joins text. Convert input with `Number()` before you calculate.
Using `let` for everything. Prefer `const` so that accidental changes become errors.
Comparing decimals with `===`. Round them first or store whole numbers.

content.text: Your task

items: Change the code so that `students` goes up by 10 and print a message with a template string.
Predict the output of `'10' * '2'`, `'10' + '2'` and `true + 1`, then run them.
Write a line that uses `??` to print `'unknown'` when `city` is `null`, but `''` when `city` is an empty string.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You can explain the difference between `const` and `let`.
You can name the six falsy values.
You can say why `0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3` is false.

steps.say: A variable is a name that holds a value. const cannot be reassigned, let can.
Every value has a type, such as text, number or boolean.
Operators combine values. Watch for + joining text and for strict equality ===.
In a condition every value counts as truthy or falsy. Know the six falsy ones.

faqs.q: Should I use var?
faqs.a: No. Use const by default and let when the value must change. var has confusing rules and is only in old code.

faqs.q: What is the difference between null and undefined?
faqs.a: undefined means nothing was set yet. null means empty on purpose. Both are falsy.

faqs.q: Why use === instead of ==?
faqs.a: === compares the type as well, so it avoids surprises from automatic type conversion.

quiz.q: Which keyword should you use by default for a value that will not change?
What does 5 === "5" give?
quiz.explain: Strict equality also compares the type.

quiz.q: Which of these values is falsy?

lessons.title: JavaScript Conditions and Loops: if, switch, for and while
lessons.metaTitle: JavaScript Conditions and Loops
lessons.description: Learn how JavaScript makes decisions and repeats work: if and else, switch, the ternary operator, for, while, for of, for in, break and continue, with output.

content.text: A program that only runs from the first line to the last is not very useful. Real programs make decisions, such as *is this user an admin?*, and repeat work, such as *send an email to every customer*. In JavaScript, decisions are made with **conditions** and repetition is done with **loops**. Together with variables, they are the whole foundation of programming. A server uses them constantly: every route checks conditions, and every list of results is walked through with a loop.
Conditions: if, else if and else

An `if` statement runs a block of code only when its condition is true. You can add `else if` for more choices and `else` for the case when nothing matched. JavaScript checks the conditions from top to bottom and runs only the first block that matches. That is why the grade function below checks the highest score first. If it checked `score >= 50` first, every pass would become a `C`.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Save the code as `flow.js` and run it with `node flow.js`.

content.text: node flow.js

A B C Fail
weekend weekday
adult
Sum 1..5 = 15
First power of 2 above 100: 128
tool: node
tool: express
tool: mongo
name = Asha
city = Pune
odd 1
odd 3
odd 5

Notice the `return` statements in `grade`. When a function returns, it stops, so the lines after it do not run. Many programmers use this to write **early returns**: handle the unusual cases first and return, and keep the normal path flat and readable. You will see early returns in every Express route that checks input first.
switch and the ternary operator

When you compare one value against many exact choices, `switch` can be tidier than a long chain of `else if`. Each `case` is a possible value. Without a `return` or `break`, JavaScript *falls through* into the next case, which the example uses on purpose so that both `'Sat'` and `'Sun'` give the same answer. The `default` case runs when nothing matched. The **ternary operator**, `condition ? a : b`, is a one-line choice between two values. It is good for simple choices and hard to read when nested, so do not nest it.
Loops

A loop repeats a block of code. The classic `for` loop has three parts in its brackets: where to start, when to continue, and how to step. `for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++)` starts at 1, continues while `i` is at most 5, and adds 1 each round. A `while` loop only has a condition, and it is the right tool when you do not know in advance how many rounds are needed. Be careful: if the condition never becomes false, the loop never ends and freezes your program, which is called an **infinite loop**. In the example, `while (true)` is made safe with `break`, which ends the loop at once. `continue` is the opposite: it skips the rest of the current round and goes to the next.

For walking through a collection, use `for...of` for arrays, which gives you the values one by one, and `for...in` for the keys of an object. A common beginner mistake is to use `for...in` on an array. It gives you the index numbers as text, and can include surprising extras, so use `for...of` for arrays. Later you will meet array methods such as `map` and `filter`, which do most loop work in a shorter way.
Where you use this in a back end

items: A route checks `if (!user) return res.status(404)...` before it does the real work.
A `switch` on `req.method` or on an event name decides what to do.
A loop turns a list of database rows into a list of JSON objects.
A `while` loop can retry a failed network call a few times.

content.text: Do not run a loop that waits for something on the same thread, such as a loop that checks a flag forever. Node has one thread, and a loop that never gives it back stops the whole server. Lesson 44 explains this.

The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.
Common mistakes

items: Writing `if (x = 5)` with one `=`. It stores 5 instead of comparing.
Forgetting `break` in a `switch`, so the code falls through.
An off-by-one error: using `<` when you meant `<=`, or starting from 1 instead of 0.
Changing the array while you loop over it.

content.text: Your task

items: Add a grade `A+` for scores of 98 or more.
Write a loop that prints the multiplication table of 7 from 1 to 10.
Write a `while` loop that doubles a number until it passes 1000 and counts the rounds.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Your output matches the output above.
You can say when `switch` falls through.
You can explain how a `while (true)` loop ends.

steps.say: A condition is an expression that is true or false.
if, else if and else choose one block. The first match wins.
A loop repeats a block. break ends it early and continue skips a round.
Each round produces a result, such as one line or one object in a list.

faqs.q: When should I use switch instead of if?
faqs.a: When you compare one value against several exact choices. For ranges and complex conditions, use if and else if.

faqs.q: What is an infinite loop?
faqs.a: A loop whose condition never becomes false, so it never ends. Make sure that something inside changes the condition, or use break.

faqs.q: for...of or for...in?
faqs.a: Use for...of for the values of an array. Use for...in for the keys of an object.

quiz.q: What happens in a switch case with no break or return?
options: It falls through into the next case

quiz.q: Which loop is best for the values of an array?
What does continue do inside a loop?
options: Skips the rest of this round and goes to the next

lessons.title: JavaScript Functions, Arrays, Objects and Array Methods
lessons.metaTitle: JavaScript Functions, Arrays and Objects
lessons.description: Write functions and arrow functions, work with arrays and objects, and use map, filter, find, reduce and sort to process lists of data.

content.text: Almost everything that a back end does is: take some data in, change it in some way, and send some data out. **Functions** are the reusable pieces that do the changing, and **arrays** and **objects** are the shapes that the data takes. A list of orders is an array of objects. A request body is an object. If you are comfortable with these three things, reading Express code will feel natural. This lesson also covers the array methods that replace most loops in modern JavaScript.
Functions

A function is a named block of code that you can run again and again, optionally giving it inputs, called **parameters**, and getting an output back with `return`. Without `return` a function gives back `undefined`. You can give a parameter a **default value**, as in `add(a, b = 0)`, which is used when the caller leaves that argument out. An **arrow function**, written `(a, b) => a * b`, is a shorter way to write a function. With one expression, you can leave out the braces and the `return`, and the result is returned automatically. Arrow functions are the style used in most Express code, for route handlers and for array methods. There is one more reason to know functions well: in JavaScript they are values. You can store one in a variable, pass it to another function, and return it from a function. Express uses this idea all the time: `app.get('/', handler)` hands your function to Express, and Express calls it later.
Arrays and objects

An **array** is an ordered list, written with square brackets. Positions start at 0, so the first item is `list[0]`. Useful basics are `push` to add at the end, `pop` to remove the last item, `slice` to copy a part, and `length` for the size. An **object** is a set of named values, written with curly braces: `{ name: 'Pen', price: 10 }`. You read a value with `product.name`, add one by assigning to it, and remove one with `delete`. `Object.keys` and `Object.entries` list the names and the pairs. The JSON that APIs send and receive is just text in the shape of objects and arrays.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Save the code as `arrays.js` and run it with `node arrays.js`.

content.text: node arrays.js

5 2 20 36
[ 'Keyboard', 'Mouse', 'Monitor', 'Cable' ]
3
Monitor
true true
11200
[ 'Monitor', 'Keyboard', 'Mouse', 'Cable' ]
true 2
{ name: 'Pen', stock: 50 } [ 'name', 'stock' ] [ [ 'name', 'Pen' ], [ 'stock', 50 ] ]
true undefined
d [ 'b', 'c' ] [ 'a', 'b', 'c' ]
The array methods you will use every day

items: **`map`** makes a new array by changing every item. It is how you shape database rows into API replies.
**`filter`** keeps only the items for which your function returns true. It is how you remove unpaid orders.
**`find`** returns the first matching item, or `undefined`. **`findIndex`** returns its position.
**`some`** and **`every`** answer yes-or-no questions about a whole list.
**`reduce`** combines all items into one value, such as a total. It takes a starting value, here `0`.
**`sort`** orders an array **in place**, which means it changes the original. Copy first with `[...orders]` when you must keep the original, as the example does.
**`includes`** checks if a value is in an array.

content.text: Read the output against the code. `orders.filter((o) => o.paid).length` is 3 because three orders are paid. `reduce` adds up the prices to 11200. The sort puts the highest price first because the compare function returns a negative number when the first item should come earlier. Without a compare function, `sort` orders items as **text**, so `10` would come before `2`. That is another classic surprise.
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting `return` inside the braces of an arrow function, which gives `undefined`. Without braces the return is automatic.
Using `sort` on the original array when other code still needs it.
Using `map` just to loop. If you do not use the new array, use `for...of` instead.
Reading `list[list.length]`. The last item is at `list.length - 1`.
Comparing two objects with `===`. They are equal only if they are the very same object.

content.text: The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.
Your task

items: Add a `discount` function and use `map` to give every paid order a discounted price.
Use `reduce` to count how many orders are paid and how many are not, in one object.
Write a function that takes an array of numbers and returns the largest, without using `Math.max`.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Your output matches the output above.
You can explain why `sort` needs a compare function for numbers.
You can write `map`, `filter` and `reduce` calls from memory.

steps.say: Data usually arrives as an array of objects, such as rows from a database.
filter keeps only the items that pass your test.
map turns each item into the shape that you want to send.
reduce combines the items into one value, like a total.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a function and an arrow function?
faqs.a: They do the same job. Arrow functions are shorter, and with one expression they return it automatically. They also treat this differently, which matters in classes.

faqs.q: Does map change the original array?
faqs.a: No. map, filter and slice return new arrays. sort and splice change the original.

faqs.q: What is the difference between an array and an object?
faqs.a: An array is an ordered list accessed by position. An object is a set of named values accessed by name.

quiz.q: Which method makes a new array by changing every item?
Why copy an array before calling sort when you need the original?
What does reduce do?
options: Combines all items into one value

lessons.title: JavaScript Error Handling and JSON: try, catch, throw and parse
lessons.metaTitle: JavaScript Error Handling and JSON
lessons.description: Handle errors without crashing: try, catch, finally, throw, custom errors and async errors, and learn how JSON.stringify and JSON.parse work.

content.text: Things go wrong in real programs. A user types text where a number is needed, a file does not exist, a network call fails. A beginner program crashes. A professional program **expects** problems and decides what to do about each one. In a server, the difference matters a lot: one uncaught error in a handler must not take the site down for everyone. This lesson covers how JavaScript reports errors and how you catch them, and also JSON, the text format that nearly every API uses.
throw, try, catch and finally

To report a problem yourself, you **throw** an error: `throw new Error('message')`. A thrown error stops the current function and travels up to whoever called it, then to who called them, until something **catches** it. If nothing does, the program stops with an error message. You catch errors with `try` and `catch`. The code inside `try` runs normally. If anything inside it throws, JavaScript jumps straight to the `catch` block, and the variable in brackets holds the error. An optional `finally` block runs in both cases, whether there was an error or not, which makes it the right place for cleanup, such as closing a file or a database connection.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Save the code as `errors.js` and run it with `node errors.js`.

content.text: node errors.js

29
Caught: "abc" is not a valid age
finally always runs
ValidationError email true
Async caught: network down
{"name":"Asha","skills":["js","sql"],"joined":"2026-01-15T00:00:00.000Z"}
{
  "a": 1,
  "b": [
    2,
    3
  ]
}
3
Bad JSON: SyntaxError

Look at the first three lines. The first call works and prints 29. The second call throws, so the line `console.log('not reached')` never runs, the `catch` block prints the message, and `finally` prints its line. An error object has a `message` that explains the problem, a `name` such as `TypeError` or `SyntaxError`, and a `stack` that lists the chain of calls that led to it, which lesson 45 teaches you to read.
Custom errors

You can make your own kind of error by extending `Error`. The `ValidationError` in the example has an extra `field`. In an Express app you build classes such as `NotFoundError` or `AppError` with a status code, and one error handler turns them into the right response. That is the system of lesson 38. The check `error instanceof ValidationError` lets you treat different errors differently: show a message to the user for a validation error, but only log and show a generic message for an unknown one.
Errors in asynchronous code

A `try/catch` only catches errors thrown while it is running. A callback that runs later is outside of it. With promises, the fix is `async` and `await`: when you `await` a promise that fails, the failure is thrown as a normal error at that line, and your `try/catch` catches it, as the `load` example shows. Without `await`, you would receive the failed promise and the error would become an **unhandled rejection**, which can crash a Node process. The rule is: await your promises, and put a catch around the place where you can decide what to do. In Express 5, a rejected promise from an async route handler goes to the error handler automatically.
JSON: text that carries data

**JSON** stands for JavaScript Object Notation. It is plain text that looks like a JavaScript object, with some rules: names are in double quotes, there are no comments, and the values can only be text, numbers, `true`, `false`, `null`, arrays and other objects. Because it is text, it can be sent over a network or saved in a file. `JSON.stringify(value)` turns a JavaScript value into JSON text, and `JSON.parse(text)` turns JSON text into a value. Study the output. The `note: undefined` and the `greet` function are **dropped**, because JSON has no such types, and the `Date` became a text string in a standard format, so after `parse` it is a string and not a date. A third argument to `stringify`, such as `2`, adds indentation, which is useful for reading and for saving files.

`JSON.parse` throws a `SyntaxError` when the text is not valid JSON, so you must always wrap it in `try/catch` when the text comes from outside. Express's `express.json()` does this for you for request bodies, and answers 400 for broken JSON in the course code.

The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.
Common mistakes

items: An empty `catch` block that hides the error. At least log it.
Throwing text instead of an `Error`, which loses the stack trace.
Forgetting `await`, so the error escapes the `try/catch`.
Trusting `JSON.parse` on outside text without a `try/catch`.
Expecting dates, functions or `undefined` to survive `JSON.stringify`.

content.text: Your task

items: Make `parseAge` also reject ages above 120, and test it.
Write a `NotFoundError` class with a `status` of 404 and throw and catch it.
Save an object to a file with `JSON.stringify`, read it back with `JSON.parse` and compare.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Your output matches the output above.
You can say what `finally` is for.
You can name two things that `JSON.stringify` drops.

steps.say: Code reports a problem by throwing an Error.
Inside a try block, the throw stops the rest of the block.
Control jumps to catch, where you log, convert or answer with a message.
finally runs either way, so cleanup is never skipped.

faqs.q: What is the difference between throw and return?
faqs.a: return gives a value back normally. throw signals an error, which skips the normal path until something catches it.

faqs.q: Why does JSON.parse need a try/catch?
faqs.a: It throws a SyntaxError for invalid text, and text from outside can be invalid. Without a catch, that error can crash the request.

faqs.q: What is an unhandled rejection?
faqs.a: A promise failed and nothing handled the failure. It can crash a Node process, so await your promises and catch errors.

quiz.q: When does the finally block run?
options: Only when there is no error
Whether or not there was an error

quiz.q: Why wrap JSON.parse in try/catch when the text comes from outside?
options: It throws a SyntaxError for invalid JSON

quiz.q: Which of these does JSON.stringify drop?

lessons.title: What Is Node.js? Install It and Run Your First Script
lessons.metaTitle: What Is Node.js? Install and First Script
lessons.description: Learn what Node.js is, what it is used for, how to install it, and how to run JavaScript on your own computer outside the browser. Beginner friendly.

content.text: JavaScript began as a language that runs inside web browsers. It made buttons click and menus open. **Node.js** takes the same language and lets it run on a computer or server, outside the browser. That one change means a person who knows JavaScript can also write the back end of a website: the part that stores data, checks passwords and answers requests from the front end.

Node.js is not a new language and it is not a framework. It is a **runtime**: a program that reads your JavaScript file and runs it. Under the hood it uses V8, the same engine that runs JavaScript in Chrome, plus a library of tools for things a browser does not allow, such as reading files, opening network connections and starting servers. In this course you will use Node.js to build a real back end, a small task API with login, step by step.
What people build with Node.js

items: **Web servers and APIs** that a website or a mobile app talks to. This is what you will build.
**Command line tools**, for example scripts that rename a thousand files or clean a spreadsheet export.
**Build tools.** Many front end tools you may already use, such as Vite and webpack, run on Node.js.
**Real-time apps** such as chat, using web sockets.
**Automation and scheduled jobs**, such as sending a daily report.

content.text: Node.js is a good fit when your program spends most of its time waiting for things, such as the network or a database. It is less suited to heavy number crunching on a single thread, such as video editing. We will see why in the lesson on async code.
Install Node.js

Go to the official website, nodejs.org, and download the version marked **LTS**. LTS means long-term support: it receives security fixes for a long time, so it is the safe choice for learning and for real projects. Run the installer and keep the default options. This course needs Node.js 20.11 or newer, and newer LTS versions are fine. If you already have Node.js, you only need to check the version.
Open a terminal. On Windows, use PowerShell or the Terminal app. On macOS, use Terminal. On Linux, use your usual terminal. Then type these two commands.

node -v
npm -v

Each prints a version number such as `v22.12.0` for Node and `10.9.0` for npm. The numbers on your computer will probably be different, and that is fine. **npm** is Node's package manager. It comes with Node and downloads libraries that other people wrote. You will use it from the next lesson.

If the terminal says the command is not found, close it and open a new one. The installer changes your system path, and an old window does not see the change. If it still fails, run the installer again.
The REPL: try JavaScript instantly

Type `node` on its own and press Enter. You get a prompt where you can type JavaScript and see the result straight away. This is called the REPL (read, evaluate, print, loop). It is great for quick experiments.

> 2 + 3
5
> const prices = [120, 80, 650]
undefined
> prices.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)
850
> .exit
Press Ctrl+C twice, or type `.exit`, to leave. The REPL is for testing small ideas. Real programs live in files.
Your first script
Create a new folder called `taskapi` for the whole course, and open it in your editor (VS Code is a popular free choice). Create a file named `hello.js` with the code below.
Run it from the terminal, in the same folder, and add two extra words after the file name.
node hello.js one two

Hello, Asha! You have studied for 3 hours.
Node is running
[ 'one', 'two' ]

Look at what happened. `console.log` printed to the terminal instead of the browser console. The backtick string with `${name}` is a template string, which puts a variable inside text. And `process.argv` is a list of the words typed on the command line. We removed the first two entries with `slice(2)`, because those are the path to Node and the path to your script. `process` is a global object that Node gives you. It describes the running program.
What is different from the browser?

items: There is **no** `window` and **no** `document`. A server has no web page. Code that touches the page, such as `document.getElementById`, will fail.
There **is** a `process` object, a way to read files, and a way to start a server.
Your code runs **once**, on your machine, and you control the version of Node. In a browser, your code runs on every visitor's device and version.
The rest of the language is the same: variables, functions, arrays, objects, classes, promises, `async` and `await`.

content.text: Because the language is the same, you can already read most of the code in this course. The new part is the tools Node provides, and the habits of back-end work: validating input, handling errors and protecting data.
Where this course goes

There are 15 lessons. First the basics: modules, files and async code. Then plain Node servers, then Express, a library that makes servers easier to write. Then you build and test a small task API with login, store data in a file and in MongoDB, protect it, and get it ready for a server. Every code sample in the course was run before it was written here.
Your task

items: Install the LTS version of Node.js and run `node -v` and `npm -v`.
Create the folder `taskapi` and the file `hello.js`. Change the name and the number of hours.
Run `node hello.js` with three words after it and check that all three appear in the list.
Open the REPL, work out the total of three numbers with `reduce`, and leave with `.exit`.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: `node -v` prints a version that starts with `v20` or higher.
Running `node hello.js one two` prints your greeting and the list `[ 'one', 'two' ]`.
You can explain in one sentence why `document` does not exist in Node.js.

steps.say: You write a JavaScript file, such as hello.js.
You run it with the node command. Node reads the file and runs it with the V8 engine.
Node can use your computer directly: files, the network and the command line.
The results appear in the terminal, because console.log writes there and not in a browser.

faqs.q: Is Node.js a programming language?
faqs.a: No. The language is JavaScript. Node.js is a runtime that runs JavaScript outside the browser and adds tools for files, networks and servers.

faqs.q: Which Node.js version should I install?
faqs.a: The current LTS (long-term support) version from nodejs.org. It gets security fixes for a long time. This course needs Node.js 20.11 or newer.

quiz.q: What is Node.js?
options: A runtime that runs JavaScript outside the browser
quiz.explain: It is not a new language and not a framework.

quiz.q: Which version should you download for learning and real projects?
What kind of work suits Node.js well?
options: Heavy video editing on a single thread
Programs that spend most of their time waiting for the network or a database

notes: Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser: servers and APIs, command line tools, build tools, scheduled jobs.
Check the install: `node -v` should show `v20` or higher. After installing, open a new terminal.
The REPL (`node`) is for trying one line. A file (`node app.js`) is for a real script.
Different from the browser: no `document` and no `window`, but you get files and the system.
This course builds a tasks API with Express.

lessons.title: Modules, npm and package.json Explained
lessons.metaTitle: Node.js Modules, npm and package.json
lessons.description: Understand ES modules with import and export, how npm installs packages, what package.json and node_modules are, and how to add scripts to your project.

content.text: As a program grows, you cannot keep everything in one file. A **module** is simply a file whose code you can use from other files. Node.js supports the same module system as modern browsers, called **ES modules**, with `import` and `export`. In this lesson you will split code into files, start a proper project with `package.json`, install your first package and add scripts.
Turn on ES modules

Node can read two module styles. The older one, CommonJS, uses `require`. The newer one, ES modules, uses `import`. Most new code and most documentation now use `import`, so this course does too. To tell Node that your project uses it, create a `package.json` file. The easiest way is to let npm do it. Run this inside `taskapi`.

npm init -y
npm pkg set type=module

`npm init -y` creates `package.json` with default answers. `npm pkg set type=module` adds one line, `"type": "module"`, which makes every `.js` file in the project an ES module. Without that line, using `import` gives an error such as *Cannot use import statement outside a module*.
Export and import
Create `math.js`. It shares three things: a named function, a named constant, and a default export.
A file can have many **named** exports but only one **default** export. Now create `app.js` and use them.
node app.js

5 0.18 118
number

Three rules to remember. First, named imports go inside curly braces and must match the exported names. A default import has no braces, and you choose any name for it. Second, for your own files you must write the **file extension**, `./math.js`, and not just `./math`. Browsers and bundlers sometimes let you skip it, but Node does not. Third, paths for your own files start with `./` or `../`. A name with no dot, such as `express`, means a package from `node_modules`.

The check on the last line, `typeof os.cpus().length`, prints `number` whatever your computer is, so the output is the same for everybody. Printing the real number of processor cores would differ per machine.
Built-in modules and the node: prefix

Node ships with many modules that need no installation, such as `node:fs` for files, `node:path` for file paths, `node:os` for facts about the computer, `node:http` for servers, `node:crypto` for security tools and `node:test` for tests. Write the `node:` prefix when you import them, as in `import os from 'node:os'`. It shows the reader, and Node, that this is built in and not a package from the internet.
npm and packages
Most real projects use packages that other people wrote and shared on the npm registry, a huge public library. To add one, use `npm install`. Try it with the package we will use later.
npm install express

Three things happen. A folder named `node_modules` appears with the package and everything it needs. `package.json` gets a `dependencies` section that lists `express` with a version. And a file named `package-lock.json` records the exact versions installed, so every computer gets the same result.

items: **`node_modules`** can be huge. Never edit it by hand and never commit it to git. Add `node_modules` to `.gitignore`.
**`package.json`** lists what your project needs. Commit it.
**`package-lock.json`** locks exact versions. Commit it too.
To rebuild `node_modules` on another computer, run `npm install` and npm reads the two files.

content.text: Some packages are needed only while you develop, such as test or formatting tools. Install those with `npm install --save-dev name`, and npm lists them under `devDependencies`. On a server, `npm install --omit=dev` skips them.
Version numbers

A version such as `5.3.0` has three parts: major, minor and patch. A patch is a bug fix. A minor adds features without breaking old code. A major may break old code. In `package.json` you will see something like `^5.1.0`. The caret means npm may install newer minor and patch versions, but not a new major one. That protects you from surprise breaking changes while still receiving fixes.
npm scripts
The `scripts` section of `package.json` holds short names for commands. Add these three. We will create the files they use in later lessons, so do not run them yet.

Run `npm start` or `npm test` directly. Other names need `run`, for example `npm run dev`. The flag `--watch` restarts the program every time you save a file, so you do not need a separate tool. The flag `--env-file=.env` loads settings from a file named `.env`. You will meet it in lesson 16.
Safety with packages

A package is code from strangers, and it runs with your permissions. Choose well-known packages with many users and recent updates. Read the name carefully, because fake packages with names that look like popular ones exist. Run `npm audit` now and then to see reported problems in what you have installed, and keep dependencies updated.
Your task

items: Run `npm init -y` and `npm pkg set type=module` in `taskapi`.
Create `math.js` and `app.js` as shown and run `node app.js`.
Change `TAX` to `0.05`, run again, and check that the price of 100 changes.
Run `npm install express`, then look at `package.json` and the new files.
Create `.gitignore` containing the line `node_modules`.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: `node app.js` prints `5 0.18 118` and then `number`.
`package.json` shows `"type": "module"` and a `dependencies` section with `express`.
Deleting `node_modules` and running `npm install` brings it back.

steps.say: package.json describes your project and lists the packages it needs.
npm install reads that list and downloads the packages from the npm registry.
The packages are stored in the node_modules folder. Do not edit it and do not commit it.
Your own files then load those packages and your other files with import.

faqs.q: What is the difference between dependencies and devDependencies?
faqs.a: dependencies are needed to run the app. devDependencies are only for development, such as test tools. Install them with --save-dev.

faqs.q: Why must I write the file extension in imports?
faqs.a: In Node.js ES modules, import paths for your own files must include the extension, such as ./math.js. Without it, Node cannot find the file.

quiz.q: What does "type": "module" in package.json do?
options: Makes .js files ES modules so import and export work

quiz.q: Should you commit node_modules to git?
How many default exports can a file have?
quiz.explain: A file can have many named exports but only one default export.

notes: Turn on ES modules with `"type": "module"` in `package.json`. Then use `import` and `export`.
Built-in modules are imported with the `node:` prefix: `import os from 'node:os'`.
`npm install express` adds a package. It goes in `dependencies` in `package.json`.
Commit `package.json` and `package-lock.json`. Never commit `node_modules`.
`^5.1.0` in `package.json`: the caret allows newer minor and patch versions, not a new major one. `npm run name` runs a script.
Check a package before you install it: name, downloads, last update.

lessons.title: CommonJS vs ES Modules: require, import and export
lessons.metaTitle: CommonJS vs ES Modules in Node.js
lessons.description: Understand the two module systems in Node.js: require and module.exports versus import and export, how to choose, mix them and avoid the common errors.

content.text: When you read Node.js code, you will meet two ways to share code between files, and the beginner confusion about them is real. One looks like `const express = require('express')` and the other looks like `import express from 'express'`. Both work, both are common, and they come from different times in the history of JavaScript. This lesson explains where each comes from, how they differ in practice, and how to deal with the errors that appear when they meet.
Why two systems?

Early JavaScript had no way to split code into files. When Node.js started in 2009 it needed one, so it invented **CommonJS**: each file is a module, you expose things with `module.exports`, and you load them with `require`. Years later, the JavaScript language itself got an official module system, **ES modules** (ESM), with `export` and `import`. Browsers use it, and Node.js added support for it. So today Node supports both, and the old and the new live together in a huge number of projects.
CommonJS
node mod-cjs-main.cjs

5 3.14159
string mod-cjs-main.cjs
object object

In CommonJS, `require` loads the file **synchronously**, at the moment it runs, and returns whatever that file put into `module.exports`. Every CommonJS file also gets the free variables `__dirname` (the folder of the file), `__filename`, `module`, `exports` and `require`. Files normally end in `.js` in a project without `type: module`, or in `.cjs` to mark them clearly.
ES modules
node mod-esm-main.mjs

5 3.14159 A tiny math module
undefined
true true
top-level await works
15
[ 'PI', 'add', 'default' ]

ES modules use `export` to make things available, either **named** (`export const add`) or one **default** (`export default`). You import named things with braces, `import { add }`, and the default without braces, `import describe from`. They are loaded in a way that lets tools see the imports without running the code, which allows features such as tree shaking, and they support **top-level `await`**, shown in the example, which CommonJS cannot do. They do not have `__dirname`. The example shows the replacement: `import.meta.url` holds the address of the current file, and `fileURLToPath` plus `path.dirname` give you the folder.
How Node chooses the system

items: A file ending in `.mjs` is always an ES module, and `.cjs` is always CommonJS.
A `.js` file follows the `type` field in the nearest `package.json`: `"type": "module"` means ESM, and no type or `"commonjs"` means CommonJS.
This course uses `"type": "module"`, so every `.js` file uses `import` and `export`.
In ES modules, local imports must include the file extension: `./math.js`, not `./math`.

content.text: Mixing the two

From an ES module you can load a CommonJS file with `createRequire`, as the example does, and the default import of a CommonJS package usually works too: `import express from 'express'`. Going the other way used to be an error: a CommonJS file could not `require` an ES module and received `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM`. Newer versions of Node.js, including the 22 that this lesson was run on, allow `require` of an ES module that has no top-level `await`, and the dynamic `import()` function works from both worlds on every version and returns a promise. If your project must run on older Node versions, use `import()`. Check the Node.js documentation for your version.
Which should you use?

For a new project, use ES modules. They are the standard of the language, they match what you write in front-end code, and the ecosystem has moved that way. You still need to read CommonJS, because many tutorials, tools and configuration files use it. Some tools, such as the Jest configuration in lesson 46, work in the `.cjs` style. If you see the error `Cannot use import statement outside a module`, your file is being treated as CommonJS, so add `"type": "module"` or rename it to `.mjs`. If you see `require is not defined in ES module scope`, do the opposite: you used `require` in an ES module.

The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.
Common mistakes

items: Using `require` in a file that is an ES module, and `import` in one that is not.
Forgetting the file extension in an ES module import.
Using `__dirname` in an ES module, where it does not exist.
Mixing default and named imports: `import add from` when `add` is a named export.

content.text: Your task

items: Add a `subtract` function to the ES module and import it in the main file.
Rename `mod-esm-main.mjs` to `.js` and add and remove `type: module` to see both error messages.
Convert the CommonJS math file into an ES module and update the main file.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Both examples print the output shown above.
You can name the two replacements for `__dirname` and `require` in ES modules.
You can say which system a `.js` file uses, and where Node looks to decide.

steps.say: CommonJS is the original Node system. It loads files synchronously with require.
ES modules are the language standard. They add top-level await and static imports.
The type field in package.json, or .mjs and .cjs, tells Node which one a file uses.
To mix them, use createRequire in ESM or the dynamic import() in CommonJS.

faqs.q: Should I use require or import?
faqs.a: Use import with ES modules in new projects. Know require for reading older code and tools.

faqs.q: Why is __dirname not defined in my file?
faqs.a: It exists only in CommonJS. In an ES module, use path.dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)).

faqs.q: Can I use both in one project?
faqs.a: Yes. Use the file extensions .mjs and .cjs, or the type field, to say which each file is, and bridge with createRequire or import().

quiz.q: Which file ending always means CommonJS?
What replaces __dirname in an ES module?
Which system supports top-level await?

lessons.title: Working with Files and Paths: fs, path and JSON
lessons.metaTitle: Read and Write Files in Node.js with fs
lessons.description: Read and write files with node:fs/promises, build safe file paths with node:path, store data as JSON and handle errors such as a missing file.

content.text: A browser page is not allowed to read files from your disk. Node.js is. That makes it good for tools that process files, and for small apps that save data in a file. In this lesson you will use two built-in modules, `node:fs/promises` to read and write files, and `node:path` to build file paths, and you will store data as JSON. The file store you write here is the same idea we use for the task API later.
Reading and writing a file

The `fs` module has older callback functions and newer promise functions. Use the promise version, `node:fs/promises`. It works with `async` and `await`, which you will study in the next lesson. In ES modules you can use `await` at the top level of a file, so this works as it is.
node files.js

1 Learn Node
ENOENT ENOENT: no such file or directory, open

Walk through it line by line. `writeFile` creates the file, or replaces it if it exists. `readFile` with the encoding `'utf8'` returns text, and without an encoding it returns raw bytes. `JSON.stringify(tasks, null, 2)` turns the array into text with two-space indentation, which is easy to read. `JSON.parse` turns the text back into JavaScript objects. The last part reads a file that does not exist, and the `catch` block shows the error. The text in the output above is cut short because the real message continues with the full path of the missing file, which is different on every computer.
Build paths with the path module

Never join paths by hand with `'/'` or `'\'`. Windows and Linux use different separators. `path.join` does it correctly for the system it runs on. And never depend on the **current folder**, which is wherever you started the program. If you run `node` from another folder, a path like `./tasks.json` points to a different place. Instead, build paths from the folder that contains the script.

items: `import.meta.dirname` is the folder of the current file. It is available in current Node versions (20.11 and newer).
`path.join(import.meta.dirname, 'tasks.json')` builds a full path to a file beside your script.
`path.extname('photo.png')` returns `.png`, and `path.basename('/a/b/c.txt')` returns `c.txt`.
`path.resolve('data')` turns a relative path into an absolute one, starting from the current folder.

content.text: Error codes

When a file operation fails, the error has a `code`. The most common are `ENOENT` (the file or folder does not exist), `EACCES` (no permission) and `EEXIST` (it already exists). Check `err.code` to decide what to do. A missing file at start-up is often fine, for example the first time the app runs, and the program should create an empty list. Any other error should stop the program or be reported.
The last line, `throw err`, passes the problem on instead of hiding it. Silent failures are the hardest bugs to find.
Other useful file functions

items: `readdir(folder)` lists the names inside a folder.
`mkdir(folder, { recursive: true })` creates a folder and any missing parent folders, and does nothing if it already exists.
`appendFile(file, text)` adds text to the end of a file. It suits simple logs.
`rename`, `copyFile` and `rm` move, copy and delete files. Be careful with `rm`: it does not use a recycle bin.
`stat(file)` returns information such as size and last modified time.

content.text: Limits of storing data in a file

A JSON file is a very good way to learn, and it is fine for a tiny personal tool. But it has real limits. The whole file must be rewritten on every change. If two requests write at the same moment, one change can be lost. It cannot search large data quickly. And if the program crashes in the middle of writing, the file can be left half written. Databases solve these problems. Later in this course you will use a file first, because it is simple, and then MongoDB.
Never save passwords, tokens or secrets as plain text in a file that is committed to git or served to the public. We will deal with secrets properly in lesson 16.
Your task

items: Create `files.js` as shown and run it. Open `tasks.json` in your editor and look at it.
Add a second task to the array and run again. Check that the file has two tasks.
Write a function `loadTasks(file)` that returns an empty list when the file is missing, and test it with a file name that does not exist.
Use `appendFile` to write a line with the current date and time to `log.txt` each time the script runs.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: `node files.js` prints `1 Learn Node` and then an `ENOENT` line.
`tasks.json` contains your tasks with two-space indentation.
`loadTasks('nothing.json')` returns `[]` instead of crashing.

steps.say: Your data lives in memory as JavaScript objects and arrays.
JSON.stringify turns it into text that can be saved.
writeFile saves the text in a file on disk.
Later, readFile and JSON.parse bring the data back as objects.

faqs.q: What does ENOENT mean?
faqs.a: It means the file or folder does not exist. It is the usual error code when you read a missing file.

faqs.q: Why use path.join instead of joining strings?
faqs.a: path.join uses the right separator for the operating system and cleans up extra slashes, so the same code works on Windows, macOS and Linux.

quiz.q: Why use path.join instead of joining paths with "/" by hand?
options: Windows and Linux use different separators

quiz.q: What does the error code ENOENT mean?
options: The file or folder does not exist

quiz.q: What does readFile return without an encoding?
quiz.explain: Use the encoding 'utf8' to get text.

notes: Use `fs/promises` with `await`: `readFile`, `writeFile`, `appendFile`, `readdir`, `mkdir`.
Build paths with `path.join(import.meta.dirname, 'tasks.json')`. It works on every system.
`ENOENT` means the file does not exist. Catch it and return a safe default, such as `[]`.
`mkdir(folder, { recursive: true })` is safe to run twice.
`rm` has no recycle bin. A file store is fine for learning, not for many users.
Never save secrets as plain text in a committed file.

lessons.title: Async JavaScript in Node: Promises, async/await and the Event Loop
lessons.metaTitle: Async Node.js: Promises, await, Event Loop
lessons.description: Understand why Node.js is asynchronous, how promises and async/await work, how to handle errors, run tasks in parallel and avoid blocking the event loop.

content.text: Almost everything useful in a server takes time: reading a file, asking a database, calling another service. If the program stopped and waited for each one, a single slow request would freeze every other visitor. Node.js avoids this with **asynchronous** code. This lesson is the most important idea in the whole course, so take your time.
One thread and an event loop

Your JavaScript runs on a single thread, which means one line at a time. But slow work, such as file and network operations, is handed to the operating system. While the system works, Node carries on with other code. When the work is done, the result is put in a queue, and the **event loop** takes it from the queue and runs your code that was waiting for it. Think of a waiter in a restaurant. The waiter does not stand at the kitchen door until your meal is ready. They take your order, serve other tables, and bring your food when the kitchen calls.

This design handles thousands of waiting connections with little memory. The price is one rule: **never block the thread** with long work. If you run a loop that takes five seconds, no other request is answered for five seconds.
Promises

A **promise** is an object that stands for a value that is not ready yet. It is in one of three states: pending, fulfilled (with a value) or rejected (with an error). You attach code to it with `.then` for success and `.catch` for failure. Most modern Node functions, including `fs/promises` and `fetch`, return promises.
async and await

`async` and `await` let you write promise code that reads from top to bottom. Putting `await` before a promise pauses **that function** until the promise settles, and gives you the value. The program as a whole is not paused: other work continues. You can use `await` only inside an `async` function, or at the top level of an ES module file. Run this example.
node async.js

1 start
2 end of script
2.5 promise
3 timer
{ id: 1, name: 'Asha' }
caught: No user 2
parallel ok true Asha Asha

Study the order of the first four lines. The code runs from top to bottom: line `1`, then it schedules a timer and a promise, then line `2`. Only after the main script finishes does Node run the waiting work. Promise callbacks run **before** timer callbacks, even a timer set to zero milliseconds. This surprises many beginners, and you do not need to memorise it. Just remember that async results never appear in the middle of your current code.
Handling errors

When an awaited promise is rejected, `await` throws the error, and you catch it with an ordinary `try` and `catch`, as shown with `getUser(2)`. If you forget, an unhandled rejection can crash your program or leave a request hanging. Two habits help: use `try` and `catch` where you can do something useful about the error, and let other errors travel upwards to one central place. In Express, that central place is an error handler, which you will build in lesson 15.
Sequential or parallel?

Two awaits one after the other run one after the other. If the two tasks do not depend on each other, start both first and wait for both together with `Promise.all`. In the example, two 50 ms calls finish in about 50 ms in total, not 100 ms. If one promise in `Promise.all` rejects, the whole thing rejects. Use `Promise.allSettled` when you want every result, whether it worked or failed.
A common mistake: forgetting await

If you forget `await`, you get a promise object instead of the value. You will see output such as `Promise { <pending> }`, and a later line fails with an odd error. When a value looks strange, check that every async call has `await`. Another mistake is using `await` inside `forEach`. The loop does not wait. Use a `for...of` loop, or `Promise.all` with `map`.
Do not block the event loop

items: Avoid long synchronous work in request code, such as huge loops or reading a big file with `readFileSync`.
Functions ending in `Sync` block the thread. They are fine in a start-up script, but not while serving requests.
For truly heavy computing, use worker threads or a separate service.

content.text: You do not need to understand every detail of the event loop to write good Node code. The practical rules are: use `await` for slow work, use `Promise.all` for independent work, catch errors, and never run long loops inside a request.
Your task

items: Create `async.js` and run it. Predict the order of the first four lines before you run it.
Add `getUser(3)` and `getUser(4)` inside `Promise.all` and measure the time with `Date.now()`.
Change `Promise.all` to `Promise.allSettled` and print the results. Make one of the calls fail on purpose.
Remove one `await` on purpose and see what is printed. Then put it back.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The first four lines print in the order `1`, `2`, `2.5`, `3`.
The parallel version takes about 50 ms, not 100 ms, and prints `parallel ok true`.
You can say what `await` does in your own words.

nodes.label: Your code
nodes.sub: runs one line at a time

steps.say: Your code runs on one thread. When it asks for slow work, it does not wait.
The slow work is handed to the system, such as reading a file or waiting for the network.
When the work is done, its result is put in a queue.
The event loop takes results from the queue and runs the code that was waiting, such as the code after await.

faqs.q: Is Node.js single-threaded?
faqs.a: Your JavaScript runs on one thread, but slow work like file and network operations is done by the system and its results come back through the event loop. Heavy computing can still block it.

faqs.q: When should I use Promise.all?
faqs.a: When you have several independent async tasks. Start them together and wait for all, which is faster than awaiting them one after the other.

quiz.q: What is a promise?
options: An object standing for a value that is not ready yet

quiz.q: Why should you avoid long synchronous work in request code?
options: It is not allowed by Node
It blocks the thread and no other request is answered meanwhile

quiz.q: What happens if you forget await before a promise?
options: You get the promise object, not its value

notes: Node has one thread and an event loop. Slow work (files, network) runs in the background.
A Promise is a value that arrives later. `await` waits for it inside an `async` function.
Handle errors with `try` / `catch` around `await`.
Independent jobs: `await Promise.all([a(), b()])` is faster than one after the other.
Forgot `await`? You get a Promise, not the value.
Do not block the event loop with long loops or `*Sync` functions inside a server.

lessons.title: Your First HTTP Server with Plain Node.js
lessons.metaTitle: Build a Plain Node.js HTTP Server
lessons.description: Learn how HTTP requests and responses work and build a small server with node:http. See why frameworks like Express exist and how to test with curl.

content.text: Before using Express, it is worth building one tiny server with only what Node provides. It takes five minutes, and afterwards Express will make sense, because you will see the work that it does for you. In this lesson you will learn how a web request is structured, write a server with the built-in `node:http` module and test it with `curl`.
What happens in a web request

HTTP is the conversation between a client, such as a browser, a phone app or `curl`, and a server. The client sends a **request**: a **method** (what to do), a **path** (which thing), headers (extra information) and sometimes a body (data). The server sends back a **response**: a **status code** (how it went), headers and usually a body. Learn these methods first.

items: **GET** reads data. It should not change anything.
**POST** creates something new, usually with data in the body.
**PUT** and **PATCH** change something that exists. PUT replaces it, PATCH changes part of it.
**DELETE** removes something.

content.text: And these status codes. The first digit tells the story: 2 means success, 3 means redirect, 4 means the client made a mistake, and 5 means the server had a problem.

items: **200 OK**: it worked. **201 Created**: something new was made. **204 No Content**: it worked and there is nothing to send back.
**400 Bad Request**: the request data is wrong. **401 Unauthorized**: log in first. **403 Forbidden**: you are logged in but not allowed. **404 Not Found**: no such thing.
**429 Too Many Requests**: slow down. **500 Internal Server Error**: the server broke.

content.text: A server in a few lines
Create `server.js` in a new folder, or in `taskapi` for this lesson.

`http.createServer` takes a function that runs for **every** request. It receives `req`, which describes the request, and `res`, which you use to answer. `res.writeHead` sets the status code and headers, and `res.end` sends the body and finishes the response. `server.listen(3000)` starts waiting for connections on port 3000. A port is like a door number on your computer. Run it.
node server.js
Listening on http://localhost:3000

The program does not finish. It keeps running and waiting for requests. Leave it running, open a **second** terminal, and test it with `curl`, a command line tool for making requests. Windows 10 and 11, macOS and most Linux systems include it. Or just open the address in a browser.

curl http://localhost:3000/
curl http://localhost:3000/api/time
curl -i http://localhost:3000/nope
The time in your output will be the time on your computer. The `-i` flag makes curl print the status line and headers as well. Stop the server with Ctrl+C in the first terminal.
If you see an error saying the address is already in use (`EADDRINUSE`), another program, or an old copy of your server, is using port 3000. Stop it, or change the number.
Why people use Express

Look at what you had to do by hand. You compared `req.method` and `req.url` with an `if` chain. You set the content type each time. You turned objects into JSON text yourself. For a real API, you would also have to read the request body in pieces, parse the JSON, split the query string from the path, pull out values from URLs such as `/api/tasks/7`, handle errors in one place and check logins. That is a lot of repeated, easy-to-get-wrong code.

Express is a small, popular library that handles all this for you. It is built directly on `node:http`, so everything you learned here still applies. In the next lesson you will build the same server in about half the lines.
Do not leave the server open to the world

By default, a server started on your own computer is reachable from your own machine, and on some systems also from the local network, depending on your firewall. While learning, that is fine. Do not put real passwords or private data into a practice server, and never expose a practice server to the internet.
Your task

items: Create `server.js` and start it. Test all three URLs with curl or the browser.
Add a route `GET /api/hello` that returns `{ "message": "Hello" }` as JSON.
Change the port to 3010 and test again.
Use `curl -i` and find the status code and the `Content-Type` header of each response.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: `curl http://localhost:3000/` prints `Hello from plain Node`.
An unknown path returns status 404 and a JSON error.
You can name one thing Express would do for you that you wrote by hand here.

steps.say: A client, such as a browser, a phone app or curl, wants some data.
It sends a request with a method and a path, for example GET /api/time.
Your server function runs for the request and decides what to answer.
It sends a response with a status code and a body, and the client shows or uses it.

faqs.q: What is the difference between 401 and 403?
faqs.a: 401 means the client is not logged in or has no valid login. 403 means the client is logged in but is not allowed to do that action.

faqs.q: Do I need Express to build a server?
faqs.a: No. node:http is enough, but you must write much repeated code for routing, JSON bodies and errors. Express removes most of that.

quiz.q: What does a 404 status code mean?
quiz.explain: The 4xx codes mean the client made a mistake; 5xx means a server problem.

quiz.q: Which HTTP method is for reading data and should not change anything?
The error EADDRINUSE usually means…
options: Another program or an old copy of your server is using the port

notes: Request in, response out. Methods: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH changes part, DELETE removes.
Status codes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 bad request, 401 log in, 403 not allowed, 404 not found, 429 slow down, 500 server broke.
A plain Node server works but gets long. Express makes routing short.
`EADDRINUSE` means another program, or an old copy of your server, is using the port.
Do not leave a test server open to the world.

lessons.title: Your First Express Server: Routes, Requests and Responses
lessons.metaTitle: Your First Express Server Step by Step
lessons.description: Install Express, create a server with routes, learn what req and res contain, send text and JSON, and restart automatically while you edit with node --watch.

content.text: Express is the most used web framework for Node.js. It is small, it has been around for many years and a huge amount of documentation and examples exist for it. Express does not change how Node works. It adds a clean way to describe which code answers which request. In this lesson you will build the same kind of server as in lesson 10, but with far less code.
Install and start

Inside your `taskapi` folder, you already ran `npm install express` in lesson 6. If not, run it now. Create a file `server.js` with this code. This course uses Express 5, which is the current major version. Most of what you learn also applies to Express 4, and we point out the differences where they matter.
Start it with `node server.js`, or better, with `npm run dev` after you have added the scripts from lesson 6. Then test it.

curl http://localhost:3000/
curl http://localhost:3000/api/health

Hello from Express
{"ok":true,"time":"2026-10-28T04:00:00.000Z"}
The time you see will be your current time. Now look at the code in four parts.

items: `express()` creates the **app**, an object that holds your routes and settings.
`app.get(path, handler)` says: when a GET request arrives for this path, run this function. There are matching methods `app.post`, `app.patch`, `app.put` and `app.delete`.
The handler receives `req` (the request) and `res` (the response).
`app.listen(port, callback)` starts the server. The callback runs once it is ready.

content.text: The request object, req
The request object describes what the client sent. You will use these parts all the time.

items: `req.method` and `req.originalUrl`: the method and the full URL path with the query string.
`req.params`: values taken from the path, such as the `7` in `/api/tasks/7`. Lesson 12 covers this.
`req.query`: values after the question mark, such as `?done=true`.
`req.body`: the data sent in the body of a POST or PATCH. It needs a body parser, which lesson 13 covers.
`req.get('Authorization')`: reads one request header.
`req.ip`: the address of the client.

content.text: The response object, res
You must send exactly one response for each request. If you never send one, the client waits until it times out. If you send two, Node throws an error. These are the methods you will use.

items: `res.send('text')` sends text, HTML or a buffer, and sets the content type for you.
`res.json(object)` converts a JavaScript object into JSON and sets `Content-Type: application/json`. This is the main method for APIs.
`res.status(404)` sets the status code and returns `res`, so you can chain: `res.status(404).json({ error: 'Not found' })`.
`res.status(204).end()` sends an empty response, used after a delete.
`res.set('Header-Name', 'value')` sets a header.
`res.redirect('/other')` sends the client to another URL.

content.text: A very common beginner mistake: writing `res.json(...)` and then, in the next line, running more code that also calls `res.send`. After you respond, use `return`, as in `return res.status(404).json(...)`, so that the function stops.
Restart automatically while you work

Node reads your file once at start-up. If you change the code, the old version keeps running until you restart. Instead of stopping and starting by hand, run `node --watch server.js`. Node watches the files it loaded and restarts whenever one changes. That is what the `dev` script from lesson 6 does.
Ports and the PORT variable

We used the fixed port 3000. On a real server, you often cannot choose the port yourself, because a hosting service or a process manager gives it to you through an environment variable called `PORT`. Lesson 16 shows how to read it with a fallback, so the same code runs on your laptop and on a server.
Express 5 handles async errors

In Express 4, if an `async` handler threw an error or rejected a promise, the error was not caught and you had to wrap every handler by hand. Express 5 catches rejected promises from handlers and passes them to the error handler for you. That makes async handlers much simpler, and you will rely on it from lesson 14.
Common problems

items: **`Cannot GET /something`**: no route matches. Check the path and the method. A POST route does not answer a GET request.
**The browser shows old content**: your code did not restart. Use `--watch`.
**`EADDRINUSE`**: the port is already used by another copy of the server. Stop it.
**`Error [ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND]`**: you forgot `.js` in a file import, or the package is not installed.

content.text: Your task

items: Create `server.js` with the code above and start it with `node --watch server.js`.
Add a route `GET /api/hello/world` that returns `{ "message": "Hello, world" }`.
Change the text of the home page while the server runs and refresh. Check that the change appears.
Use `curl -i` on `/api/health` and find the `Content-Type` header.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The browser shows `Hello from Express` at `http://localhost:3000/`.
`/api/health` returns JSON with `ok` set to `true`.
After saving a change, the terminal shows that the server restarted and the new text appears.

steps.say: A request arrives, for example GET /api/health.
Express looks for a route that matches the method and the path.
It calls your handler function and gives it the request and response objects.
Your handler sends one response, for example with res.json.

faqs.q: What is the difference between res.send and res.json?
faqs.a: res.send sends text, HTML or a buffer. res.json converts an object to JSON and sets the JSON content type. Use res.json for APIs.

faqs.q: Why does my browser show the old version after I edit the code?
faqs.a: Node does not reload code by itself. Restart the server, or start it with node --watch so it restarts when files change.

quiz.q: What does app.get(path, handler) say?
options: When a GET request arrives for this path, run this function

quiz.q: What is req.query?
options: Values after the question mark in the URL, such as ?done=true

quiz.q: What does res.json(object) do?
options: Sends the object as JSON and sets the content type

notes: `app.get(path, handler)` runs the handler for a GET on that path. `app.listen(port)` starts the server.
`req.params` (from the path), `req.query` (after `?`), `req.body` (needs a body parser).
`res.json(object)` is the main way to answer an API call. `res.status(404).json({ error: '...' })` chains.
`res.status(204).end()` is an empty answer, used after a delete.
Send one response per request. A second `res.send` causes an error.
`node --watch` restarts on every save. Use `process.env.PORT` for the port.
`Cannot GET /x` = no route for that path and method.

lessons.title: Express Routing: URL Params, Query Strings and Routers
lessons.metaTitle: Express Routing, Params and Query Strings
lessons.description: Learn how Express routes work: method and path, URL parameters, query strings, status codes, route order and splitting routes into files with Router.

content.text: Routing means deciding which code answers which request. Each route is a combination of an HTTP method and a path. A good API uses the method to say what to do and the path to say which thing, for example `GET /api/tasks/7` means read task 7 and `DELETE /api/tasks/7` means remove it. In this lesson you will build read-only task routes with parameters and filters, and then learn how to organise routes in separate files.
Route parameters

A segment of the path that starts with a colon is a **parameter**. Express puts the matching part of the real URL into `req.params`. For the route `/api/tasks/:id` and the request `/api/tasks/2`, `req.params.id` is the **text** `'2'`. Parameters are always strings, so convert them with `Number()` when you need a number.
Query strings

The part of the URL after a question mark is the **query string**, such as `?done=true&sort=title`. Express parses it into `req.query`. Use the path for *which thing*, and the query string for *how to filter, sort or page the list*. Query values are also strings, and a key can come as an array if it is repeated, so check the value before using it. Try the next example.

curl "http://localhost:3000/api/tasks?done=false"
curl http://localhost:3000/api/tasks/2
curl -i http://localhost:3000/api/tasks/99

Notice the filter. We compare `done` with the text `'true'` and `'false'`, because the query string only holds text. Any other value, such as `?done=maybe`, simply returns the full list here. In a stricter API you could answer 400. Notice also that the one-task route answers `404` with a JSON message when the id is not found. A request to `/api/tasks/abc` also gets 404, because `Number('abc')` is `NaN`, which matches no id.
Put quotation marks around a URL that contains `?` or `&` when you use curl, as above. Otherwise your terminal may treat the `&` as a command separator.
Choose good status codes

items: `200` for a successful read or update.
`201` after creating something, ideally with a `Location` header that gives its address.
`204` for a successful delete with nothing to return.
`400` when the client's data is invalid, `404` when the thing does not exist.
Do not return `200` with a body that says `{ error: ... }`. Clients, tests and monitoring tools rely on the status code.

content.text: Route order matters

Express tries routes **in the order you wrote them** and uses the first one that sends a response. A general route placed before a specific one can swallow requests. For example, if `/api/tasks/:id` comes before `/api/tasks/stats`, then a request to `/api/tasks/stats` is matched with `id` equal to `stats`. Put the specific routes first and the ones with parameters after them.
Express 5 path syntax

Express 5 uses a stricter path syntax than Express 4. A plain `*` wildcard is no longer allowed, and `app.get('/old/*', ...)` throws an error on start-up. A wildcard must have a name, as in `/files/*splat`, and the matched parts are then found in `req.params.splat`. An optional part is written with braces, as in `/users{/:id}`, which matches both `/users` and `/users/7`. If you copy older Express 4 examples from the internet and get a `Missing parameter name` error, this is the reason.
Split routes into files with Router

When an app grows past a few routes, one file becomes hard to read. Express has `Router`, a small mini-app that holds a group of routes. You write the routes with paths that are relative to the place where you mount the router.

In the router file, the route `'/'` means the root of wherever the router is mounted. `app.use('/api/tasks', ...)` mounts it under that prefix. Wrapping the router in a function, as we did here, lets you pass dependencies in, such as a data store, and it makes the code easy to test. The final project in this course uses exactly this layout, with one router for tasks and one for login.
Keep URLs predictable

items: Use nouns in the plural for things: `/api/tasks`, `/api/users`.
Do not put verbs in paths: prefer `POST /api/tasks` over `/api/createTask`.
Use lowercase letters and hyphens.
Keep a prefix such as `/api` or `/api/v1`, so you can add a front end on the same domain, and you can change the API later without breaking old clients.

content.text: Your task

items: Create `server.js` with the routes above and test the three curl commands.
Add `?sort=title` support: when it is present, return the tasks sorted by title.
Add a route `GET /api/tasks/stats` that returns how many tasks are done and how many are not. Put it **before** the `:id` route and test it. Then move it after and see what happens.
Move the task routes into `routes/tasks.js` using `Router`.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: `/api/tasks?done=true` returns only tasks that are done.
`/api/tasks/99` returns status 404 with a JSON message.
`/api/tasks/stats` returns your counts, not a 404.

animation.title: Matching a URL to a route

steps.say: The request URL has a path and an optional query string.
Express compares the method and path with your routes in order and picks the first match.
The values in the path go to req.params and the values after the question mark go to req.query.
Your code uses them to build the response, with the right status code.

faqs.q: Why is req.params.id a string?
faqs.a: URLs are text, so every parameter and query value arrives as a string. Convert it with Number() when you need a number, and check that the result is valid.

faqs.q: Why does the order of routes matter?
faqs.a: Express uses the first matching route. A general route written before a specific one can capture requests meant for the specific one.

quiz.q: In the route /api/tasks/:id, what is req.params.id for /api/tasks/2?
Which status code should follow a successful create?
Why does route order matter?
options: Express uses the first route that sends a response
