notes: Route parameter: `/api/tasks/:id` gives `req.params.id` as text.
Query string: `/api/tasks?done=true` gives `req.query.done`. Quote the URL in curl.
Status codes: 200 read or update, 201 created, 204 deleted, 400 bad data, 404 missing.
Route order matters: put `/api/tasks/stats` before `/api/tasks/:id`.
Use `express.Router()` to split routes into files and mount them with `app.use('/api/tasks', router)`.
Keep URLs predictable: plural nouns, no verbs.

lessons.title: Express Middleware Explained: next(), Logging and express.json()
lessons.metaTitle: Express Middleware: next() and Logging
lessons.description: Understand Express middleware: functions that run in order on every request. Write a logger, parse JSON bodies and apply middleware to chosen routes.

content.text: Middleware is the idea that makes Express flexible. A middleware is a function that runs **between** the arrival of a request and your route handler. It can look at the request, change it, stop it with a response, or pass it on to the next function by calling `next()`. Logging, reading JSON bodies, checking logins, handling cross-origin requests and limiting traffic are all middleware. If you understand this lesson, the rest of Express becomes easy.
The shape of a middleware

A middleware takes three arguments: `req`, `res` and `next`. It must do one of two things. Either it sends a response, which ends the chain, or it calls `next()`, which passes control on. If it does neither, the request hangs until the client gives up. You register middleware with `app.use`. Here is a small logger and a JSON body parser.

The first middleware records the start time, asks Node to run a function when the response is finished, and then calls `next()`. When the response finishes, it prints the method, the URL, the status code and the time taken. The second one, `express.json()`, is built into Express. It reads the request body, and if the content type is JSON, it parses it and puts the result in `req.body`. Then the route can use `req.body`. Try it.
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/echo -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"title":"Hi"}'
{"youSent":{"title":"Hi"}}

The server terminal prints one line for each request, such as `POST /api/echo 200 9ms`. The number of milliseconds will differ on your computer. If you use Windows PowerShell, quoting rules for curl are different. A simple way is to test with a tool such as the REST Client extension for VS Code, or to use `curl.exe` with the data in a file. The code works the same.
Order is everything

Middleware and routes run in the order you write them. The logger must be registered **before** the routes you want it to log. `express.json()` must come before any route that reads `req.body`. If you put a route first, its response ends the chain and the middleware below never runs. When something does not work, a good first check is the order of the `app.use` lines.
What express.json() does when things go wrong

items: If the request has no JSON content type, `req.body` is `undefined` in Express 5, not an empty object. A line such as `req.body.title` then throws an error. Always check the body before you use it, which is what the validation helper in lesson 15 does.

If the body is not valid JSON, the parser rejects the request with a 400 error. Without your own error handler, Express answers with an HTML page that contains a stack trace. Lesson 15 replaces that with a clean JSON message.
By default, the parser accepts bodies up to 100 kilobytes. You can set a smaller limit with `express.json({ limit: '10kb' })`, which is a good protection for an API that only receives small objects.

content.text: Middleware for some routes only

You do not have to apply middleware to everything. You can give a path to `app.use('/api', mw)`, or put middleware as an argument before a handler. We will do this in lesson 18 to protect the task routes and leave the login route open.
Middleware that other people wrote

Many packages are middleware. You install them with npm and add them with `app.use`. Some you will use in this course: `cors` (lesson 19), `helmet` (security headers, lesson 19) and `express-rate-limit` (limit repeated requests, lesson 19). Express itself includes `express.json()`, `express.urlencoded()` for HTML form data, and `express.static('public')`, which serves files from a folder, such as a built React app or images.
Passing data along with the request

A middleware can attach information to `req` so that later functions can use it. For example, an authentication middleware can set `req.user`, and then every route that comes after can read `req.user.id`. That is exactly how the login check in lesson 18 will work. Choose clear names, and do not overwrite built-in properties of `req`.
A word about error middleware

There is a special kind of middleware with **four** parameters: `(err, req, res, next)`. Express recognises it by the count and uses it for errors. It must be registered **after** the routes. You will build one in lesson 15.
If you ever see `next is not a function` or a request that never finishes, check that each middleware either responds or calls `next()` exactly once, and that you did not forget the third parameter.
Your task

items: Add the logger and `express.json()` to your server and the `/api/echo` route. Send a JSON body with curl and check the log line.
Move the logger below the echo route and see why it stops logging that route.
Send an invalid JSON body such as `{bad` and see the HTML error. Keep this in mind for lesson 15.
Write a middleware called `addRequestId` that sets `req.id` to a random value from `crypto.randomUUID()` and add it to the log line.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Each request prints one log line with method, URL, status and time.
`/api/echo` returns the JSON you sent.
Moving the logger after the route proves to you that order matters.

steps.say: A request comes in. Express runs your middleware in the order you wrote it.
The logger notes the start time and calls next() to pass the request on.
express.json() reads the body, parses the JSON and stores it in req.body.
Finally the route handler runs and sends the response. If a middleware had responded earlier, the chain would have stopped there.

faqs.q: What happens if middleware never calls next()?
faqs.a: If it also sends no response, the request hangs until the client times out. A middleware must either respond or call next().

faqs.q: Why is req.body undefined in my route?
faqs.a: The body parser did not run or did not match. Check that express.json() is registered before the route, and that the client sends the Content-Type: application/json header.

quiz.q: A middleware must either send a response or…
quiz.explain: Otherwise the request hangs until the client gives up.

quiz.q: Where must express.json() be placed?
options: Before any route that reads req.body

quiz.q: In Express 5, what is req.body if the request had no JSON content type?

notes: Middleware is a function `(req, res, next)`. It either answers, or calls `next()`.
Order is everything: middleware runs in the order you write `app.use`.
`express.json()` reads a JSON body into `req.body`. Bad JSON gives a 400 error.
Use middleware for some routes only: `app.get('/x', check, handler)`.
Pass data along with `req.user = ...` or `res.locals`.
Request hangs? A middleware forgot to answer or to call `next()`.

lessons.title: Build a REST API: Create, Read, Update and Delete Tasks
lessons.metaTitle: Build a REST API with Express: CRUD Routes
lessons.description: Build a complete Express task API with routes to create, read, update and delete tasks, correct status codes and curl tests. Data is kept in memory first.

content.text: Now you will put the pieces together. A **REST API** is a set of URLs where each URL stands for a thing, and the HTTP method says what to do with it. For the task list, the pattern is always the same: list, read one, create, update and delete. Programmers call these four jobs **CRUD**: create, read, update, delete. Almost every app you will ever build is CRUD with extra rules added on top.
The five routes

items: `GET /api/tasks`: list all tasks. Answer `200`.
`GET /api/tasks/:id`: one task. Answer `200`, or `404`.
`POST /api/tasks`: create a task from the JSON body. Answer `201` with the new task.
`PATCH /api/tasks/:id`: change some fields of a task. Answer `200` with the updated task, or `404`.
`DELETE /api/tasks/:id`: remove it. Answer `204`, or `404`.

content.text: We start with the data in a plain JavaScript array in memory. That keeps the code simple. The data disappears when the server stops, and we fix that in lesson 16. Create `server.js` like this.

Read each handler and notice the pattern. For the routes with an id, we find the task in the array, and if it does not exist, we `return` a 404 straight away. Then we do the work. `nextId++` gives each new task a new number, and the `++` adds one **after** the value is used. The delete route filters the task out and checks that the array became shorter, which tells us the task really existed.
Test every route with curl

curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/tasks -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"title":"Ship it"}'
curl -X PATCH http://localhost:3000/api/tasks/3 -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"done":true}'
curl -i -X DELETE http://localhost:3000/api/tasks/3
curl http://localhost:3000/api/tasks

Each call matches what you expect: the new task has id 3, the update marks it done, the delete answers with status 204 and no body, and the last list is back to the two original tasks. Doing this by hand is slow but valuable. It shows you exactly what a front end will send.
What is still wrong?
This API works for polite clients, but it trusts everything. Try sending an empty object to the create route.
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/tasks -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{}'
{"id":4,"done":false}

The server created a task with no title. Worse, a client could send `{ "title": 12345 }`, a huge text, or the wrong type for `done`, and `PATCH` would store it. Never trust data from outside your program. In the next lesson you will add validation and proper error handling. Other limits of this version: anyone can see and change every task, because there is no login yet, and everything is lost on restart.
PUT or PATCH?

Both change an existing thing. **PUT** means replace the whole thing with the data sent, so the client must send every field. **PATCH** means change only the fields that were sent. For task apps, where you might only tick a box, PATCH is the more practical one. Many APIs support both. We use PATCH.
Why return the new object?

After a create or an update, we send back the full task as the server now stores it. The client then has the id and any fields that the server added, so it does not need a second request. It is a small habit that makes front-end code much simpler.
Using the API from a front end

A React app can now call this API with `fetch`. For example, `fetch('http://localhost:3000/api/tasks')` returns the list. A browser blocks requests from one origin to another unless the server allows it. That rule is called CORS and we will configure it in lesson 19, together with the other security settings.
Your task

items: Create `server.js` with the CRUD routes and test all five routes with curl.
Send a PATCH to a task that does not exist. Check the status code is 404.
Add `GET /api/tasks?done=false` support to the list route (you did it in lesson 12).
Write down three kinds of bad data a client could send that this code would accept.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Create, update, delete and list all return the results shown above.
The delete route returns 204 with no body, and a second delete of the same id returns 404.
You listed at least three bad inputs the server does not reject yet.

steps.say: A client uses four kinds of requests to work with tasks: create, read, change and delete.
Each request goes to the same API address, and the method tells the API what to do.
The API reads or changes the list of tasks. For now the list lives in memory.
The API answers with a status code, such as 200, 201, 204 or 404, and usually the task as JSON.

faqs.q: What does CRUD mean?
faqs.a: Create, read, update and delete: the four basic jobs most apps do with data. In HTTP they are POST, GET, PATCH or PUT, and DELETE.

faqs.q: Why return 201 instead of 200 after creating something?
faqs.a: 201 Created tells the client that a new resource was made. It is more precise than 200, and many tools and clients expect it.

quiz.q: Which method and path create a new task?
What status does the lesson use after a successful delete with nothing to return?
Why is data kept in a plain array at first?
options: To keep the code simple; the data disappears when the server stops

notes: Five routes: `GET /api/tasks`, `GET /:id`, `POST` (201), `PATCH /:id`, `DELETE /:id` (204).
Test every route with curl, including the failing cases.
PUT replaces the whole thing. PATCH changes some fields.
Return the new or updated object so the front end does not need a second call.
Early version problems: no validation, data lost on restart, ids not safe.

lessons.title: Validation and Error Handling in Express
lessons.metaTitle: Validate Input and Handle Errors in Express
lessons.description: Never trust client data: validate request bodies, return clear 400 and 404 errors, and write one central Express error handler with no leaked stack traces.

content.text: A server receives data from strangers, so everything in `req.body`, `req.params` and `req.query` must be treated as untrusted until you have checked it. Validation is your first line of defence against broken data and many attacks. Error handling is the second: it makes sure that when something fails, the client receives a clear, safe message and not a crash or a page of internal details. In this lesson you will add both to the task API.
Write a validation function

You can use a library such as Zod or Joi, and many teams do. For a small API a short function is enough, and it shows exactly what validation means. This function checks a task. It returns either a clean value or an error message. The `partial` option is for PATCH, where fields are optional.

items: It checks the **type** of every field. A title must be a text, not a number or an array.
It **trims** spaces and sets a **maximum length**.
It builds a **new object** with only the allowed fields. Extra fields sent by the client, such as `id` or `ownerId`, are ignored. This stops a client from changing fields they should not control.
It returns the first problem as a plain message that the client can show to a user.

content.text: Use it in the routes

In the create and update routes, call it first, and answer 400 if there is an error. `400 Bad Request` means the client sent something wrong. Compare this with 500, which means the server itself failed. Never use 500 for bad input.
404 for unknown routes

When no route matches a request, Express sends a plain HTML message by default. For an API you want JSON. Add a middleware **after** all routes. Because it comes last, it only runs when nothing else answered.
One central error handler

The error handler is a middleware with four parameters, registered **last**. Express sends to it any error that is thrown in a handler, passed to `next(err)`, or caused by a rejected promise in an async handler (this works automatically in Express 5). It is the one place where you decide how errors look to the client.

items: Errors you can predict, such as invalid JSON or a body that is too big, get a clear 400 or 413 message. Those errors come from `express.json()` and have an `err.type`.
Everything else is a surprise. Log the full error on the **server** with `console.error`, and send the client only a general `Something went wrong` with status 500.
Never send `err.stack` or `err.message` of unexpected errors to the client. They can reveal file paths, library versions and database details that help an attacker.

content.text: The sample above includes a route `GET /api/crash` that throws on purpose. Test the handler.

curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/tasks -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{}'
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/tasks -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{bad'
curl http://localhost:3000/api/crash
curl http://localhost:3000/nothing

Each failure now returns clean JSON with the right status code. In the server terminal you will see the full stack trace for the crash, which is what you want for debugging. The client never sees it. Remove the `/api/crash` route after testing, because it is only for practice.
Express 4 note

If you ever work on an Express 4 project, async handlers need extra care. Wrap them, or call `next(err)` inside `catch`, because errors in promises are not caught by Express 4. That is the main reason many older tutorials contain wrappers such as `asyncHandler`. In Express 5 you do not need them.
Use consistent error responses

items: Always the same shape, for example `{ "error": "message" }`, so the front end can handle all errors in one place.

Use codes that people can act on: 400 invalid data, 401 not logged in, 403 not allowed, 404 not found, 409 conflict (for example, an email already used), 413 too large, 429 too many requests, 500 server error.
Write messages for the person who will read them. They should say what to fix. They should not reveal how the server works.

content.text: Validation on the front end is for convenience. Validation on the server is for security. A client can always bypass your front end, so the server must check everything again.
Your task

items: Add `validate.js` and call `checkTask` in the create route. Test an empty body, a number as title and a 200-character title.
Add the 404 middleware and the error handler at the end of the file. Test the four curl commands above.
Change the validation to also accept an optional `priority` that must be `low`, `medium` or `high`.
Make `GET /api/tasks/:id` return 400 when the id is not a whole number, and 404 when it is a number that does not exist.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: An empty or wrong-typed title returns 400 with a clear message.
Invalid JSON returns 400 JSON, not an HTML page.
The crash route returns `Something went wrong`, and the stack trace is only in the server terminal.

steps.say: Everything that arrives from a client is untrusted until you check it.
The validation step checks types, length and allowed fields. Bad data is turned away with a 400 message.
Good data goes on to the real work, such as saving the task.
If anything fails, the central error handler logs the details and sends a safe, short message to the client.

faqs.q: Should I use a validation library?
faqs.a: For bigger projects, yes: libraries like Zod or Joi save time and handle many cases. For a small API, a short function is enough and shows what validation does.

faqs.q: Why not send the error message to the client?
faqs.a: Unexpected error messages and stack traces can reveal file paths, library versions or database details that help attackers. Log them on the server and send a general message.

quiz.q: Which status code should an API send for invalid input?
Why build a new object with only the allowed fields?
options: Extra fields like id or ownerId sent by the client are dropped

quiz.q: Where is the central error handler registered?

notes: Never trust the request. Check every field on the server.
Write a validation function and return `400` with a clear message when the data is wrong.
Add a `404` handler after all routes for unknown URLs.
One central error handler `(err, req, res, next)` gives every error the same JSON shape.
Front-end validation is for convenience. Server validation is for security.
Do not leak details such as stack traces to the client.

lessons.title: Environment Variables and Saving Your Data to a File
lessons.metaTitle: Env Variables and a File Store in Node.js
lessons.description: Keep settings and secrets out of your code with environment variables and a .env file, and save API data to a JSON file so it survives a restart.

content.text: Two problems remain in the task API. The settings, such as the port number, are written inside the code, and the data vanishes every time the server restarts. In this lesson you will fix both. First you will learn about **environment variables**, the standard way to give a program its settings and secrets. Then you will move the data into a small store that saves tasks to a JSON file.
Why settings do not belong in code

Your program runs in different places: your laptop, a test machine and a live server. Each place needs different values: the port, the address of the database, the secret used for logins. If these values sit inside your code, you must edit the code for each place, and passwords end up in git, where many people can see them and where they stay in the history forever. The fix is to keep settings **outside** the code, in the environment, and have the code read them.
process.env

Every running program has a set of **environment variables**: named values given to it by the system that starts it. In Node.js they are in the object `process.env`. All values are strings, or `undefined` when missing. Read the port like this.
const port = Number(process.env.PORT) || 3000;

The `Number(...)` converts text to a number. If `PORT` is not set, `Number(undefined)` is `NaN`, which counts as false, so `|| 3000` supplies the default. Hosting services and process managers often set `PORT` for you, which is why the code should always read it.
A .env file

Typing variables in the terminal for every run is tedious. The usual solution is a text file named `.env` in the project folder, with one `NAME=value` per line. Recent versions of Node.js can load it directly with the flag `--env-file=.env`, which is what the `start` and `dev` scripts from lesson 6 use. You do not need an extra package.

# .env  (never commit this file)
PORT=3100
JWT_SECRET=change-me-to-a-long-random-string
DATA_FILE=./data/tasks.json

items: Add `.env` to `.gitignore` **now**, before your first commit.
Commit a copy named `.env.example` with the variable names and harmless sample values, so other people know what to set.
No spaces around `=`, and no quotes needed for simple values.
On a live server, do not upload a `.env` file at all if your host has a place to set environment variables. Use that instead.

content.text: If you ever commit a real secret by mistake, deleting it in the next commit is not enough, because it stays in the history. Change the secret straight away, as if it had been stolen.
Fail early when something is missing

If a required setting is missing, the program should stop at start-up with a clear message, and not fail in a confusing way later. You will see this in the final `server.js` in lesson 20, where a missing or short `JWT_SECRET` stops the server.
A store that saves to a file

Now the data. We move all work with tasks into a separate module, a **store**. The routes will call the store and will not care how data is kept. Today the store uses a file. In the next lesson, you can replace it with a database without changing the routes much. That is why separating the two is a good habit.

Take your time with this file. `createStore(file)` returns an object with five functions. The `ready` promise loads the file once at start-up. If the file does not exist, which is normal the first time, `ENOENT` is ignored and the list starts empty. Any other error is thrown, so a damaged file is not silently replaced. Each function starts with `await ready`, so requests that arrive during start-up wait for the data to load. After each change, `save()` writes the whole list to the file. The next id is the highest id so far plus one, so ids stay unique after a restart.

Now use the store in the server. The routes become short, because the store does the work and `checkTask` from lesson 15 does the validation. Put `validate.js` (from lesson 15) and `store.js` (this lesson's store) in the project folder next to `server.js`.
Start the server with `npm run dev`, create a task, then stop the server and start it again. The task is still there, and `data/tasks.json` contains it.

curl -X POST http://localhost:3100/api/tasks -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"title":"Saved"}'
curl http://localhost:3100/api/tasks

{"id":1,"title":"Saved","done":false,"createdAt":"2026-10-28T04:10:56.259Z"}
[{"id":1,"title":"Saved","done":false,"createdAt":"2026-10-28T04:10:56.259Z"}]
The dates in your output will show the time of your own request. Create the `data` folder first if it does not exist, because `writeFile` creates files but not folders.
Honest limits of a file store

items: It rewrites the whole file on every change, so it slows down as data grows.
If two changes arrive at the same moment, the second write can overwrite the first. Writes of tiny files are quick, so this is rare in a practice project, but it is a real risk on a busy server.
It lives on one machine. If you run several copies of the server, each has its own data.
There are no searches, indexes or relationships.
On many hosting services, the file system is wiped on every deploy. A file store is for learning and tiny tools. Anything that matters belongs in a database, which is the next lesson.

content.text: Your task

items: Create `.env` and `.env.example`, and add `.env` to `.gitignore`.
Use `process.env.PORT` in the server and start it on a different port by changing `.env`.
Add `store.js` and move the routes to use it. Create a task, restart the server and check that it survived.
Delete `data/tasks.json` and start the server. Check it starts with an empty list and does not crash.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: `npm run dev` starts on the port from `.env`.
A task created before a restart is still listed after it.
`git status` does not list `.env`.

animation.title: Settings and data outside the code

steps.say: Settings and secrets live in a .env file that is not committed to git.
Node loads the file and your code reads the values from process.env.
The server uses the settings and calls the store to work with tasks.
The store saves the tasks to a file after every change, so they survive a restart.

faqs.q: Why not put secrets directly in the code?
faqs.a: Code is shared and stored in git, so a secret in it can leak and stays in the history. Environment variables keep secrets outside the code and let each machine use its own values.

faqs.q: Do I need the dotenv package?
faqs.a: Not with current Node.js versions. The --env-file flag loads a .env file for you. The dotenv package is still common in older projects.

quiz.q: Why do settings and secrets not belong in the code?
options: They are faster in the environment
Each place needs different values and secrets must not be committed

quiz.q: What type are all values in process.env?
What should you commit instead of your real .env?
options: A .env.example with names and harmless sample values

notes: Settings and secrets do not belong in code. Read them from `process.env`.
Put them in a `.env` file and list `.env` in `.gitignore`.
Commit a `.env.example` with names but no real values.
Fail early at startup if a required variable is missing.
A leaked secret stays in git history. Change the secret, do not only delete the line.
A file store is fine to learn. For real apps use a database.

lessons.title: MongoDB and Mongoose: Store Your API Data in a Real Database
lessons.metaTitle: MongoDB and Mongoose with Express
lessons.description: Connect your Express API to MongoDB with Mongoose: schemas, models, CRUD queries, validation and bad ids. Use a local install or an Atlas cluster.

content.text: A file is fine for learning, but real applications keep data in a database. MongoDB is a popular choice for Node.js projects, and it is the M in the MERN stack. It stores data as **documents**, which look like JavaScript objects, grouped in **collections**, which are like tables. **Mongoose** is a library that sits between your code and MongoDB and adds structure: schemas, validation and handy query functions. In this lesson you will replace the file store with MongoDB.

Set-up note: the code in this lesson follows the Mongoose documentation. You need a running MongoDB to try it. Install the free Community Server on your computer, or create a free cluster on MongoDB Atlas, the company's hosted service. Both are explained on mongodb.com. The free hosted tier has limits and its terms can change, so check the current page. Never use production data while you practise.
Install and connect

Install the library in your project, and add the connection string to `.env`. For a local server it looks like `mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/taskapi`. Atlas gives you a longer address that includes a user name and a password, and so it is a secret: it belongs in `.env` and never in git.
npm install mongoose

# .env
MONGODB_URI=mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/taskapi

`mongoose.connect` returns a promise. `await` it before you start the server, so no request arrives before the database is ready. The option `serverSelectionTimeoutMS` makes the program fail after five seconds if it cannot reach the database, and not wait for a long time. In `server.js`, put the connect step before `app.listen`.
Schemas and models

A **schema** describes the shape of a document: its fields, their types and rules. A **model** is built from a schema and gives you the functions to read and write that collection. Mongoose creates the collection from the model name, in lowercase and plural, so `Task` becomes `tasks`.

items: `required` with a message: saving without a title fails with that message.
`trim` removes spaces at both ends. `maxlength` limits the length.
`default: false` fills in `done` when it is not given.
`timestamps: true` adds `createdAt` and `updatedAt` and keeps them up to date.
Mongoose adds an `_id` field to every document. It is an `ObjectId`, a 24-character identifier, and not a small number like our earlier ids.

content.text: You can check a document without a database by calling `await new Task({ title: '   ' }).validate()`. It rejects with an error whose `errors.title.message` is `title is required`, because trimming leaves an empty text. A document with the title ` Read docs ` passes, and its title becomes `Read docs`. Schema rules are a second layer of protection after your own `checkTask` function.
The routes with Mongoose
The routes now call the model. Compare them with the store version. Every function is async, which Express 5 handles for us.

Look at the functions used. `Task.find(filter)` returns the matching documents, `.sort({ createdAt: -1 })` puts the newest first and `.limit(100)` caps the list, so one request can never pull in a million documents. `findById` finds one. `Task.create(value)` validates and inserts. `findByIdAndUpdate` changes a document, and the option `returnDocument: 'after'` returns the new version, while `runValidators: true` applies the schema rules to updates, which Mongoose does not do by default. `findByIdAndDelete` removes it.

The small `validId` middleware matters. If a client calls `/api/tasks/abc`, Mongoose cannot turn `abc` into an `ObjectId`, and it throws a `CastError`. We check with `mongoose.isValidObjectId` first and answer 404, which is what the client should see.
Handling database errors

items: A **duplicate key** error (code `11000`) happens when a unique field repeats, for example two users with the same email. Catch it and answer 409.
A **validation** error from Mongoose has the name `ValidationError`. Answer 400.
A connection problem is a server problem. Let it reach the error handler, which answers 500 and logs the details.

content.text: Safety rules for databases

items: Never build a query from raw request data. For example, `Task.find(req.body)` lets a client send operators such as `{ "$gt": "" }` and change the meaning of the query. This kind of attack is called NoSQL injection. Pick the fields you accept yourself, as `checkTask` does, and check that they are the types you expect.
Do not let clients choose which fields to update. `checkTask` copies only `title` and `done`.
Use a database user with only the rights the app needs, never an admin account.
Limit the size of lists with `.limit()` and paging.
Keep backups, and test restoring one.

content.text: When you are ready, ask which indexes your queries need. An index lets MongoDB find documents without reading the whole collection. A field you search or sort by often, such as `owner` or `createdAt`, is a candidate. Add `index: true` to the field, and measure before you add many, since indexes cost space and slow down writes.
Your task

items: Set up MongoDB locally or on Atlas. Put the connection string in `.env`.
Install Mongoose, add `models.js` and connect before `app.listen`.
Replace the store with the Mongoose routes. Create, read, update and delete a task with curl, and look at the document in a viewer such as MongoDB Compass.
Try `/api/tasks/abc` and a valid-looking id that does not exist. Both should give 404.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: A task you created is still there after you restart the server.
Updating `done` returns the document with the new value.
`/api/tasks/abc` returns 404 JSON and not a 500 error.

steps.say: An Express route receives a request and checks the input.
It calls the Mongoose model, for example Task.create or Task.find.
Mongoose applies the schema rules and sends the query to MongoDB, which stores or returns documents.
The result comes back and the route sends it to the client as JSON.

faqs.q: What is the difference between MongoDB and Mongoose?
faqs.a: MongoDB is the database. Mongoose is a Node.js library that adds schemas, validation and convenient query functions on top of it.

faqs.q: Why is my _id not a number?
faqs.a: MongoDB creates a 24-character ObjectId for every document. Treat it as text, and check ids with mongoose.isValidObjectId before querying.

quiz.q: In MongoDB, data is stored as…
What does a Mongoose schema describe?
options: The shape of a document: fields, types and rules

quiz.q: Why await mongoose.connect before starting the server?
options: So no request arrives before the database is ready

notes: MongoDB stores documents. Mongoose adds schemas and models.
Connect once at startup with `mongoose.connect(process.env.MONGODB_URI)`.
A schema sets the rules: `required`, `trim`, `maxlength`, `default`, `timestamps: true`.
Routes use `find`, `findById`, `create`, `findByIdAndUpdate`, `findByIdAndDelete`.
A bad id like `/api/tasks/abc` should give a 404 or 400, not a 500.
Never put the database address in code. Do not open the database to the whole internet.

lessons.title: User Login: Password Hashing and JSON Web Tokens
lessons.metaTitle: Login in Node.js: Password Hashing and JWT
lessons.description: Add registration and login to your API: hash passwords with bcrypt, issue and verify JSON Web Tokens, and keep each person’s tasks private.

content.text: So far anyone can read and change every task. A real app needs accounts, and it needs to know who is making each request. In this lesson you will add registration, login and a check that protects the task routes, so each user sees only their own tasks. Authentication is easy to get subtly wrong, so we will go slowly and explain the reason for each choice.
Rule one: never store a password

A database can be stolen, and staff can read it. If it holds real passwords, every account is at risk, and because people reuse passwords, accounts on other sites too. Instead, store a **hash**: the result of a one-way mathematical function. You cannot turn a hash back into the password, but you can hash what the user types at login and compare the two. Use a slow function made for passwords, such as **bcrypt**, which also adds a random **salt** so that two users with the same password have different hashes. Never use plain SHA or MD5 for passwords, and never invent your own method.
npm install bcryptjs jsonwebtoken

We use `bcryptjs`, a pure JavaScript version that installs without a compiler on any system. The `bcrypt` package is faster, but it has native parts. The functions are the same: `bcrypt.hash(password, 10)` and `bcrypt.compare(password, hash)`. The number 10 is the cost: higher is slower and harder to break.
Rule two: prove who you are with a token

HTTP has no memory. Each request stands alone, so after login, the client needs a way to prove its identity on every later request. One common way is a **JSON Web Token (JWT)**. At login, the server creates a signed text that contains the user's id and an expiry time. The client sends it back in the `Authorization` header with every request: `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. The server checks the signature with its secret. If the signature is valid and the token has not expired, the server trusts the contents. Nobody can change the contents without the secret, because the signature would no longer match.

items: A JWT is signed, **not encrypted**. Anyone who holds it can read what is inside. Never put passwords or private data in it.
The secret must be long and random, and stored only in the environment. Whoever has it can create tokens for any user.
Give tokens a short life, as we do with `expiresIn: '1h'`. A stolen token then stops working soon.
Always use HTTPS in production, so tokens and passwords cannot be read on the way.

content.text: The login routes
The router handles registration and login. Read it carefully, especially the comments in the text below the code.

items: The check of the email and password length happens **before** any work is done. The minimum of 8 characters is a modest rule. Longer is better, and it is wise to allow long passphrases.
The email is lowercased, so `Asha@Example.com` and `asha@example.com` are the same account.
A duplicate email returns `409 Conflict`.
At login, a wrong email and a wrong password give **the same** message. A different message would tell an attacker which emails have accounts.
`await bcrypt.compare` is slow on purpose, so guessing is slow.

content.text: In this course the users are kept in a `Map` in memory, so they disappear when the server restarts. That is only to keep the lesson short. In a real application, store users in your database, with a unique index on the email, as lesson 17 showed. The hashing and tokens work in exactly the same way.
The check that protects routes
This middleware reads the header, verifies the token and sets `req.user`. Any route placed after it can trust `req.user`. If the token is missing or wrong, it answers 401 and the route never runs.
Each user sees only their own tasks

Logging in is not enough. The routes must also use `req.user.id` so that one user cannot read or change another user's tasks. In the store, every function now takes the owner's id, and finds a task only if both the id and the owner match. Other users' tasks then look like they do not exist, so the answer is 404 and not 403. Here is the complete store. Compare it with lesson 16: every function now takes `ownerId` first.
And the task router. The first argument of each store call is `req.user.id`, which the middleware set. Create a task, and the owner is stored with it.
The app mounts everything: the auth routes are open, and the task routes sit behind `requireAuth`.

app.use('/api/auth', authRouter({ secret, users }));
app.use('/api/tasks', requireAuth(secret), tasksRouter(store));
Try the whole flow

# 1. register and keep the token
curl -X POST http://localhost:3100/api/auth/register -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"email":"asha@example.com","password":"correct-horse"}'

# 2. no token: refused
curl -X POST http://localhost:3100/api/tasks -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"title":"x"}'

# 3. with the token: works
curl -X POST http://localhost:3100/api/tasks -H "Authorization: Bearer PASTE_TOKEN_HERE" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"title":"Learn Express"}'

The token in your output will be a different long text. We also tested the other cases: registering the same email twice returns 409 with `That email is already registered`, a wrong password returns 401 with `Wrong email or password`, and a bad token returns 401. Notice that the task response includes `ownerId`. For this exercise that is harmless, but in a real API you would decide which fields to send, and leave out internal ones.
What this does not cover

items: **Logout and revoking tokens.** A pure JWT cannot be cancelled before it expires. Short lifetimes help. Bigger apps add refresh tokens or a server-side list.

**Where the client keeps the token.** Browser storage is easy but readable by any script on the page. A cookie with the `HttpOnly` flag is safer against script theft but needs protection against cross-site requests. Each choice has trade-offs. Read about both before you build a real front end.
**Password reset, email checks, two-step login.** Use a tested service or library for these, and do not write them from scratch for real users.
**Roles.** Add a `role` to the token for things like admin pages and check it in a middleware.

content.text: Your task

items: Install `bcryptjs` and `jsonwebtoken` and add the auth router and the `requireAuth` middleware.
Register two users. Create a task as the first user and check that the second user cannot see it, and gets 404 when asking for its id.
Decode the middle part of a token with `Buffer.from(part, 'base64url').toString()` and look at what is inside. Confirm that there is no password in it.
Set `expiresIn` to `'5s'`, wait, and try again. You should get the message about an expired token.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Registering returns 201 and a token, and registering the same email returns 409.
A request without a token gets 401, and with a valid token it works.
The second user cannot read, change or delete the first user's tasks.

steps.say: The user sends an email and a password to the login route.
The server compares the password with the stored hash using bcrypt. The real password is never stored.
If it matches, the server signs a token that holds the user id and an expiry time.
On later requests, the client sends the token. The requireAuth middleware verifies it before any task route runs.

faqs.q: Why hash passwords instead of encrypting them?
faqs.a: Encryption can be reversed with a key. A hash cannot be reversed, so a stolen database does not give attackers the passwords. Use a slow password hash such as bcrypt.

faqs.q: Is a JWT secret or private?
faqs.a: The signature stops people changing it, but the contents are only encoded, not encrypted. Anyone with the token can read it, so never put private data in it.

quiz.q: What should you store instead of a password?
A JWT is…
options: Signed, but not encrypted, so never put secrets inside it

quiz.q: Where should the JWT secret be stored?
options: Only in the environment, long and random

notes: Never store a password. Store a hash made with `bcrypt`. `bcrypt.compare` is slow on purpose.
After login, the server gives a signed token (JWT). The client sends it on each request.
A middleware checks the token and sets `req.user` before protected routes.
Each user sees only their own tasks: filter by the user id.
Give the same error for a wrong email and a wrong password.
Not covered: logout, refresh tokens, password reset, roles. Use tested libraries for these.

lessons.title: Secure Your Express API: CORS, Helmet and Rate Limiting
lessons.metaTitle: Secure an Express API: CORS, Helmet, Limits
lessons.description: Harden your Express API: set CORS for your front end, add Helmet headers, limit repeated requests, cap body size and avoid common mistakes.

content.text: An API on the internet will be probed by strangers and by automated scripts within hours. You do not need to be a security expert to block the most common problems. A few well-known libraries and some careful habits remove a great deal of risk. This lesson adds them to the task API, and ends with a checklist to use before every launch. Security is never finished, and no list can promise that an app is safe. Treat this as a solid beginning.
CORS: allow your front end, and only it

Browsers have a rule: a web page may only call APIs on its **own origin** (the same protocol, domain and port) unless the API says otherwise. If your React app runs at `http://localhost:5173` and your API at `http://localhost:3100`, the browser blocks the calls. The API opts in with **CORS** headers, and the `cors` package sets them. Allow the exact origin of your front end, and not every origin.
npm install cors helmet express-rate-limit
app.use(cors({ origin: allowedOrigin || false }));   // false: no cross-origin access

items: CORS is enforced by **browsers**. It does not protect your API from `curl` or scripts. Authentication and validation do that.
Do not use `origin: '*'` together with logins, unless you understand the effect.

When you test with curl and a different `Origin` header, the server still answers. A string origin makes the package always send your configured origin, and it is the **browser** that refuses to give the response to a page from another origin.
Read the allowed origin from `.env`, so development and production can differ.

content.text: Helmet: safer headers

`helmet` is a middleware that sets a group of HTTP headers that tell browsers to be careful. For example, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` stops browsers guessing types, `Strict-Transport-Security` asks them to use HTTPS, and `Content-Security-Policy` limits where scripts may load from. It is one line, and it is a good default for any Express app. Express also announces itself with an `X-Powered-By: Express` header, which only helps attackers, so switch it off with `app.disable('x-powered-by')`.
Rate limiting

Without a limit, a script can try thousands of passwords a minute against your login, or overload your server. `express-rate-limit` counts requests per client address and answers `429 Too Many Requests` after a limit. Use a strict limit on login and registration, and a more relaxed one for the rest.

We tested it: the first 20 login attempts get `401` (wrong password), and the 21st and 22nd get `429` with a `Retry-After` header. The store behind this limiter is the memory of one process. If you run several copies of your server, or restart often, use a shared store such as Redis. Also, behind a proxy like nginx, every request seems to come from the proxy's address unless you tell Express to trust it with `app.set('trust proxy', 1)`. Do that only when a proxy really sits in front of Node, because otherwise clients can fake their address.
Limit what you accept

items: `express.json({ limit: '10kb' })`: a task needs only a few hundred bytes. A small limit prevents huge bodies from using up memory. Bigger bodies get `413`, which our error handler explains.
Validate every field, as in lesson 15.
Cap list sizes and page through them.
Do not let users choose file paths or run commands with their input.

content.text: The full app so far

Here is the whole `app.js` with everything combined. It exports a function that builds the app, which is useful for testing in the next lesson, and it is the only place that knows the order of middleware.

Read the order. Security headers and CORS come first, then the body parser, then the logger. The login routes are limited. The task routes need a login. The 404 handler and the error handler are last. We checked the headers with curl and saw `Content-Security-Policy`, `Strict-Transport-Security` and `X-Content-Type-Options`, and no `X-Powered-By`.
Habits that protect you

items: **Keep secrets out of git** and out of logs. Do not log passwords, tokens or full request bodies.
**Keep dependencies updated.** Run `npm audit` regularly and read what it says before you run automatic fixes.
**Use HTTPS** everywhere in production.
**Give each secret one job**, and replace it if you think it leaked.
**Check ownership** of every record, not just login.
**Return the same error for a wrong email and a wrong password.**
**Run the app as a normal user**, not as root, on your server.
**Back up your data** and test restoring.

content.text: These steps reduce common risks. They do not make an app unhackable. If your app holds sensitive data such as health, payment or children's information, rules and laws apply in many countries, and you should get qualified advice.
Your task

items: Install `cors`, `helmet` and `express-rate-limit` and add them to `app.js` in the order shown.
Run `curl -I` on `/api/health` and check for the security headers. Check that `X-Powered-By` is gone.
Send 22 wrong logins in a loop and watch the status change to 429.
Send a JSON body of more than 10 kilobytes and see the 413 response.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The health check response has `X-Content-Type-Options` and no `X-Powered-By`.
The 21st login attempt within 15 minutes returns 429.
A request with an oversized body returns 413 with a JSON message.

steps.say: Requests arrive from anywhere on the internet, some friendly and some not.
Helmet adds safe headers and CORS only lets your own front end call the API from a browser.
The rate limiter slows down clients that send too many requests, which blocks password guessing.
Login checks and validation make sure only the right people send only valid data to your routes.

faqs.q: Does CORS protect my API from attackers?
faqs.a: No. CORS is enforced by browsers to protect users of web pages. Scripts and tools such as curl ignore it, so you still need authentication, validation and rate limits.

faqs.q: What is a good rate limit?
faqs.a: It depends on your app. Use a strict limit for login and registration, such as a few dozen attempts per 15 minutes per client, and a more relaxed one for ordinary routes. Watch real traffic and adjust.

quiz.q: Does CORS protect your API from curl or scripts?
options: No, it is enforced by browsers only
quiz.explain: You still need authentication and validation.

quiz.q: What does express-rate-limit answer after the limit is passed?
What does the helmet middleware do?
options: Sets HTTP headers that tell browsers to be careful

notes: CORS: allow only your own front end origin.
`helmet()` sets safer HTTP headers.
Rate limiting stops too many requests, especially on login routes.
Limit the body size: `express.json({ limit: '10kb' })`.
Keep secrets out of git and logs. Run `npm audit` and keep packages updated.
Use HTTPS in production, check ownership of every record, and take backups.
These steps reduce risk. They do not make an app unhackable.

lessons.title: Test and Deploy Your Node.js API: node:test, pm2 and nginx
lessons.metaTitle: Test and Deploy a Node.js API
lessons.description: Write API tests with the built-in node:test runner, then take your Express API live with pm2, an nginx proxy, HTTPS and a launch checklist.

content.text: You now have a working API with validation, login and security. Two jobs remain, and both are about trust. **Tests** let you change code without fear, because a failing test tells you what you broke. **Deployment** puts the API on a server where other people can reach it. In this final lesson you will write tests with the test runner that is built into Node.js, then walk through the steps to run the API on a Linux server.
Make the app testable

In lesson 19, `app.js` exports a function `createApp` and does not call `listen`. A separate `server.js` reads the settings, creates the app and starts it. This split is what makes testing easy: a test can create its own app with its own settings, start it on a random free port and talk to it with `fetch`, with no need for any extra library.

The server file also does two production jobs. It refuses to start without a long enough secret. And it listens for `SIGTERM`, the signal that process managers send to stop a program, and closes the server tidily so running requests can finish.
Tests with node:test

Node.js includes a test runner. A test is a function with a name. `assert` checks that things are as expected. The file below tests the main paths: a login is required, a user can register and create a task, bad input is rejected, and a task can be updated and deleted.

Look at the structure. `test.before` starts the app on port `0`, which means the system picks any free port, and `test.after` stops it. The small `call` helper sends JSON and adds the token when we have one. Each `test(...)` block checks one behaviour. The tests run in order and share the `token` variable, which is simple, but it also means that one failure can cause later ones to fail. For bigger suites, give each test its own setup.
npm test

ok 1 - tasks need a login
ok 2 - register, then create and read a task
ok 3 - bad input is rejected with 400
ok 4 - a task can be updated and deleted
# tests 4
# pass 4
# fail 0

The real output also shows timings and other details, and the timings will be different on your computer. The `test` script runs `node --test`, which finds files that end in `.test.js` and runs them. Make a habit of running the tests before every commit. When you find a bug, write a test that fails because of it, then fix the code until the test passes. The bug can then never return unnoticed.
Preparing for production

items: Set `NODE_ENV=production`. Express and many libraries then switch to faster, safer behaviour. For example, the default error page no longer shows stack traces.
Install only what you need: `npm install --omit=dev`.
Set every secret and setting in the server's environment: `JWT_SECRET`, `MONGODB_URI` or `DATA_FILE`, `CLIENT_ORIGIN`, `PORT`.
Use a **long random** `JWT_SECRET` that exists only on the server. You can make one with `node -e "console.log(require('crypto').randomBytes(48).toString('base64url'))"`.
Use a database, not a JSON file, for anything you cannot afford to lose.

content.text: Keep it running with pm2

If you start the API with `node server.js` in a terminal, it stops when you close the terminal or when it crashes. A **process manager** keeps it running, restarts it after a crash and starts it again after a reboot. **pm2** is a popular one for Node.js. These commands run on your server.

npm install -g pm2
pm2 start server.js --name taskapi --node-args="--env-file=.env"
pm2 logs taskapi          # watch the logs
pm2 restart taskapi       # after deploying new code
pm2 save                  # remember the list of processes
pm2 startup               # prints a command to start pm2 on boot
The program listens on a port on the server, such as 3100. You do not want visitors to type that port, and you want HTTPS.
Put nginx in front

A **reverse proxy**, usually nginx, accepts connections on the normal ports 80 and 443, handles HTTPS, and passes requests to your Node.js program on its own port. Here is a minimal server block. It is a sketch to adapt, and not a complete production setup.

items: Get a free certificate for HTTPS from Let's Encrypt, with a tool such as `certbot`, and let it set up the renewal.
Because nginx now sits in front, add `app.set('trust proxy', 1)` to the app, so the rate limiter sees real client addresses and not the proxy's.
Only open ports 80 and 443 to the world. Keep the Node port closed in the firewall.
`example.com` is a placeholder. Use your own domain.

content.text: Health checks and logs

The `/api/health` route gives monitoring tools and load balancers something to call. Check it after each deploy. Read logs with `pm2 logs`, and watch for repeated errors. Do not log passwords, tokens or personal data. For a busy service, send logs to a central service, so they survive a server loss.
A deploy routine

items: Run the tests on your machine. Commit and push.
On the server, pull the new code: `git pull`.
Install what is needed: `npm install --omit=dev`.
Restart: `pm2 restart taskapi`.
Check `/api/health` and read the first lines of the logs.
If something is wrong, go back to the last good commit and restart.

content.text: Before you launch: a short checklist

items: Tests pass, and secrets are not in git.
HTTPS works, and the secret is long and random.
CORS allows only your front end.
Rate limits are on for login and registration.
The database has a restricted user, and backups run.
Errors show a general message to clients and full detail in the logs.
You know who to call, and what to do, if something breaks.

content.text: Where to go next

You now know the core of back-end work with Node.js: modules, async code, Express, validation, storage, login, security, tests and deployment. Next, connect a front end. Our [MERN stack course](/learn/mern-stack-full-course) builds a complete app with React on top of an API like this one. Add features to your task API: due dates, tags, paging, password reset with email. And read the official documentation for Node.js, Express and Mongoose when you meet something new, because it is the most reliable source. The [career roadmaps](/roadmaps) show how this skill fits into back-end and full stack roles.
Your task

items: Add `test` and `start` scripts, write the tests above and run `npm test`.
Write a new test for a case of your own, for example that a second user cannot read the first user's task, and make it pass.
Make a plan for deployment of your API: where it would run, where the secrets would be kept, and how you would roll back.
If you have a server, deploy the API with pm2 and check `/api/health`.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: `npm test` shows all tests passing.
The server refuses to start when `JWT_SECRET` is missing, and prints a clear message.
You can describe, in your own words, what pm2 and nginx each do.

animation.title: From your laptop to a live API

steps.say: Before anything goes live, the tests must pass on your machine.
On the server you pull the new code and install the packages you need.
A process manager such as pm2 starts the API, restarts it after a crash and starts it again after a reboot.
nginx accepts public HTTPS requests and passes them to your Node.js program.

faqs.q: Why export createApp instead of calling listen in app.js?
faqs.a: It lets tests create their own app and start it on a random port, without side effects. The separate server.js reads settings and starts the real server.

faqs.q: Why do I need nginx if Node can serve requests itself?
faqs.a: nginx handles HTTPS, standard ports, compression and static files efficiently, and protects the Node process from direct exposure. It is a common and well-tested setup, though not the only one.

quiz.q: Why is it useful to have tests for your API?
options: They catch problems when you change the code

quiz.q: Which Node feature runs tests without extra packages, as in the course?
Where should live-server settings and secrets come from?

notes: Make the app testable: export `app` and call `listen` in a separate file.
Tests with the built-in `node:test`. `npm test` should pass before every deploy.
For production set `NODE_ENV=production`, use real secrets and a real database.
Keep it running with `pm2`. Put nginx in front with HTTPS.
Add a `/api/health` route and check the logs.
Deploy routine: pull, install, test, restart. Test your backup, and have a way to go back.

lessons.section: JavaScript and Node Core in Depth
lessons.title: JavaScript Essentials for Node: Destructuring, Closures, Promises and the Event Loop
lessons.metaTitle: JavaScript Essentials for Node Developers
lessons.description: Review the JavaScript that Node and Express use daily: destructuring, spread and rest, closures, higher-order functions, promises and the event loop.

content.text: Node.js is JavaScript outside the browser, so everything you know about the language applies. Express code, though, uses a particular slice of it again and again: pulling values out of objects, copying objects without changing the original, functions that return functions, and asynchronous code written with promises. If one of these feels shaky, backend code will feel confusing. This lesson is a fast review of exactly those parts, with one small file that you can run.

If you are new to JavaScript, read this lesson slowly and try each line in the REPL. If you already know the language well, skim the headings and read the last section on the event loop, because it explains why Node can serve many users at once.
Destructuring, spread and rest

**Destructuring** takes values out of an object or array and gives them names. In Express you will write `const { title, price } = req.body` hundreds of times. **Spread** (`...`) copies the items of an object or array into a new one, which is how you change data without changing the original. **Rest** is the same three dots used the other way round, to collect the remaining items. The rule that decides which is which is simple: on the left of an assignment or in a function's parameter list it collects (rest), and everywhere else it expands (spread).

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Save the code below as `essentials.js` and run it with `node essentials.js`.

content.text: node essentials.js

Asha Pune js [ 'sql' ]
30 29 6
count 2
[ 4, 8, 12 ]
A B
Caught: Something failed

Look at the second line: `older.age` is 30 and `user.age` is still 29. Spread made a new object, so the original is untouched. This matters in servers, because code that quietly changes shared objects causes bugs that appear only under load.
Closures and higher-order functions

A **closure** is a function that remembers the variables around the place where it was created. The `counter` function returns an inner function that still sees `count`, even after `counter` has finished. Closures are how middleware factories work: `rateLimit({ max: 5 })` returns a function that remembers `max`. A **higher-order function** is a function that takes another function as input or returns one. `filter`, `map` and `reduce` take functions. Express itself is built on this idea: you hand `app.get` a function and Express calls it later.
Callbacks, promises and async/await

Slow things, such as reading a file or asking a database, must not freeze the server, so Node starts them and carries on. When the result is ready, it calls a function you provided, a **callback**. Nested callbacks quickly become hard to read, so JavaScript added **promises**: an object that stands for a value that will arrive later. `async` and `await` let you write promise code in a straight line. In the example, `Promise.all` waits for two promises at the same time, which is much faster than waiting for one and then the other. A rejected promise becomes an exception that `try/catch` can handle.

items: Always `await` a promise, or return it. A promise you forget about can fail silently.
Use `Promise.all` when the tasks do not depend on each other, and `await` one by one when they do.
Wrap awaited code in `try/catch`, or let Express 5 pass the error to your error handler.

content.text: JSON and modules

**JSON** is text in the shape of JavaScript objects, and it is the language of APIs. `JSON.stringify` turns an object into text and `JSON.parse` turns text back into an object. Remember that JSON has no functions, no `undefined`, and no dates: a date becomes a text string. For code organisation, ES modules use `export` and `import`, which this course uses throughout. Older code uses `require`, which you will still meet in many projects.
The event loop in one picture

JavaScript runs your code on **one thread**, which means one thing at a time. Node serves many users because slow work, such as network and disk, is handed to the operating system, and your code is called again when it finishes. The **event loop** is the part that keeps checking for finished work and runs the waiting callbacks. The practical rule is: never block the loop. A long calculation or a synchronous file read inside a request handler stops every other user until it ends. Lesson 23 shows how to move heavy work to other threads.

The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.
Your task

items: Change the example so that `counter` takes a starting number and a step.
Write a function `pick(object, ...keys)` that returns a new object with only those keys.
Make one of the two `wait` promises reject, and see what `Promise.all` and `Promise.allSettled` do.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Your output matches the output shown above.
You can say whether `...` is spread or rest in any line.
You can explain why a long synchronous loop in a handler hurts every user.

steps.say: Requests arrive. Node runs your handler on a single thread.
When the handler starts slow work, it is handed over and the loop carries on.
The operating system does the disk or network work in the background.
When it finishes, the loop runs your callback or resumes your await.

faqs.q: Is JavaScript really single-threaded?
faqs.a: Your code runs on one thread, but Node uses other threads inside for things such as file and network work, and you can start more with worker threads.

faqs.q: Should I use callbacks, promises or async/await?
faqs.a: Use async/await in new code. Callbacks still appear in older libraries, and util.promisify can turn many of them into promises.

faqs.q: What is the difference between spread and rest?
faqs.a: They look the same. Rest collects the remaining items into one variable. Spread expands items out of a variable.

quiz.q: What does spread do in { ...user, age: 30 }?
options: Copies the properties into a new object, leaving user unchanged

quiz.q: What is a closure?
options: A function that remembers the variables around where it was created
A function that cannot be called
A way to close a file

quiz.q: Why must you not block the event loop in a handler?
options: Every other user waits until it finishes

lessons.section: JavaScript and Node Core in Depth
lessons.title: Node Core Modules: EventEmitter, Streams, Buffers, os and process
lessons.metaTitle: Node Core Modules: Events, Streams, Buffers
lessons.description: Learn the Node.js built-in modules back ends rely on: EventEmitter, streams with pipeline, Buffers, and the os and process modules.

content.text: Node.js ships with a standard library that needs no installation, and several of its parts show up in every serious project. You have already used `fs` and `path`. This lesson adds the ones you meet next: **events** for letting parts of a program talk without knowing each other, **streams** for handling big data in small pieces, **buffers** for raw bytes, and the **os** and **process** modules for information about the machine and the running program. Express itself is built on them: a request is a readable stream, a response is a writable stream, and the server is an event emitter.
EventEmitter: announce, do not call

An `EventEmitter` lets one part of a program announce that something happened, while other parts listen. The sender does not need to know who listens. When an order is placed, the order code announces `placed`. The email code, the stock code and the analytics code each listen and do their own work. Adding a fourth listener needs no change to the order code. That is the idea behind event-driven design, and it returns in later lessons about queues and sockets.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Save each example below as its own file in the same folder and run it with `node`.

content.text:
Email sent for Keyboard
Stock reduced for Keyboard
First order ever!
Email sent for Mouse
Stock reduced for Mouse
Listeners: 2

Listeners run in the order you added them, and they run **synchronously**, one after another, when you call `emit`. A listener that throws stops the others, so keep listeners small and careful. The special event name `error` is different: if you emit `error` and nobody listens, Node throws and the process can crash. Always attach an `error` listener to emitters that can fail.
Streams: big data in small pieces

Reading a 2 GB file into memory with `readFile` could crash the server. A **stream** reads it in small chunks, passes each chunk along, and forgets it, so memory use stays small whatever the file size. There are four kinds: readable, writable, duplex and transform. A transform changes data as it passes, such as compressing or converting to upper case. `pipeline` connects streams, passes errors along, and closes everything properly. Prefer it to the older `.pipe()` method, which does not clean up when something fails.

[ 'HELLO', 'STREAMS', 'ARE', 'USEFUL' ]
<Buffer 4e 6f 64 65> 4 4e6f6465 Tm9kZQ==
Node JS

In an Express route, `fs.createReadStream(path).pipe(res)` sends a large download without loading it, and `req` is a stream too, which is how upload libraries read big files in parts. Streams also have **backpressure**: if the receiver is slow, the sender is told to wait. `pipeline` handles this for you.
Buffers: raw bytes

A `Buffer` is a fixed block of bytes. Files, network packets, images and encrypted data are bytes, not text. The same buffer can be read as text with `toString('utf8')`, as hexadecimal with `'hex'`, or as base64 with `'base64'`. You saw in the output that the text `Node` is four bytes, `4e 6f 64 65`. Security code uses buffers constantly, for example to compare two secrets safely, and upload code uses them to check the first bytes of a file.
os and process

The `os` module tells you about the machine: the number of CPU cores, total and free memory, the platform. You use it to decide how many workers to start. The `process` object is the running program. `process.argv` holds the command-line words, `process.env` the environment variables, `process.exitCode` the result code, and `process.on('exit')` and `process.on('SIGTERM')` let you clean up when the program ends. A server should listen for `SIGTERM`, stop taking new requests, finish the current ones and then exit. Hosting tools send that signal when they restart your app.

Platform: linux | Node: v22.23.4
CPU cores: true
Total memory > 0: true
Arguments after the script name: []
PORT from the environment: (not set)
Exiting with code 0

Your platform and version will differ. Two more things to remember: global objects such as `process`, `Buffer`, `setTimeout`, `console` and `URL` need no import, and `globalThis` is the standard name for the global object. Avoid putting your own data on it.

The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.
Your task

items: Make the order service in the first example emit an `error` event for an empty item name and add a listener that logs it.
Write a transform stream that turns each line into a numbered line, and use `pipeline` to process a text file.
Run the os example with `PORT=4000 node n17-os-process.js a b c` and read the output.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You can explain why `pipeline` is safer than `.pipe()`.
You can name the four kinds of streams.
You can say why a large download should be streamed.

steps.say: A readable stream produces data in small chunks.
A transform changes each chunk as it passes.
A writable stream receives the chunks, and slows the sender if it is busy.
pipeline connects them, passes errors and closes everything when done.

faqs.q: When should I use streams instead of readFile?
faqs.a: When the data can be large or arrives over time, such as big files, uploads, downloads and logs. For small files, readFile is simpler.

faqs.q: What is backpressure?
faqs.a: A way for a slow receiver to tell a fast sender to pause, so memory does not fill up with data nobody has processed yet.

faqs.q: Why must I add an error listener to an EventEmitter?
faqs.a: An unhandled error event throws an exception, which can crash the whole process.

quiz.q: Why use pipeline instead of .pipe()?
options: It passes errors along and cleans up all streams
It is the only way to read files

quiz.q: What happens if an EventEmitter emits error and nothing listens?
options: The event is queued for later
Node throws and the process can crash

quiz.q: What is a Buffer?
options: A fixed block of raw bytes
