lessons.title: Scaling Node: Worker Threads, Child Processes and the Cluster Module
lessons.metaTitle: Worker Threads, Child Processes, Cluster
lessons.description: Use more than one CPU core in Node.js: worker threads for heavy work, child processes for other programs, and cluster to run copies of a server.

content.text: Node runs your JavaScript on a single thread, which is fine for work that mostly waits, such as database and network calls. It is not fine for work that keeps the processor busy, such as resizing images, hashing many passwords, or a big calculation. While that runs, nobody else is served. Modern computers have many cores, and Node gives you three tools to use them. Each fits a different problem, and choosing the right one is a common interview question.
Worker threads: heavy calculations

A **worker thread** is another JavaScript thread inside the same Node process. It has its own event loop and its own memory, and it talks to the main thread by sending messages. Use it for CPU-heavy JavaScript. The example below calculates slow Fibonacci numbers in three workers at once. The main thread only starts them and waits for the messages, so it could keep answering requests meanwhile.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Save the code as `worker.js` and run it with `node worker.js`.

content.text: Notice that the same file contains both sides. `isMainThread` tells which side is running. Data sent between threads is copied, not shared, except for special shared memory. Starting a worker costs a few tens of milliseconds, so for a real server you create a small **pool** of workers at start and reuse them, using a library such as Piscina. Do not start a new worker for every request.
Child processes: other programs

A **child process** is a separate operating-system process. Use it to run another program, such as `ffmpeg` for video, a Python script, or `git`, or to run a second Node script that must be isolated. `execFile` runs a program and gives you its output. `fork` starts another Node script with a built-in message channel.

Child program printed: 42
Forked child replied: { doubled: 42 }

Security rule: never build a command from user input. `exec` runs its text in a shell, so a user who sends `; rm -rf ~` could run anything. Use `execFile` or `spawn` with the arguments as an array, and validate the values anyway.
Cluster: copies of your server

The **cluster** module starts several copies of the same server, one per core, that share one port. The operating system or Node spreads new connections between them. If one copy crashes, the others keep serving, and the primary process can start a replacement. This is the simplest way to use all the cores for a normal web server, because each request is handled completely by one copy.
Answers came from 2 worker process(es)

The number may vary: the system may happen to give all four requests to the same worker. In practice you rarely write cluster code yourself. The process manager **pm2**, which lesson 48 uses, can run your app in cluster mode with one setting. Container platforms and load balancers do the same by starting several copies.
Choosing the right tool

items: **Waiting work** (database, network): nothing special. The event loop already handles many at once.
**Heavy JavaScript calculation**: worker threads, ideally from a pool.
**Another program or language**: child process, with `execFile` and an argument array.
**More throughput for a web server**: cluster, pm2, or more containers behind a load balancer.
**Very heavy or slow work**: a background job queue, as in lesson 40, so the web request does not wait at all.

content.text: One warning applies to all copies of a server. Each copy has its own memory. A user logged in on copy A is unknown to copy B if you keep sessions or caches in a normal variable. Store shared state in a database or in Redis, and keep your servers stateless.

The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.
Your task

items: Change the worker example to take the numbers from `process.argv` and compare the time with and without workers.
Run the child example, then change it to run `node --version` and print the result.
Run the cluster example with three workers, and print the process id each answer came from.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Your outputs match the outputs above.
You can say which tool fits an image resize, a call to ffmpeg and a normal web server.
You can explain why an in-memory session breaks with several copies.

steps.say: The main thread serves requests and must never be blocked.
Heavy JavaScript goes to a worker thread, which reports back with a message.
Other programs run as child processes with safe arguments.
To use all cores for the web server itself, run copies with cluster or pm2.

faqs.q: Do worker threads share variables?
faqs.a: No. Each has its own memory and they communicate with messages, which copy the data. SharedArrayBuffer is the exception for special cases.

faqs.q: Is cluster the same as worker threads?
faqs.a: No. Cluster starts separate processes that share a port. Worker threads are threads inside one process, meant for CPU work.

faqs.q: Do I need cluster if I use Docker or Kubernetes?
faqs.a: Usually not. You run several containers and a load balancer spreads traffic, which gives the same benefit.

quiz.q: Which tool fits a heavy JavaScript calculation?
Why use execFile with an argument array instead of exec with a built string?
options: User input cannot inject extra shell commands

quiz.q: Why does an in-memory session break when you run several copies of a server?
options: Sessions are not allowed in cluster mode
Each copy has its own memory

lessons.section: Express Structure and REST in Depth
lessons.title: Express Project Structure: MVC, Static Files and App Settings
lessons.metaTitle: Express Structure, MVC and Static Files
lessons.description: Split an Express app into store, controller and routes files, serve static files, use app settings, and finish with a 404 handler and one error handler.

content.text: A tutorial server often lives in one file, and that is fine for learning. A real project grows to dozens of routes, and one file becomes painful to read, test and change. This lesson shows a simple structure that you will see in most Express projects. It is usually called **MVC**, short for model, view and controller, though in an API the view is just JSON. The goal is not to follow a rule. The goal is that each file has one job, so you always know where to look.
Who does what

items: **Store (model):** reads and writes data. It knows nothing about HTTP. Later you can swap it for MongoDB without touching anything else.
**Controller:** receives the request values, calls the store, and decides the response and status code.
**Routes:** a list that connects a method and a path, such as `GET /api/books/:id`, to a controller function.
**App:** creates the Express app, adds middleware, mounts the routes, and adds the 404 and error handlers.
**Server:** a tiny file that calls `app.listen`. Keeping it separate lets tests import the app without opening a port.

content.text: The separation has a practical payoff: you can test the controller with a fake store, or test the whole app with Supertest and no real port. Both are used later in the course. The example below is a small book API in four files plus a web page.
The store and the controller

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Install what the lesson needs: `npm install express`.
Save the files below in one folder, with the names shown in the comments at the top of each block. Put the web page in a folder called `s19-public`.

content.text: The store keeps books in an array and gives each an id. The controller functions take `(req, res)` and use the store. Notice that they are factory functions that receive the store as an argument. That is the simplest form of **dependency injection**: the controller does not create its own store, so a test can pass a different one.
Routes and the app

Read the app file from the top. `app.disable('x-powered-by')` removes a header that tells everyone you use Express, which gives attackers a small hint for free. `app.set('trust proxy', 1)` tells Express that one proxy, such as nginx, sits in front, so `req.ip` and `req.protocol` show the real visitor. Without it, every visitor looks like the proxy. `json spaces` makes JSON replies readable while you develop; remove it in production to save bytes.

`express.static` serves the files of a folder as they are. A request to `/` returns `s19-public/index.html`, and a request to `/style.css` returns that file if it exists. Static files are meant for your front-end build, images and a favicon. Never point it at a folder that contains code or secrets, because every file inside is public.
404 and the error handler

Express runs middleware in the order you add it. The two functions at the bottom of the app are the safety net. The first has no path, so it catches any request that no route handled, and returns a JSON 404. The second has **four** parameters, `(err, req, res, next)`. That fourth parameter is how Express recognises an error handler, so keep it even if you do not use `next`. Any error thrown in a route reaches it, and in Express 5 that includes errors from async functions. The handler logs the real error for you and sends the client a short, safe message. Lesson 38 expands this into a full logging and error system.
Order matters. Put the 404 handler after all routes and the error handler last. A route added after them is never reached.
Environment settings

The behaviour of the app should change with the environment, not with edited code. `process.env.NODE_ENV` is `production` on a live server, and several libraries, including Express, use it to turn on faster, quieter behaviour. Read the port, database address and secrets from environment variables as well. Lesson 36 builds a validated configuration file for this.

The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.

The test for this lesson starts the app with Supertest, fetches the home page, creates a book, reads it back, deletes it, and checks that a missing id returns 404. It passes, and you can find it in the course code as `s19.test.js`.
Your task

items: Add a `PATCH /api/books/:id` route that changes only the fields sent.
Add a second store file that saves the books in a JSON file and swap it in without changing the controller.
Add a route that deliberately throws an error and check that the client sees only the safe message.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: `GET /` returns the web page.
A wrong URL returns a JSON 404, not an HTML error page.
You can say which file you would open to change a status code, and which to change where data is saved.

steps.say: The router matches the method and path and picks a controller function.
The controller reads the request and decides what to do.
The store reads or writes data. It knows nothing about HTTP.
Anything that fails travels on to the error handler, which hides the details from clients.

faqs.q: Is MVC required in Express?
faqs.a: No. Express has no fixed structure. MVC is a common convention because it keeps files small and testable.

faqs.q: Why separate app.js from server.js?
faqs.a: Tests can import the app and call it with Supertest without opening a network port.

faqs.q: Why does the error handler need four parameters?
faqs.a: Express decides a function is an error handler by counting its parameters. With three it is treated as normal middleware.

quiz.q: What does the controller do in the structure shown?
options: Reads the request, calls the store and decides the response

quiz.q: Why keep app.js and server.js separate?
options: Tests can import the app without opening a port

quiz.q: How does Express recognise an error handler?

lessons.title: REST API Design: Status Codes, Versioning, Paging, Filtering and Search
lessons.metaTitle: REST API Design: Paging and Search
lessons.description: Design a clean REST API in Express with correct status codes, URL versions, safe paging limits, filtering, sorting and search, with a tested working example.

content.text: A REST API is a promise to other programmers, including the front-end developer who joins next year. If the URLs and replies are predictable, they can use your API without asking you questions. If they are not, every endpoint becomes a small mystery. This lesson collects the habits that make an API predictable, and shows each one in a tested example of 45 products.
Nouns for URLs, verbs for methods

A URL names a **thing**, and the HTTP method says what to do with it. Use plural nouns: `/api/v1/products` is the collection and `/api/v1/products/7` is one item. `GET` reads, `POST` creates, `PUT` replaces, `PATCH` changes part of it, and `DELETE` removes it. Avoid verbs in paths such as `/getProducts` or `/deleteProduct`, because the method already says that. For relations, nest only one level: `/users/5/orders` is clear, while `/users/5/orders/9/items/3/notes` is a sign to flatten.
Status codes that tell the truth

items: **200** OK for a successful read or update. **201** Created after a `POST`, with a `Location` header holding the new URL. **204** No Content for a delete.
**400** when the request is malformed. **401** when the user is not logged in. **403** when the user is logged in but not allowed. **404** when the item does not exist.
**409** Conflict when the request clashes with the current state, for example a duplicate email. **422** when the data is well-formed but fails the rules, for example a negative price.
**429** when the client sent too many requests. **500** for your own bugs. Never send 200 with an error message inside; clients and monitoring tools trust the code.

content.text: The most common mistakes are using 200 for everything and mixing up 401 and 403. 401 really means *unauthenticated*: we do not know who you are. 403 means we know you, and the answer is still no.
Paging, filtering, sorting and search

A list endpoint that returns every row works on your laptop and fails in production. The fix is **paging**: the client asks for a page and a size. The server must also set a **maximum size**, otherwise a client can ask for `limit=1000000`. In the code, `clamp` keeps numbers inside a safe range and falls back to a default when the value is not a number at all. Filtering, sorting and search then narrow the list. Sorting only accepts a short list of allowed field names, never a field name copied straight from the URL, because a free field name can expose private fields or break database queries.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Install what the lesson needs: `npm install express`.
Save the code as `api.js`. The test below it needs `npm install -D supertest` and runs with `node --test`.

content.text: Try these URLs once the app is listening: `/api/v1/products?page=2&limit=5`, `/api/v1/products?category=books&sort=price&order=desc`, and `/api/v1/products?q=item 0`. Return a small envelope with the data and the paging details, such as the current page, the size and the total count, so a front end can draw page buttons. For very large or fast-changing data, **cursor paging** ("give me the items after this id") is more stable than page numbers, but page numbers are simpler and enough for most projects.

ok 1 - paging
ok 2 - limit is capped and bad numbers fall back
ok 3 - filter, sort and search
ok 4 - status codes
ok 5 - version 2 has its own shape
Versioning

Once other people use your API you cannot freely change replies, or their apps break. A **version in the URL**, `/api/v1` and `/api/v2`, lets you publish a new shape while the old one keeps working. The example has a version 2 that changes the shape of the list reply. Do not create a new version for every small change. Adding a new field is safe in the same version. Renaming or removing a field is the kind of change that needs v2. Announce the end date of an old version in advance, and keep it running until then.
Treat every query-string value as text that a stranger typed. Convert, check and clamp it before use, and only use values from a list you chose for sort and filter fields.

The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.
Your task

items: Add `DELETE /api/v1/products/:id` that returns 204, and 404 for a missing id.
Add a `fields` query, for example `?fields=name,price`, that returns only the allowed fields.
Return the total number of pages in the reply and write a test for the last page.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Your five tests pass.
`limit=9999` returns at most 50 items.
A bad `sort` value falls back to `id` instead of crashing.

animation.title: One list request, safe at each step

steps.say: The client sends page, limit, sort and search words in the URL.
The server converts them, caps the limit and allows only known sort fields.
Only then are the filters, the sort and the page slice applied.
The reply carries the items plus the page, size and total so a front end can draw page buttons.

faqs.q: Should I use PUT or PATCH?
faqs.a: Use PUT when the client sends the complete new version of the item, and PATCH when it sends only the fields that change.

faqs.q: When do I need API versions?
faqs.a: When you must change or remove a field that other apps already use. Adding new fields normally needs no new version.

faqs.q: Page numbers or cursors?
faqs.a: Page numbers are simpler and fine for most apps. Cursors suit very large or constantly changing lists, where page numbers can skip or repeat items.

quiz.q: Which status code means the user is logged in but not allowed?
quiz.explain: 401 means not authenticated, 403 means not allowed.

quiz.q: Why set a maximum limit on a list endpoint?
options: A client could ask for a huge number of rows at once

quiz.q: When do you need a new API version such as /v2?
options: When you must rename or remove something clients already use

lessons.title: Document Your API: OpenAPI, Swagger UI and Postman
lessons.metaTitle: API Docs: OpenAPI, Swagger, Postman
lessons.description: Describe an Express API in an OpenAPI file, serve interactive Swagger UI documentation, and test the same endpoints in Postman, with a tested working example.

content.text: An API without documentation is only half finished. The front-end developer, the mobile developer and your own future self all need to know the URLs, the fields and the possible errors. Writing that in a chat message goes out of date in a week. The standard solution is an **OpenAPI** file: a machine-readable description of the API. Tools turn that one file into interactive pages, test requests and even client code.
What an OpenAPI file contains

OpenAPI, which many people still call by its old name Swagger, is a JSON or YAML file with a fixed structure. It lists each path, each method on that path, the parameters it accepts, the body it expects, and every response it can return, with the status code and shape. The `components` section holds shapes you reuse, such as a `Product`, so you describe them once. The file for our product API is below. Read the `paths` first, then `components`.

Notice that the file documents the errors as well as the success cases. A client developer needs to know that a missing item returns 404 and that a wrong body returns 422 with a list of problems. Good documentation answers the question "what can go wrong?", not only "what do I send?".
Serving interactive docs with Swagger UI

**Swagger UI** reads the file and draws a web page where each endpoint can be opened, filled in and tried with a button. With the `swagger-ui-express` package it takes three lines. You also serve the raw file at `/openapi.json`, because other tools, such as Postman, can import it from there.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Install what the lesson needs: `npm install express swagger-ui-express`.
Save the OpenAPI file as `r21-openapi.json` next to the code. For the test, install `npm install -D supertest`.

content.text: The test confirms that the spec is served as JSON and that the docs page loads. The docs usually live at a path such as `/docs`. In a real product, think about whether the documentation should be public. Public APIs benefit from open docs. For a private internal API, put the docs behind a login or serve them only in development, because they give an attacker a complete map of your endpoints.
Keeping the file true

The danger is a document that disagrees with the code. There are two ways to avoid it. You can **write the spec first** and build the code to match, which makes the file the agreement between front end and back end. Or you can **generate** the spec from comments or schemas in the code, for example with Zod and a conversion library. Whichever you choose, add a test that checks real replies against the described shapes, and review the file in every pull request that changes an endpoint.
Testing by hand with Postman

**Postman** is an app for sending requests and saving them. Import `http://localhost:3000/openapi.json` and it creates a collection with one request for every endpoint. Use an *environment* with a variable such as `baseUrl`, so the same collection works on your laptop and on the live server by switching one setting. Postman can also run simple checks on each reply, for example that the status is 201 and the body has an `id`, and can run a whole collection in a row, which is a gentle introduction to automated API tests. Insomnia and the VS Code extension Thunder Client do the same job, and `curl` always works from a terminal.

items: Document every status code you return, including 401, 403, 404 and 422.
Give each field a type and one example value.
Never put real passwords, tokens or customer data in examples.
Commit the spec to Git so its history shows when the API changed.

content.text: The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.
The Swagger UI package ships its own copy of the front-end files and its version changes, so run the test again after you update it.
Your task

items: Add the `DELETE` operation to the file and see it appear in the docs page.
Import the spec in Postman and send a request to create a product.
Protect `/docs` so that it only loads when `NODE_ENV` is not `production`.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: `/openapi.json` returns the spec.
`/docs` shows every endpoint and the Try it out button works.
You can say which status codes each endpoint can return without opening the code.

steps.say: You describe the API once in an OpenAPI file and keep it in Git.
Swagger UI turns the file into pages where each endpoint can be tried.
Postman imports the same file into a ready collection of requests.
The front-end developer builds against the agreement without asking you.

faqs.q: Is Swagger the same as OpenAPI?
faqs.a: OpenAPI is the specification. Swagger was its old name and is now the name of a set of tools, such as Swagger UI, that read it.

faqs.q: Should my API docs be public?
faqs.a: For a public API, yes. For an internal API, serve them only in development or behind a login.

faqs.q: How do I stop the docs going out of date?
faqs.a: Write the spec first or generate it from your schemas, and add a test that compares real replies with the described shapes.

quiz.q: What is an OpenAPI file?
options: A machine-readable description of your API

quiz.q: What does Swagger UI do with the file?
options: Draws interactive docs where you can try each endpoint

quiz.q: Why document the error responses too?
options: Client developers need to know what can go wrong

lessons.title: File Uploads in Express: Multer, Validation and Cloud Storage
lessons.metaTitle: File Uploads in Express with Multer
lessons.description: Accept uploads safely in Express with Multer: size limits, checking real file types by their first bytes, random file names, and a storage driver for the cloud.

content.text: Letting users upload files is one of the riskiest features you can add. A profile photo or a PDF resume feels harmless, but the file is data from a stranger that you will store, and perhaps show to other people. Careless upload code has led to servers being taken over, disks being filled and private files being leaked. This lesson shows the safe way, using the **Multer** package, and a tested example.
How uploads work

A normal JSON body cannot carry a file well, so browsers use **multipart/form-data**, which splits a request into named parts, some text and some files. Express does not read this format, so Multer does. It reads the parts and gives you `req.file` for one upload or `req.files` for many. You choose where the bytes go: to the disk, or into memory as a Buffer.
Five rules for safe uploads

items: **Set a size limit.** Without one, a single request can fill your memory or your disk. Here it is 1 MB.

**Check the real type.** The `Content-Type` and the file name come from the client, who can lie. Look at the first bytes of the file, which are called the *magic number*. A PNG always starts with the same eight bytes, a PDF with `%PDF-`.
**Use an allow-list** of types you accept, instead of a block-list of bad ones.
**Make your own file name.** A random UUID plus the extension you decided. Never use the original name to build a path, because a name such as `../../app.js` is an attack called path traversal.
**Do not serve uploads as code.** Store them outside your source folders, or in cloud storage, and send them with the correct type.
Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Install what the lesson needs: `npm install express multer`.
Save the code as `upload.js`. The test needs `npm install -D supertest`.

content.text: Read the code in the order a request travels. Multer's `memoryStorage` puts the file in `req.file.buffer`, and the `limits` option stops anything over 1 MB. Then `sniff` compares the first bytes with the known signatures. If the result is not in the allow-list, the route replies 415 or 422 and nothing is saved. Only a passed file is given a random name and handed to the **storage driver**.
A storage driver keeps your options open

Look at `localStorageDriver`: it has one method, `save`, that takes a buffer and a name and returns a URL. Everything else in the app uses that method only. When the project grows and local disk is no longer enough, because you have several servers or want a content delivery network, you write another driver with the same method that sends the file to Cloudinary, ImageKit or Amazon S3, and change one line where the app is created. That is the idea of a stable interface in front of a changeable detail, and project 8 in this course shows an ImageKit driver.
Handling Multer errors

When a limit is exceeded, Multer raises a `MulterError`, such as `LIMIT_FILE_SIZE`. If you do nothing, the client sees a confusing 500. The example catches it and returns **413 Payload Too Large** with a clear message. Also reject requests that have no file at all, with 400.

The test sends a real PNG, a text file that pretends to be a PNG, a file that is too large, and a request with no file. Only the first is accepted. Run it with `node --test` and read what each case returns.
Cloud driver code for Cloudinary and ImageKit is shown in project 8 but was not run, because those services need an account and keys. Check their current documentation before you copy it.
Beyond the basics

For large files, such as video, do not pass them through your server at all. Ask the cloud provider for a short-lived **signed upload URL**, and let the browser send the file straight to it. Your server only records the result. For images, resize and convert them on upload, because a 12 MB phone photo does not belong on a web page. For files that others will open, such as PDF resumes, consider a virus scan, which cloud storage services and tools like ClamAV can provide.

The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.
Your task

items: Add GIF support, including its magic bytes, and a test.
Change the limit to 200 KB for a profile photo and watch the 413 reply.
Write a second driver that saves into a `uploads-b` folder and swap it in.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: A real PNG returns a URL and a fake PNG is refused.
A big file returns 413.
No saved file uses the name the user sent.

steps.say: The browser sends the file as multipart form data.
Multer reads it and rejects anything above the size limit.
The first bytes are compared with known file signatures, not the name the client gave.
Only then is the file saved under a random name through the storage driver.

faqs.q: Why check the first bytes instead of the file extension?
faqs.a: The extension and the Content-Type come from the client and can be faked. The first bytes are part of the real file format.

faqs.q: Should uploads go on my server disk?
faqs.a: It is fine for a small app. With several servers or a lot of files, use cloud storage, so every copy of your app sees the same files.

faqs.q: How do I handle very large uploads?
faqs.a: Use signed upload URLs so the browser sends the file directly to cloud storage, and only record the result on your server.

quiz.q: Why check the first bytes of an uploaded file?
options: The name and Content-Type come from the client and can be faked

quiz.q: Why create your own random file name?
options: A user-supplied name can contain a path such as ../../ that escapes your folder

quiz.q: What does the storage driver idea give you?
options: You can switch from disk to cloud storage by changing one piece

lessons.title: Calling Third-Party APIs and Webhooks: Timeouts, Retries, Signatures
lessons.metaTitle: Third-Party APIs and Webhooks in Node
lessons.description: Call other services from Node.js with timeouts and safe retries with backoff, and verify webhooks with an HMAC signature and a constant-time comparison.

content.text: Almost every real back end talks to other services: a payment provider, an email service, a maps API, an AI model, a government database. Those services are outside your control. They are sometimes slow, sometimes down, and sometimes send you data you did not expect. A server that assumes they always work will fail in the worst possible moment. This lesson has two halves: calling other APIs defensively, and receiving **webhooks**, where another service calls you.
Calling an API: three habits

Node 18 and later has `fetch` built in, so you need no extra package for simple calls. Raw `fetch` has no timeout, though, so a service that never answers can leave your request waiting forever and use up your server. Build one small wrapper function that every call goes through, and put these habits in it.

items: **A timeout.** `AbortSignal.timeout(2000)` cancels the request after two seconds.
**Retries for temporary failures.** Network errors, 5xx replies and 429 (too many requests) are often gone a moment later, so try again.
**No retry for your own mistakes.** A 400, 401, 403 or 404 will fail the same way every time, so retrying only wastes time.
**Exponential backoff.** Wait a little, then longer, for example 50, 100, 200 milliseconds, so you do not hammer a service that is already struggling.
**A limit on attempts,** then a clear error that the rest of your app can handle.
Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Save the code as `client.js`. The test uses only Node, with no extra packages.

content.text: In `fetchJson`, a loop runs up to `retries + 1` times. Inside it, the `fetch` call carries the timeout signal. A 4xx reply other than 429 is thrown straight away. A network error, a timeout or a 5xx makes the loop sleep for `baseDelayMs * 2 ** attempt` and try again. The test starts a small fake server that fails twice and then answers, one that always returns 404, and one that is too slow, and checks that the wrapper behaves correctly in each case.

Only retry requests that are safe to repeat. A `GET` is safe. A `POST` that charges a card is not, unless the provider supports an **idempotency key**, a unique value you send so the provider ignores the repeat. Lesson 42 shows this.
Receiving webhooks

A **webhook** is a request that a service sends to your server when something happens, for example "payment succeeded" or "new commit pushed". Instead of asking again and again, you give them a URL and they call it. The risk is obvious: anyone on the internet can send a request to that URL and claim that a payment succeeded. You must check that the request really came from the provider.

The usual method is an **HMAC signature**. You and the provider share a secret. For each webhook the provider calculates a hash of the exact body using the secret and sends it in a header. You calculate the same hash and compare. An attacker who does not know the secret cannot produce a matching signature. Three details matter. First, hash the **raw bytes** of the body, before `express.json()` changes them, or the hash will not match. Second, compare with `crypto.timingSafeEqual`, because an ordinary `===` stops at the first different character and can leak information through timing. Third, reject requests with a missing or wrong-length signature before comparing.

In Express, use `express.raw({ type: 'application/json' })` on the webhook route only, so the body arrives as a Buffer, verify it, and then `JSON.parse` it yourself. Always answer quickly with a 200 after you have verified and saved the event, and do slow work later in a queue, because providers resend if you take too long. Since they can resend, store the event id and ignore ids you have already handled.

The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.
Your task

items: Add jitter, a small random amount, to the backoff delay, and explain why it helps when many clients retry together.
Make the wrapper read the `Retry-After` header on a 429.
Write an Express route that receives a webhook, verifies the signature and answers 401 for a bad one.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: All four tests pass.
A 404 is tried once, not three times.
You can say why the raw body is needed for the signature.

animation.title: Safe calls out, trusted calls in

steps.say: Calls to other services go through one wrapper with a timeout.
Temporary failures are retried with a growing delay. 4xx errors are not retried.
When a service calls you, the signature is checked against the raw body.
Only a verified, not-yet-seen event is saved and answered with 200.

faqs.q: Which errors should I retry?
faqs.a: Network errors, timeouts, 5xx replies and 429. Do not retry 4xx errors such as 400 or 404, because they will fail again.

faqs.q: Why use timingSafeEqual?
faqs.a: A normal comparison stops at the first difference, and the time it takes can leak how much of a guess was correct. timingSafeEqual takes the same time either way.

faqs.q: What if the provider sends the same webhook twice?
faqs.a: Store the event id and skip ids you have already processed, so the work is done only once.

quiz.q: Which failure should you retry?
options: A 503 reply or a network timeout

quiz.q: Why does a webhook signature check need the raw body?
options: JSON is not allowed in webhooks
The hash is calculated over the exact bytes that were sent

quiz.q: Why use timingSafeEqual to compare signatures?
options: A normal comparison can leak information through timing

lessons.title: MongoDB Relationships, Populate, Indexes and SQL versus NoSQL
lessons.metaTitle: MongoDB Relations, Indexes and SQL vs NoSQL
lessons.description: Model related data in MongoDB with Mongoose references and populate, add indexes for the queries you really run, and learn when SQL fits better than NoSQL.

content.text: Real data is connected. A user writes posts, a customer places orders, an employee belongs to a department. How you store those connections decides how simple your queries are and how fast the app is. This lesson covers the choices you have in MongoDB with Mongoose, the indexes that keep queries fast, and an honest comparison with SQL databases, which interviewers love to ask about.
SQL and NoSQL in plain words

A **SQL** database, such as PostgreSQL or MySQL, stores data in tables with fixed columns, and connects tables with keys and **joins**. It is strong when data is highly connected and correctness matters, for example banking, bookings and inventory, because it supports strict rules and multi-table transactions. A **NoSQL** document database, such as MongoDB, stores flexible JSON-like documents in collections. It is comfortable when records have varied shapes, when the data is read as a whole document, and when the structure changes often. Neither is better in general. A good answer in an interview is: *it depends on the shape of the data and the queries*. Many companies use both.
Embed or reference?

In MongoDB you choose for each relation. **Embedding** puts the related data inside the document, for example the address inside the user. One read returns everything, and it is the right choice when the child data is small, belongs to one parent and is always read together. **Referencing** stores the id of the other document, like a foreign key. Use it when the data is large, grows without limit, or is shared. A post has an author and may have thousands of comments, so the post holds the author's id and the comments live in their own collection. A document cannot grow beyond 16 MB, so never embed something that can grow forever.

The `author` field of a post is an `ObjectId` that points at a `User`. With a connection you replace it by the real user using **populate**, as shown in the comment at the bottom: `Post.findById(id).populate('author', 'name email')`. Populate runs a second query behind the scenes, so use it on purpose, ask only for the fields you need, and avoid it inside loops. Use `.lean()` for read-only lists; it returns plain objects and skips Mongoose's extra work, which is faster.
Validation in the schema

The schema is also your first line of validation. The post requires a title of at most 120 characters, trims spaces, lowercases tags, limits `status` to two words with `enum`, and fills in a default. The next file runs those rules **without a database**, since validation happens in memory, and prints the result.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Install what the lesson needs: `npm install mongoose`.
Save both files and run `node db24-check.js`. No database is needed for this check.

content.text:
Errors on: [ 'author', 'title' ]
Tags cleaned: [ 'js', 'node' ]
Default status: draft
User errors on: [ 'name' ]
Email lowercased: asha@example.com
Post indexes: [ 'author+createdAt', 'status+tags', 'title+body' ]
In Mongoose 9, the synchronous `validateSync` method is deprecated, so the example awaits `validate()` and catches the error. Check the Mongoose release notes when you upgrade.
Indexes: the biggest speed-up you can buy

Without an index, MongoDB reads every document to answer a query, which is called a collection scan. That is fine for 500 documents and painful for 5 million. An **index** is a sorted lookup structure on one or more fields. The three indexes in the example match three real questions: *my posts, newest first* uses `author` and `createdAt`; *published posts with a tag* uses `status` and `tags`; and *search the text* uses a text index. The order of fields in a compound index matters, because it can only be used from the left. An index on `{ author: 1, createdAt: -1 }` helps a query on `author` alone, but not one on `createdAt` alone.

items: Create indexes for the queries you actually run, not for every field.
Every index makes writes a little slower and uses memory and disk.
Use `unique: true` for values that must not repeat, such as an email. It is enforced by an index.
Use `explain()` in the shell, or the Atlas performance tools, to confirm that a query uses its index.

content.text: A word about MongoDB Atlas

**MongoDB Atlas** is the hosted service from the makers of MongoDB. It has a free tier that is enough for learning. You create a cluster, add your server's IP address to the access list, create a database user, and copy the connection string into an environment variable such as `MONGODB_URI`. Never write that string in your code. Atlas clusters are replica sets, which is why transactions work there, as the next lesson shows.

The code in this lesson was syntax-checked, but the queries that need a running MongoDB, such as populate and the index speed-up, needs a service that was not available when the lesson was written, so that part was not run. The parts that do not need the service were run and their tests passed. Check the current documentation of the library before you rely on a detail.
Your task

items: Add a `Comment` model that references both a post and a user, with an index for `post` and `createdAt`.
Add a `slug` field to `Post` with `unique: true` and see how the index list changes.
Write down one thing that you would embed and one that you would reference in your own project, and say why.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The check prints the same six lines.
You can explain embed versus reference using the 16 MB limit.
You can explain why `{ author, createdAt }` does not help a query on `createdAt` alone.

steps.say: A post stores only the id of its author, so the user data is not copied everywhere.
populate asks for the user in a second query and puts the result in place of the id.
The user document is read from its own collection.
Indexes decide whether those lookups take microseconds or scan the whole collection.

faqs.q: When should I choose SQL instead of MongoDB?
faqs.a: When data is strongly connected, needs strict rules and multi-table transactions, or you do a lot of reporting with joins. MongoDB suits flexible documents read as a whole.

faqs.q: Does populate use a join?
faqs.a: No. Mongoose runs a separate query for the referenced documents and combines the results. For database-side joins use the $lookup stage of aggregation.

faqs.q: How many indexes are too many?
faqs.a: Each one slows writes and uses memory. Keep only the indexes your real queries use, and drop unused ones.

quiz.q: When should you reference instead of embed?
options: When the related data is large, shared or grows without limit
When the data is tiny and always read together

quiz.q: What does populate do?
options: Replaces a stored id with the referenced document using another query

quiz.q: An index on { author: 1, createdAt: -1 } helps a query on which field alone?
quiz.explain: A compound index is used from the left.

lessons.title: MongoDB Aggregation Pipelines and Transactions in Node
lessons.metaTitle: MongoDB Aggregation and Transactions
lessons.description: Use MongoDB aggregation stages like match, group, sort and lookup to build reports, and use transactions so several writes succeed together or not at all.

content.text: Sooner or later someone asks a question that no simple `find` can answer: *Who are our top five customers this year? How many orders came in each day? What is the average salary per department?* Doing that in JavaScript, by loading everything and looping, is slow and wastes memory. MongoDB can do the work inside the database with an **aggregation pipeline**. This lesson also covers **transactions**, which protect you when several changes must happen together.
A pipeline is a list of stages

Think of an assembly line. Documents enter the first stage, each stage transforms them, and the output of one becomes the input of the next. The most useful stages are: `$match` to keep only some documents, like `find`; `$group` to combine documents by a key and calculate totals; `$sort` and `$limit` to order and cut the list; `$lookup` to join another collection; `$unwind` to turn an array into separate documents; and `$project` to choose and rename the output fields.

Read the pipeline top to bottom. It keeps only paid orders of one year, groups them by customer while adding up `amountCents` and counting orders, sorts by total from largest to smallest, keeps five, joins the user documents to get names, flattens the joined array, and returns only the name, total and count. The first stage is always a `$match` if you can manage it, because it reduces the number of documents early, and a `$match` at the start can use an index.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Install what the lesson needs: `npm install mongoose`.
The pipeline is a plain array, so you can print it without a database. Save `db25-check.js` and run it.

content.text: $match -> $group -> $sort -> $limit -> $lookup -> $unwind -> $project

Amounts are stored in **cents as whole numbers**, not as decimals such as 19.99. Computers cannot store many decimal fractions exactly, so adding prices as floating-point numbers drifts by tiny amounts. Whole numbers in the smallest unit stay exact. Convert to rupees or dollars only when you show the value.
Why transactions exist

Imagine moving stock from one warehouse to another. You subtract from the first and add to the second. If the server crashes between the two writes, the stock has vanished. A **transaction** groups writes so that either all of them are saved or none are. In the example, `session.withTransaction` runs the callback, commits if it finishes, and rolls everything back if it throws. The first update also contains the condition `stock: { $gte: quantity }`, so checking that there is enough stock and subtracting it happen in one step. That prevents two simultaneous requests from both thinking there is enough.

MongoDB transactions need a replica set. MongoDB Atlas always is one. A plain local `mongod` is not, unless you start it as one, so the example fails on a default local install with an error about transactions. This is expected, not a bug in your code.
When you do not need a transaction

In MongoDB, a change to **one document** is atomic, even if it touches many fields. So if you design the data so that things that must change together live in one document, you often need no transaction at all. Use `$inc`, `$push` and `findOneAndUpdate` with a condition for counters and stock. Reach for a transaction when a rule really spans several documents, as with transfers, bookings and payments. Transactions cost performance, so keep them short and never call a slow external API inside one.

items: Put `$match` first and `$project` last.
Store money as integers in the smallest unit.
Use conditional updates, such as `stock >= quantity`, to avoid race conditions.
Use a transaction when several documents must change together, and keep it short.

content.text: The code in this lesson was syntax-checked, but the pipeline and the transaction, which need a running MongoDB replica set, needs a service that was not available when the lesson was written, so that part was not run. The parts that do not need the service were run and their tests passed. Check the current documentation of the library before you rely on a detail.
Your task

items: Write a pipeline that counts orders per day for the last 30 days.
Add a `$facet` stage that returns both the top five and the overall total.
Write a transaction that creates an order and reduces stock, and make it fail on purpose to see the rollback.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You can name the seven stages in the example and say what each does.
You can explain why the stock check and the update are one operation.
You can say what a replica set has to do with transactions.

steps.say: The first stage keeps only the documents that matter and can use an index.
The group stage combines documents by customer and adds up the amounts.
Sort and limit keep the five biggest customers.
Lookup joins the names and project shapes the final result for the API.

faqs.q: Is aggregation faster than doing the work in JavaScript?
faqs.a: Usually yes, because the database works close to the data and returns only the result, instead of sending every document to your server.

faqs.q: Why store money as cents?
faqs.a: Decimal fractions cannot always be stored exactly as floating-point numbers, so whole numbers in the smallest unit keep totals exact.

faqs.q: Do I need transactions for every write?
faqs.a: No. A write to a single document is already atomic. Use transactions only when several documents must change together.

quiz.q: Which stage keeps only matching documents, like find?
Why store money as whole numbers of cents?
options: Decimal fractions cannot always be stored exactly as floating-point numbers

quiz.q: What do MongoDB transactions need?
options: A replica set, such as MongoDB Atlas

lessons.title: Validate Requests with Zod, and Meet Prisma with PostgreSQL
lessons.metaTitle: Zod Validation, Prisma and PostgreSQL
lessons.description: Validate and clean request data with Zod in an Express middleware, then see how Prisma and PostgreSQL model the same data with a schema file and typed queries.

content.text: Everything that enters your server from outside is untrusted: the body, the query string, the headers and the URL parameters. If you use it without checking, you get crashes at best and security holes at worst. **Validation** means checking that the data has the right shape and obeys your rules before the rest of your code sees it. This lesson uses **Zod**, a popular schema library, and then introduces **Prisma** and **PostgreSQL**, which are the usual next step for people who want a SQL database.
One schema, three jobs

A Zod schema describes the shape of data, the rules, and, in TypeScript, its type. It can also **clean** data as it checks: `trim` removes spaces, `toLowerCase` normalises an email, and `z.coerce.number()` turns the text `"25"` from a form into the number 25. The registration schema below shows all of these, and the `validate` function turns any schema into an Express middleware.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Install what the lesson needs: `npm install express zod`.
Save the file as `zod.js`. For the test, install `npm install -D supertest`.

content.text: The middleware calls `safeParse`, which never throws and returns either `success: true` with the cleaned data or a list of issues. On failure it sends **422** with one message per field, so the front end can show each message beside the right input. On success it replaces `req.body` with the cleaned value, so later code never sees the raw input. Use the same idea for `req.query` and `req.params`: a `page` that is not a number should be a 422, not an internal error.

The test sends a good body, a body with several mistakes, and a body with extra fields, and checks the replies. Zod removes unknown keys by default in an object schema, which protects you from **mass assignment**: a client adding `"role": "admin"` to a registration body. Always list the fields you accept. Never pass `req.body` directly to `User.create`.

Validation on the server is not optional, even if the front end also validates. The front end is for helping users. The server is for protecting the system, because anyone can send requests without using your front end.
Meeting PostgreSQL

**PostgreSQL**, often called Postgres, is a free, mature SQL database. Data lives in tables with typed columns. Related tables are connected by a foreign key, and a **join** combines them in a query. It enforces rules in the database itself, such as `NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE` and foreign keys, so even a bug in your code cannot store an order for a customer that does not exist. That strictness is a major reason why companies choose it for payments, bookings and accounts.
Prisma: a schema file and typed queries

**Prisma** is a tool that sits between Node and the database. You describe your models in one `schema.prisma` file. Prisma then generates a client with functions such as `prisma.user.create` and `prisma.post.findMany`, and creates the tables for you with *migrations*, which are versioned scripts that change the database step by step. With TypeScript you get autocomplete and compile-time errors for wrong field names.

Compare the model with the Mongoose model in lesson 29. The ideas are the same, a user and many posts, but here the relation is declared in the schema, the database enforces it, and you fetch related data with `include`. The common workflow is: edit `schema.prisma`, run `npx prisma migrate dev` to create and apply a migration, then use the client in your code. In production you apply migrations with `npx prisma migrate deploy`.

The code in this lesson was syntax-checked, but Prisma and PostgreSQL, which need a running database server and a generated client, needs a service that was not available when the lesson was written, so that part was not run. The parts that do not need the service were run and their tests passed. Check the current documentation of the library before you rely on a detail.

Prisma changes between major versions, including how the client is generated and configured, so follow the current official guide when you set it up, and treat the files above as the idea rather than a copy-paste recipe. The Zod example was run and its tests pass.

items: Validate `body`, `query` and `params` at the edge of every route.
Accept only listed fields and ignore the rest.
Return 422 with messages per field.
Keep validation schemas in their own files and reuse them in tests and documentation.

content.text: Your task

items: Write a `loginSchema` and a `createPostSchema` with a maximum title length.
Validate `req.query` for a list route with `page` and `limit`.
Write the Prisma model for `Order` and `OrderItem` with a one-to-many relation.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: A body with `role: "admin"` does not reach your handler with the role.
A bad email returns 422 with a message for the email field only.
You can say two reasons why teams pick PostgreSQL.

steps.say: Everything in the request is treated as untrusted text.
The schema checks the shape, trims and converts values, and drops unknown fields.
Only the cleaned result reaches the handler. Errors stop here with a 422.
The handler saves it, and a strict database such as Postgres checks the rules again.

faqs.q: Why validate on the server if the front end already does?
faqs.a: Anyone can call your API without your front end, so only the server can protect your data.

faqs.q: Should I choose Prisma or Mongoose?
faqs.a: Mongoose is the natural choice with MongoDB. Prisma is a strong choice with PostgreSQL or MySQL, especially with TypeScript.

faqs.q: What is a migration?
faqs.a: A versioned script that changes the database structure step by step, so every environment can reach the same structure.
