options: Anyone can call the API without your front end

quiz.q: Which status code fits well-formed data that breaks your rules?
What is a Prisma migration?
options: A versioned script that changes the database structure step by step

lessons.title: Access and Refresh Tokens, Logout and Role-Based Access Control
lessons.metaTitle: Refresh Tokens, Logout and Role Access
lessons.description: Build login with short-lived access tokens and rotating refresh tokens, support real logout, and protect admin routes with role checks that clients cannot fake.

content.text: An earlier lesson showed how to log a user in and give them a JSON Web Token (JWT). That works, but it leaves two problems. If the token lasts a week and someone steals it, the thief has a week. If the token lasts five minutes, the user must log in again every five minutes. Real systems solve this with **two tokens**. This lesson builds that system with a tested example, and then adds **roles**, so that normal users and admins are treated differently.
Access token and refresh token

items: The **access token** is a short-lived JWT, for example 15 minutes. The client sends it with every request. If it leaks, the damage ends quickly.
The **refresh token** lives longer, for example 7 days. It is used only to ask for a new access token, and it is never sent to normal routes.
The server **stores a hash** of each refresh token, so it can see which ones are valid and can cancel one at any time.
On every refresh, the server issues a **new** refresh token and cancels the old one. This is called **rotation**.

content.text: Why store anything on the server when JWTs are meant to be stateless? Because *logout* needs memory. A JWT alone cannot be cancelled before it expires. By keeping the refresh tokens in a database, you can delete one on logout, delete all of them when a user changes their password, and notice **reuse**: if a refresh token that was already rotated is used again, someone has a copy, and you can end the whole session family. The access token stays stateless and fast, and the refresh token is where you keep control.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Install what the lesson needs: `npm install express jsonwebtoken bcryptjs`.
Save the code as `auth.js`. The test needs `npm install -D supertest`.

content.text: Walk through the routes. `/register` hashes the password with bcrypt, and the code never stores the plain password. `/login` compares the hash and returns both tokens. `/refresh` checks that the presented refresh token is on the list of valid hashed tokens, removes it, and returns a new pair. `/logout` removes the token. `/me` is protected by `requireAuth`, which verifies the access token. `/admin/stats` is protected twice, first by `requireAuth` and then by `requireRole('admin')`.
Roles: decide on the server

**Authentication** asks *who are you?* **Authorization** asks *what may you do?* The simplest model is **role-based access control (RBAC)**: each user has a role such as `user`, `editor` or `admin`, and each route lists the roles that may use it. The rule that matters most is where the role comes from. It must come from your database, put into the token by your server, and **never from the request body**. In the code, `/register` ignores any `role` that the client sends. If it copied the field, anyone could register as an admin with one extra line of JSON.
The test registers a user, logs in, refreshes, shows that the old refresh token no longer works, logs out, and checks that a normal user gets 403 on the admin route. It passes.
Where should the client keep the tokens?

There is no perfect answer. A refresh token in an **httpOnly cookie** cannot be read by JavaScript on the page, which protects it from XSS theft, but a cookie needs CSRF protection, which lesson 35 covers. A token in `localStorage` is easy to use but any injected script can read it. A common compromise is to keep the access token in memory and the refresh token in an httpOnly, secure, sameSite cookie.
This example keeps users and tokens in memory so that you can run it without a database. In a real app, store them in your database, and delete expired refresh tokens regularly.

The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.
Your task

items: Make the refresh token travel in an httpOnly cookie instead of the JSON body.
Add an `editor` role and a route that both editors and admins can use.
Add a `/logout-all` route that removes every refresh token for the user.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The old refresh token fails after it is used once.
A user cannot make themselves admin by sending `role` in the body.
You can explain why logout needs the server to remember something.

steps.say: A correct password gives the client two tokens.
The short-lived access token is sent with each request. If stolen, it soon expires.
The refresh token is only used to get a new pair, and the server remembers its hash so it can cancel it.
Admin routes check the role that the server put in the token, never one sent by the client.

faqs.q: Why not make one long-lived access token?
faqs.a: If it leaks, the thief has access for the whole time, and you cannot cancel it. Short access tokens limit the damage.

faqs.q: What is refresh token rotation?
faqs.a: Each use of a refresh token returns a new one and cancels the old one. If an old token appears again, you know it was copied.

faqs.q: Where does the user role come from?
faqs.a: From your database, set by your server code. Never trust a role field sent by the client.

quiz.q: Why is the access token short-lived?
options: Short tokens are faster to sign
If it leaks, the damage ends quickly

quiz.q: What is refresh token rotation?
options: Sending the token in a cookie
Each use returns a new refresh token and cancels the old one

quiz.q: Where must a user role come from?
options: Your database, set by your server
A cookie the client can edit

lessons.title: Forgot Password, Email Verification and OTP Login with Nodemailer
lessons.metaTitle: Password Reset, Email Verification and OTP
lessons.description: Build email verification, a safe forgot and reset password flow, and one-time passcodes with expiry and attempt limits, sending mail through Nodemailer.

content.text: Every account system needs the same three side features: confirm that an email address is real, let people recover a lost password, and sometimes log in with a one-time code. They look simple, and they are some of the most commonly attacked features, because an attacker who takes over the reset flow takes over the account. This lesson builds all three with a fake mailer, so you can run and test it without sending real email.
The pattern behind all three

Each feature uses a **secret token that is sent by email**. The server generates a long random value, stores only its **hash** with an expiry time, and emails the plain value as a link or code. When the user comes back with it, the server hashes what it received, compares, checks that it has not expired, and **deletes it so it cannot be used twice**. Storing the hash means that someone who reads your database cannot use the tokens. Use `crypto.randomBytes(32)` for tokens, never `Math.random()`, which is predictable.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Install what the lesson needs: `npm install express`.
Save the code as `account.js`. The test needs `npm install -D supertest`.

content.text: Email verification

When someone registers, the account starts as unverified, and the server emails a link that contains a token. `/verify` checks the token and marks the email as verified. This stops people from registering with someone else's address, and keeps fake accounts out of your email list. Decide what an unverified user may do. Most apps let them log in but block sensitive actions until they verify.
Forgot and reset password

Look closely at `/forgot-password`. It answers with the **same message** whether or not the email exists: *If that address has an account, we have sent a link*. If it said *no such user*, an attacker could test thousands of addresses and learn which people use your site. The reset token expires after 15 minutes, works once, and, in a full system, should also cancel the user's refresh tokens when the password changes, so a thief who had a session is thrown out. The reset link should lead to a page on **your** domain. Never build it from the `Host` header of the request, because an attacker can send a fake one and get your server to email a link that points to their site.
One-time passcodes

An **OTP** is a short code, usually six digits, that is sent by email or SMS and proves the user has access to that address or phone. Short codes are easy to guess, so three limits are required: a short life such as five minutes, one use, and a limit on wrong attempts. With six digits there are one million possibilities, so without a limit an attacker could simply try them all. The example locks the code after five wrong guesses. Generate it with `crypto.randomInt`, and store its hash.

The test uses a fake mailer that remembers the messages, and a fake clock that the test can move forward. That is why `createApp` takes `mailer` and `now` as arguments: two small pieces of dependency injection that make time-based rules testable in milliseconds, with no waiting.
Sending real email with Nodemailer

**Nodemailer** is the usual Node package for sending mail. You create a transport with the details of an SMTP server, and call `sendMail` with `from`, `to`, `subject` and `html`. For development, use a service that catches mail without delivering it, such as Mailtrap or Ethereal. For production, use a proper provider such as Amazon SES, Brevo, Postmark or SendGrid, and set up **SPF, DKIM and DMARC** records on your domain, or your messages will land in spam. Send email in the background rather than inside the request, so a slow mail server does not slow your API.

The code in this lesson was syntax-checked, but sending real mail through Nodemailer, which needs an SMTP account, needs a service that was not available when the lesson was written, so that part was not run. The parts that do not need the service were run and their tests passed. Check the current documentation of the library before you rely on a detail.
Your task

items: Add rate limiting to `/forgot-password`, three requests per hour per address.
Cancel all refresh tokens from lesson 32 when a password is reset.
Change the OTP length to 8 digits and write a test for the new lock behaviour.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Unknown and known emails get the identical reply.
A reset token cannot be used twice or after 15 minutes.
The OTP locks after five wrong tries.

steps.say: The user asks to verify, reset or log in with a code. The reply is the same for any address.
The server creates a random token and stores only its hash and an expiry.
The plain token goes to the email address, not back in the HTTP reply.
When it comes back, the hash matches, the time is checked and the token is deleted.

faqs.q: Why show the same message for unknown emails?
faqs.a: Different messages let an attacker discover which email addresses have accounts. One identical message hides that.

faqs.q: Why store a hash of the reset token?
faqs.a: If someone reads your database, they still cannot use the tokens, the same way a hashed password is protected.

faqs.q: Is a six-digit OTP safe?
faqs.a: Only with a short expiry, one use and a limit on wrong tries. Without a limit, all one million codes can be tried.

quiz.q: Why show the same message whether or not the email exists?
options: So attackers cannot discover which emails have accounts

quiz.q: Why store only a hash of the reset token?
options: A leaked database cannot be used to reset accounts

quiz.q: What limits make a six-digit OTP safe enough?
options: Short expiry, one use and a limit on wrong tries

lessons.title: Cookies, Sessions and Sign In with Google (OAuth)
lessons.metaTitle: Cookies, Sessions and Google Sign-In
lessons.description: Understand cookies and server sessions, set secure cookie flags, compare sessions with JWT, and add Sign in with Google by verifying the ID token on the server.

content.text: JWTs are not the only way to remember a user. Many sites, including big ones, use **sessions**, which are older, simple and very solid. You also meet **cookies** everywhere, and nearly every product wants a **Sign in with Google** button. This lesson explains how these fit together, with a tested session example and the server side of Google sign-in.
Cookies in one minute

A **cookie** is a small piece of text that the server asks the browser to keep and to send back with every later request to the same site. The server sets it with a `Set-Cookie` header. Four flags decide how safe it is. **httpOnly** hides it from JavaScript on the page, so a script injected by an attacker cannot read it. **secure** sends it only over HTTPS. **sameSite** (`lax` or `strict`) stops the browser from sending it along with requests that start on other sites, which blocks most CSRF attacks. **maxAge** or **expires** says how long it lives.
A session in practice

With sessions, the cookie holds only a random **session id**, and the real data lives on the server. When a request arrives, the server looks up the id and knows who the user is. Logging out is easy, because you delete the record. The example below goes a little further and signs the cookie, so that a client that changes the value is detected.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Install what the lesson needs: `npm install express cookie-parser`.
Save the code as `sessions.js`. The test needs `npm install -D supertest`.

content.text: The test logs in, reads the protected `/me` route using the cookie, logs out, and shows that the same cookie no longer works. Notice that the cookie is `httpOnly` and `sameSite`, and in production it must also be `secure`.
Sessions or JWT?

items: **Sessions** are simple, easy to cancel, and work well for a website where the front end and the back end share a domain. They need shared storage, such as Redis or a database, once you run more than one server.
**JWT** is handy when many separate services or mobile apps must check the user without a shared store. It is harder to cancel, which is why lesson 32 adds refresh tokens.
Many teams use sessions for websites and JWT with refresh tokens for mobile apps and public APIs. Neither is wrong. State why you chose one.

content.text: The default in-memory session storage of many libraries is only for development. It loses everything when the server restarts and cannot be shared between servers. Use Redis or a database in production.
Sign in with Google

Sign in with Google uses **OAuth 2.0** and **OpenID Connect**. You never see the user's Google password. The browser shows Google's button, Google asks the user to agree, and then gives the browser a signed **ID token**. The front end sends that token to your server. Your server must **verify** it, not just decode it: check the signature against Google's public keys, check that the audience is your own client ID, check that it has not expired, and check that `email_verified` is true. The `google-auth-library` package does these steps for you.

After verification, you look for a user with that Google id or email. If one exists, log them in. If not, create an account without a password. Then issue your own session or tokens, exactly as for a password login, so the rest of your app does not need to know which method was used. Link accounts by the **verified** email carefully: if you trust an unverified email, an attacker can claim somebody else's account.

The code in this lesson was syntax-checked, but Google sign-in, which needs a Google Cloud OAuth client and a real token, needs a service that was not available when the lesson was written, so that part was not run. The parts that do not need the service were run and their tests passed. Check the current documentation of the library before you rely on a detail.
Your task

items: Add `secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production'` to the cookie options.
Make the session expire after 30 minutes of no activity.
Write the route that receives the Google token, calls `verifyGoogleToken` and starts a session.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: A changed cookie value is refused.
Logging out makes the old cookie useless.
You can say what `httpOnly`, `secure` and `sameSite` each protect against.

steps.say: A successful login, by password or by a verified Google token, starts a session.
The server stores the data and creates a random session id.
Only the id travels in a signed, httpOnly, sameSite cookie.
The browser sends it back, and the server looks up the record. Deleting the record is logout.

faqs.q: Can I use a session and JWT in the same app?
faqs.a: Yes. Many teams use sessions for the website and JWT with refresh tokens for the mobile app.

faqs.q: Do I get the user's Google password?
faqs.a: No. Google gives you a signed ID token that says who the user is, and your server verifies it.

faqs.q: Why must I verify the Google token on the server?
faqs.a: The front end can be bypassed. Only a server-side check of the signature, audience and expiry proves the token is real.

quiz.q: What does the httpOnly cookie flag do?
options: Hides the cookie from JavaScript on the page

quiz.q: What must your server do with a Google ID token?
options: Verify its signature, audience, expiry and email_verified

quiz.q: What is an advantage of sessions over JWT?
options: They need no storage at all
Logging out is easy because you delete the server record

lessons.title: Web Attacks: XSS, CSRF, NoSQL Injection, Sanitisation and Brute Force
lessons.metaTitle: XSS, CSRF, NoSQL Injection and Brute Force
lessons.description: Learn how XSS, CSRF, NoSQL injection and brute force work, and defend against each in Express with escaping, a CSRF token, key stripping and lockouts.

content.text: Attackers do not need to be clever to break most web apps. They try the same few well-known tricks on thousands of sites, and the sites that did not prepare lose. The good news is that the defence against each trick is also well known. This lesson explains four common attacks in plain words, shows a small defence for each, and tests every one. It is for defence only: the examples show how to stop attacks on your own code.
1. Cross-site scripting (XSS)

**XSS** happens when your site shows text that a user typed, and the browser treats it as code. If a comment contains a script tag and you place it into a page unchanged, the script runs in every visitor's browser, and it can steal sessions or perform actions as them. The defence is to **escape output**: turn the characters that have a special meaning in HTML, such as `<`, `>`, `&` and quotes, into harmless entities. Modern front-end frameworks such as React do this by default. The danger returns when you build HTML strings yourself, or when you use features with names like `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` or `innerHTML`. If you must show user HTML, clean it with a library such as DOMPurify.
2. Cross-site request forgery (CSRF)

**CSRF** works because browsers attach cookies automatically. If you are logged in to your bank in one tab and visit a bad page in another, the bad page can make your browser send a request to the bank, and the cookie goes along. The defences are: `sameSite` cookies, which already stop most cases, and a **CSRF token**. In the *double-submit cookie* method the server sets a random value in a cookie and requires the same value in a header. A page on another site can make the browser send the cookie, but it cannot read it, so it cannot copy it into the header. APIs that use an `Authorization` header with a token instead of cookies are not exposed to CSRF in the same way.
3. NoSQL injection

With MongoDB, an attacker does not need SQL. If your login code is `User.findOne({ email: req.body.email, password: req.body.password })` and the client sends JSON such as `{"email": "a@b.com", "password": {"$ne": null}}`, the query asks for a user whose password is *not null*, and the check passes without knowing the password. The defence is to never pass raw input into a query. Validate the type, since an email must be a string, with Zod from lesson 31, and strip keys that start with `$` or contain a dot.
4. Brute force

Automated tools can try thousands of passwords per minute. Defences are: a slow password hash, bcrypt or Argon2, which makes every guess expensive; **rate limiting**, such as the `express-rate-limit` package; and a **lockout** that counts failures per account and per address, and pauses further tries for a time. Be careful with lockouts: an attacker can lock out a real user on purpose, so a temporary pause is kinder than a permanent block.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Install what the lesson needs: `npm install express`.
Save the code as `defences.js`. The test needs `npm install -D supertest`.

content.text:
ok 1 - xss escaping
ok 2 - operator injection is removed
ok 3 - csrf double-submit cookie
ok 4 - brute force lock

In the CSRF test, three requests are made. One carries the cookie but not the header, and gets **403**. One carries both, and passes. One comes from a client that has no cookie, as a hostile site would, and gets **403**. The brute-force test makes five failures, sees the lock, and then moves the fake clock past the lock time to see the account unlock.

These small helpers show the idea. For production, also use proven libraries: `helmet` for headers, `express-rate-limit` for limits, `csrf-csrf` or a similar maintained package for CSRF, and DOMPurify for user HTML. Check their current documentation.

items: Escape output, and validate input.
Never put raw request data into a database query.
Use `sameSite` cookies and a CSRF token wherever cookies authenticate.
Slow down and limit login attempts.

content.text: The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.
Your task

items: Write a test that sends a body with `{ "$gt": "" }` as a password and confirm that it is cleaned.
Add `express-rate-limit` to the login route, five attempts per 15 minutes.
Try printing user text into an HTML string without escaping, and then fix it.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: All four tests pass.
You can describe each attack in one sentence.
You can say why a CSRF token cannot be copied by another site.

steps.say: XSS: user text becomes code in the page. Escape it on the way out.
CSRF: the browser sends cookies for you. A secret header the attacker cannot read stops it.
Injection: query operators hide in the JSON. Check the types and remove $ keys.
Brute force: many guesses. Hash slowly, limit requests and pause after repeated failures.

faqs.q: Does React protect me from XSS?
faqs.a: It escapes text by default. You are exposed again if you use dangerouslySetInnerHTML or build HTML strings yourself.

faqs.q: Do I need CSRF protection for a token API?
faqs.a: If authentication uses an Authorization header that the browser does not attach by itself, CSRF is not the same problem. If it uses cookies, yes.

faqs.q: Is MongoDB safe from injection?
faqs.a: Not automatically. Raw request data in a query can carry operators such as $ne, so validate types and strip operator keys.

quiz.q: What is the main defence against XSS?
options: Escape output so user text is not treated as code

quiz.q: How does a double-submit CSRF token stop another site?
options: The other site can send the cookie but cannot read it to copy it into a header

quiz.q: How can { "password": { "$ne": null } } break a login?
options: The query asks for a password that is not null, so it matches

lessons.title: Production Security: Secrets, HTTPS, JWT Best Practices, Helmet and Audits
lessons.metaTitle: Production Security: Secrets, HTTPS, Helmet
lessons.description: Harden an Express app: validate secrets at start, set secure headers with Helmet, use HTTPS, follow JWT best practices and audit your dependencies.

content.text: The last lesson was about attacks on your logic. This lesson is about the **settings and habits** around your code that decide whether an attack succeeds: where secrets live, whether traffic is encrypted, which headers you send, and whether the packages you installed have known holes. None of it is difficult, and all of it is routinely skipped. A short checklist done once is worth more than any clever code.
Secrets and environment variables

items: Keep secrets such as database passwords, JWT keys and API keys **out of Git**. Put them in environment variables, loaded from a `.env` file in development, and make sure `.env` is listed in `.gitignore`.
If a secret is ever committed, treat it as stolen, even if you delete it afterwards, because Git keeps history. Change it at the provider.
Use a different secret in each environment, and make them long and random.
On a server, set them in the host's settings or a secrets manager rather than a file in the project.

content.text: Read your configuration **once, at start**, and check it. The example below uses Zod to require a `JWT_SECRET` of at least 32 characters, accepts only three values for `NODE_ENV`, and turns the port into a number. If something is wrong the app refuses to start with a clear message, which is far better than starting and failing at three in the morning.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Install what the lesson needs: `npm install express helmet jsonwebtoken zod`.
Save the code as `hardening.js`. The test needs `npm install -D supertest`.

content.text: JWT best practices

The two functions `signToken` and `verifyToken` hold the rules. Fix the **algorithm** in both places. Some older attacks worked because a library accepted whatever algorithm the token claimed, including `none`, which means no signature at all. Set an **issuer** and an **audience** so a token made for another service is not accepted by yours. Use a **short expiry**. Keep the payload small and never put secrets in it, because a JWT is signed but **not encrypted**; anyone can read it. The test proves that a token with the `none` algorithm, a token with the wrong audience and a token signed with another secret are all refused.

ok 1 - helmet headers and no x-powered-by
ok 2 - environment is checked at start
ok 3 - token checks: alg none, wrong audience and wrong secret are refused
Helmet: security headers in one line

**Helmet** is a middleware that sets a group of HTTP headers that tell browsers to behave more safely. Among them are `Strict-Transport-Security`, which asks browsers to use HTTPS only, `X-Content-Type-Options`, which stops a browser from guessing file types, and a basic `Content-Security-Policy`, which limits where scripts may load from. You add it with `app.use(helmet())`. If your front end loads scripts or images from other sites, you may need to adjust the policy, so test the pages after turning it on.
HTTPS and CORS

**HTTPS** encrypts the traffic between the browser and your server, so passwords and tokens cannot be read on the way. Production sites must use it. Lesson 48 shows how to get a free certificate with Let's Encrypt. **CORS** is a different matter: it controls which *websites* may call your API from a browser. Do not use `origin: '*'` together with cookies. List the exact origins that you trust.
Dependencies

Your app contains thousands of packages that you did not write. Run `npm audit` regularly to list known problems, update packages in small steps, commit `package-lock.json`, and use `npm ci` in builds so that exactly the locked versions are installed. Remove packages that you do not use. Turn on Dependabot or a similar service to receive update pull requests. A package that is no longer maintained is a risk even when it has no known bug today.
Treat this lesson as a starting checklist, not a complete security programme. Large or regulated systems need reviews, monitoring and testing by security specialists.

The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.
Your task

items: Start the app without `JWT_SECRET` and read the error.
Run `npm audit` in your project and read the report.
Add `helmet()` to an existing app and check the response headers in your browser's network tab.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The app refuses to start with a missing or short secret.
A token with the wrong audience is refused.
Your `.env` file is in `.gitignore`.

steps.say: Secrets live in the environment, are never committed and are checked at start.
Tokens are signed and verified with a fixed algorithm, issuer, audience and a short life.
Helmet sets safe headers and HTTPS encrypts everything in transit.
Packages are audited and locked, so known holes are fixed before an attacker finds them.

faqs.q: Is a JWT encrypted?
faqs.a: No. It is signed, so it cannot be changed, but anyone can read its contents. Never put secrets in it.

faqs.q: I committed a secret by mistake. What now?
faqs.a: Treat it as public. Change it at the provider first, then remove it from the code. Deleting it from Git history alone is not enough.

faqs.q: Does Helmet make my app secure?
faqs.a: It removes some easy risks by setting headers. It does not replace validation, authentication and updates.

quiz.q: You committed a secret to Git by mistake. What first?
options: Change it at the provider, because Git keeps history

quiz.q: Is a JWT encrypted?
options: No, it is signed but anyone can read it

quiz.q: What does npm audit check?

lessons.title: Clean Architecture in Express: Repository, Service, Dependency Injection and SOLID
lessons.metaTitle: Express Architecture: Service, Repository
lessons.description: Organise a growing Express app into controller, service and repository layers, use dependency injection to test rules without HTTP, and apply SOLID.

content.text: Lesson 24 split an app into store, controller and routes. That is enough for a small API. As an app grows, a new problem appears: **business rules**. Rules such as "a task title cannot be empty" or "a finished task cannot be edited" end up inside route handlers, mixed with HTTP details, and then they are hard to test and easy to copy by mistake. The cure is one more layer, and a habit of passing in what a piece of code needs instead of creating it inside.
Four layers, each with one job

items: **Controller:** speaks HTTP. It reads the request, calls the service and turns the result into a status code and JSON. It contains no business rules.
**Service:** holds the **rules** of your application. It knows nothing about requests, responses or the database engine.
**Repository:** the only place that talks to the database. It offers methods such as `findById` and `save`.
**Errors:** the service raises its own kinds of error, for example `NotFoundError` or `RuleError`, and one small mapper turns them into 404 or 409.

content.text: The direction of dependency matters. The controller depends on the service, and the service depends on a repository *interface*, but never the other way round. The service never imports Express and never imports Mongoose. That is why you could change from MongoDB to PostgreSQL by writing a new repository, and why the business rules stay untouched.
Dependency injection without a framework

Look at how `TaskService` is built: `new TaskService(repository)`. The service does not create its repository. It receives it. This is **dependency injection**, and in JavaScript it needs no special library, just constructor or function parameters. The place where everything is wired together, here `createApp`, is called the **composition root**. In a test you pass a memory repository, and in production you pass the real one.

The first test below does not use HTTP at all: it creates a service with a memory repository and calls its methods directly. It runs in a few milliseconds. The second test goes through HTTP with Supertest and checks that the error mapper gives the right status codes. Both pass.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Install what the lesson needs: `npm install express`.
Save the code as `layers.js`. The test needs `npm install -D supertest`.

content.text: SOLID, in one paragraph each
**SOLID** is a set of five design ideas that interviewers like to ask about. You do not need to memorise them as rules. They describe the same habits you just used.

items: **S, single responsibility:** a piece of code has one reason to change. The controller changes when the API shape changes, the service when the rules change, the repository when the database changes.
**O, open/closed:** you can add behaviour without editing working code. A new payment provider is a new file, not an edit of the old ones.
**L, Liskov substitution:** any repository that follows the same methods can replace another. The memory repository and the MongoDB repository are interchangeable.
**I, interface segregation:** keep contracts small. A service that only reads should not need a repository with ten write methods.
**D, dependency inversion:** depend on a contract, not on a concrete tool. The service depends on "a repository", not on Mongoose.

content.text: Do not over-build

Layers cost files and indirection. For a three-route API they are more than you need, and a pile of empty "manager" classes helps nobody. Add a layer when it solves a problem you have: rules scattered across handlers, tests that need a database, a plan to change the data store. **Clean architecture**, the name for pushing this idea all the way, is a direction, not a goal. Start simple, and refactor towards layers when the pain appears.

The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.
Your task

items: Add a `complete` rule to the service: a completed task cannot be completed again, and make it return 409.
Write a second repository that stores tasks in a JSON file and pass it to the service.
Write a service test with a fake repository that throws, and see how the error is handled.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The service test passes with no HTTP.
You can explain what the composition root is.
You can name the layer that you would change when moving from MongoDB to PostgreSQL.

steps.say: The controller turns an HTTP request into a plain method call.
The service applies the rules. It does not know about Express.
The repository is passed in, so tests use memory and production uses the database.
Rule errors are mapped to the right status code in one place.

faqs.q: Is dependency injection the same as using a framework like NestJS?
faqs.a: No. DI is just passing what a piece of code needs as a parameter. NestJS adds a container that does it for you, but you can do it by hand.

faqs.q: Do small projects need all these layers?
faqs.a: No. Add a layer when you feel the pain it solves, such as business rules duplicated in handlers or tests that need a database.

faqs.q: What is a composition root?
faqs.a: The single place where the app creates its parts and connects them, usually the file that builds the app.

quiz.q: What does the service layer contain?
options: The business rules, with no HTTP or database details

quiz.q: What is dependency injection in this lesson?
options: Passing what a class needs, such as a repository, as an argument

quiz.q: When should you add more layers?
options: When you feel the pain they solve, such as rules scattered in handlers

lessons.title: Error Handling and Logging in Express: Winston, Morgan and Request IDs
lessons.metaTitle: Express Error Handling and Logging
lessons.description: Build one reliable error system for Express: custom AppError classes, safe client messages, JSON logs with Winston, request logs with Morgan and request ids.

content.text: When something goes wrong in production, you cannot sit beside the server and watch. You have two sources of truth: the reply that the client received and the logs that your server wrote. If the reply leaks a stack trace, you have given attackers a map. If the logs are missing, you cannot find the cause. This lesson builds a small but complete system that gets both right.
Two audiences, two messages

Every error has two readers. The **client** needs to know what it can fix: "Item not found", "Email is invalid". The **developer** needs everything: the full message, the stack trace, the user and the request. The rule is simple: show client errors (status 400 to 499) to the client, and **hide the details of server errors** (500 and above), while writing them in full to the log. The custom `AppError` class carries a status code, a short code and a flag `expose` that says whether its message is safe to send.

Read the code from the top. `AppError` and its helpers `notFound` and `badRequest` are the errors that your own code throws on purpose. The error handler at the end decides: if the error is an `AppError` with a status below 500, send its message and code. For anything else, such as a crash from a bug or a library, log the full error and send only `Something went wrong`. In Express 5, a rejected promise in an async handler goes to this handler automatically, so you no longer need to wrap every route in `try/catch`.
Winston: structured logs

`console.log` is fine on your laptop and poor in production. **Winston** is a logging library with **levels** (`error`, `warn`, `info`, `debug`), timestamps and several outputs, called transports, such as the console, files or a cloud service. The example writes **JSON**, one object per line, because tools like Datadog, Grafana Loki or the ELK stack can search and graph JSON easily. Set the level from an environment variable, `LOG_LEVEL`, so you can turn on `debug` for a short time without changing code.
Morgan and request ids

**Morgan** writes one line for each request: method, URL, status and the time taken. Here its output is sent *into* Winston, so every log line goes to the same place in the same format. Each request also receives a unique **request id**, taken from the incoming `x-request-id` header or generated, and returned in the response. When a user reports a problem, ask for that id, search the logs for it, and you will find every line that belongs to that one request.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Install what the lesson needs: `npm install express winston morgan`.
Save the code as `errors.js`. The test needs `npm install -D supertest`.

content.text: ok 1 - client errors show their message, server errors hide it but are logged

items: Never log passwords, tokens, card numbers or full personal data. Remove them before logging.
Log at the right level: `error` for failures you must act on, `warn` for strange but survivable, `info` for normal events.
Watch the logs, or set up alerts. A log that nobody reads does not protect you.
Also handle the two global events, `unhandledRejection` and `uncaughtException`: log them and exit, and let your process manager restart the app, because the program may be in an unknown state.

content.text: Never rely on `console.log` for security events. Write logins, failures and permission denials to the structured log, because those lines are what you search after an incident.

lessons.title: Caching in Node: Memory Cache, Redis and the Cache-Aside Pattern
lessons.metaTitle: Caching in Node: Memory, Redis, Cache-Aside
lessons.description: Speed up a Node.js API with the cache-aside pattern, time-to-live expiry and invalidation, first with a memory cache and then with Redis for several servers.

content.text: The fastest database query is the one you do not run. **Caching** means keeping a copy of an answer close at hand, so the next person who asks the same question gets it at once. A product page that 10,000 people view an hour does not need 10,000 database queries, only a few. Caching is also famous for being hard, because a copy can become wrong. This lesson teaches the one pattern that you will use most, and the rules for keeping it honest.
The cache-aside pattern

*Cache-aside* works in three steps. First, look in the cache. If the answer is there, a **hit**, return it. If not, a **miss**, load it from the database, store it in the cache with a lifetime, and return it. Your code controls the cache, and the cache never needs to know about the database.

The file has two caches with the same three methods, `get`, `set` and `del`. `memoryCache` keeps values in a `Map` inside your process and can run anywhere. `redisCache` wraps a Redis client. Because both offer the same methods, `cachedProductService` works with either, which is dependency injection again. The lifetime, **time to live** (TTL), is in seconds, and after that the entry is considered expired and the next request refills it. The memory cache takes `now` as a parameter so that a test can move the clock instead of waiting.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Save the code as `cache.js`. The test uses only Node. For the Redis version you also need a Redis server and `npm install redis`.

content.text: ok 1 - hit, miss, expiry and invalidation

The test checks four things: the first read is a miss and goes to the database, the second is a hit and does not, the value expires after the TTL, and after the product is changed, its cache entry is **deleted** so that the next read loads the new value.
Memory cache or Redis?

A cache inside the process is the fastest and simplest, and it is fine for a single server and for data that can be a little different on each copy. But each copy of a server has its **own** cache, the cache disappears on restart, and deleting an entry on one copy does not delete it on the others. **Redis** is a separate, very fast, in-memory data store that all your copies share. It is also used for sessions, rate limiting counters, queues and real-time messaging, so it earns its place in most mid-sized systems.
The hard part: invalidation

items: **Use short TTLs** for data that is allowed to be slightly old, such as a product list. Even 30 seconds removes most of the load.
**Delete on change.** When you update or delete a record, delete its cache key at once, as the test does.
**Cache only what is safe to share.** Never cache one user's private data under a key that another user could hit.

**Beware of a stampede.** When a popular key expires, many requests may miss together and hit the database at the same moment. Short random variation in TTL, or a lock so that only one request refills it, reduces this.
**Measure.** Count hits and misses. A cache with a low hit rate is only extra complexity.

The parts that do not need the service were run and their tests passed. Check the current documentation of the library before you rely on a detail.
Your task

items: Add a `stats()` function to the memory cache that returns hits and misses.
Cache the result of a list route for 30 seconds, and clear it when a product is added.
Add a little random jitter to each TTL.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The second read does not call the database.
An update removes the old value from the cache.
You can explain why two servers cannot share a memory cache.

steps.say: A request asks for a product.
The service looks in the cache first. A hit returns at once.
On a miss it loads from the database and stores the value with a lifetime.
When the product changes, its cache entry is deleted so nobody sees old data.

faqs.q: What is TTL?
faqs.a: Time to live: how long a cached value is kept before it counts as expired and must be loaded again.

faqs.q: Is Redis a database?
faqs.a: It is an in-memory data store. It can save to disk, but it is mostly used for cache, sessions, counters and queues next to a main database.

faqs.q: What is cache invalidation?
faqs.a: Removing or refreshing a cached value when the original data changes, so users do not see old data.

quiz.q: What is the first step in cache-aside?
options: Look in the cache, and only on a miss load from the database

quiz.q: Why can two servers not share an in-memory cache?
options: Each process has its own memory

quiz.q: What should you do to a cache entry when the record is updated?

lessons.title: Background Jobs in Node: Queues, Retries, Scheduling and BullMQ
lessons.metaTitle: Background Jobs: Queues, Retries and BullMQ
lessons.description: Move slow work out of web requests with a job queue, retries and a dead-letter list, run scheduled tasks, and see how BullMQ and Redis do the same at scale.

content.text: Some work is too slow for a web request: sending 500 emails, making a PDF, resizing images, calling a slow API. If the user waits for it, the page feels broken and a timeout can kill the work half way. The answer is a **job queue**. The request puts a small description of the work on a list and replies at once. A separate **worker** takes the jobs one by one. This lesson shows the idea with a small queue that you can run, and then the production tool, **BullMQ**.
The idea in four words

items: **Producer:** your route. It calls `queue.add(data)` and returns immediately, usually with status **202 Accepted**.
**Queue:** a waiting list. In production it lives in Redis, so it survives a restart.
**Worker:** code that takes a job and does the slow work.
**Retries and dead letters:** if a job fails, try again after a delay. After the last attempt, move it to a **failed** list that a person can look at, instead of losing it.

content.text: `createQueue` takes a `handler`. `add` pushes a job and returns at once. The loop inside `run` takes jobs one at a time. When the handler throws, the job's attempt count goes up, it waits a little longer each time, and goes back on the list. After `maxAttempts` it is saved in `results.failed` with the error message. That behaviour, retry with growing delay and then a failed list, is exactly what real queue systems offer.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Save the code as `jobs.js`. The test uses only Node.

content.text:
ok 1 - jobs run, retry and end in the failed list
ok 2 - every() repeats and stops
Scheduled work

Some jobs are not triggered by a user but by the clock: send a daily report, delete expired tokens, back up the database. The simplest way in Node is `setInterval`, which the `every` helper wraps. Call `unref()` on the timer so that it does not keep the process alive on its own, and always return a stop function so that tests and shutdown can clean up. For schedules such as "every day at 02:00", use a cron expression with a library like `node-cron`, or better, the scheduler of your platform. If you run several copies of your app, make sure **only one** of them runs a scheduled job, or you will send every email several times.
BullMQ and Redis

A queue in the memory of your process has two flaws: jobs vanish when the process restarts, and you cannot run a worker on another machine. **BullMQ** keeps the jobs in Redis, so they survive restarts, several workers can share the load, and you get retries with backoff, delayed jobs, repeatable jobs, priorities, rate limits and a dashboard through tools such as Bull Board. The structure of the code is the same as the small version: a `Queue` to add jobs and a `Worker` that processes them.

The code in this lesson was syntax-checked, but BullMQ, which needs a running Redis server, needs a service that was not available when the lesson was written, so that part was not run. The parts that do not need the service were run and their tests passed. Check the current documentation of the library before you rely on a detail.

items: Make jobs **idempotent**: running the same job twice must be safe, because a retry may repeat work that half succeeded.
Keep job data small, such as ids, not whole documents.
Set sensible timeouts and attempt limits, and watch the failed list.
Shut down workers gracefully, so that a running job can finish before the process exits.

content.text: Your task

items: Make `add` return a job id, and add a `status(id)` method.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: A job that fails twice and then works is retried and counted as done.
A job that always fails ends up in the failed list.
You can explain why jobs should be idempotent.

animation.title: The web request does not wait

steps.say: The route puts a small job description on the queue and replies at once.
The queue holds the job. With Redis it survives restarts.
A worker takes jobs one by one. If one throws, it is retried after a delay.
When all attempts fail, the job is kept in a failed list for a person to inspect.

faqs.q: What does idempotent mean?
faqs.a: Doing it twice has the same result as doing it once. It matters because retries and duplicate deliveries can repeat a job.

faqs.q: Why is setInterval not enough for every schedule?
faqs.a: It runs inside one process, is lost on restart and runs on every copy of the app. Use cron or a platform scheduler for important schedules.

faqs.q: BullMQ or a database table as a queue?
faqs.a: A table is fine for low volume. BullMQ adds speed, retries, delays and monitoring when the volume or the needs grow.

options: Emails are not allowed in routes
The web request can reply at once while a worker does the slow work

quiz.q: What does idempotent mean for a job?
options: Running it twice has the same result as once

lessons.title: Real-Time Apps with WebSockets and Socket.IO: Rooms, Auth and Notifications
lessons.metaTitle: Real-Time Node: WebSockets and Socket.IO
lessons.description: Build real-time features with Socket.IO: authenticate each connection with a JWT, use private rooms, show who is online and push notifications.

content.text: HTTP works like letters: the browser asks, the server answers, and the conversation ends. That is wrong for a chat, a live score, a delivery map or a notification bell, where the **server** must be able to speak first. **WebSockets** solve this. A WebSocket is one long-lived connection between browser and server, open in both directions, and either side can send a message at any time. This lesson uses **Socket.IO**, the most popular library for it in Node, which adds rooms, automatic reconnection and a fallback when WebSockets are blocked.
Core ideas

items: **Connection:** each browser tab that connects is a `socket`. It has an id and a place to keep data.
**Events:** you send and receive named messages with `socket.emit('name', data)` and `socket.on('name', handler)`.
**Rooms:** groups of sockets. Sending to a room reaches everyone inside it. A room per user is a neat way to send something to one person on all their devices.
**Broadcast:** `io.emit` goes to everyone, `io.to(room).emit` to one room.

content.text: Authenticate on connect

A WebSocket is a door into your server, so it needs the same protection as an HTTP route. A socket must not be able to join without proving who it is. In Socket.IO you add a middleware that runs once for each new connection. The example below verifies a JWT sent in the handshake. If the token is missing or wrong, it calls `next(new Error('unauthorized'))` and the connection is refused. After that, `socket.data.user` holds the verified user id, and the code never trusts a user id sent in a message.

Walk through what happens after the connection. The socket **joins a private room** named `user:<id>`. The id is added to a set of online users and everyone receives the new `presence` list. A `private-message` event is checked first: the text must be a string, not empty and at most 500 characters, because data from a client is never trusted just because it came over a socket. Then it is sent only to the room of the receiver. On `disconnect`, the user is removed from the online set only when their **last** connection closes, since a person can have a phone and a laptop open at once.
Pushing from the rest of your server

The function returns `notify(userId, payload)`. It lets any other part of your server, such as an Express route, a payment webhook or a background job, send a real-time notification to one user without knowing anything about sockets. When lesson 40's worker finishes a report, it can call `notify` and a bell appears in the browser. This is how most apps combine a normal HTTP API with real-time features: HTTP for requests, sockets for pushes.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Install what the lesson needs: `npm install socket.io jsonwebtoken`.
Save the code as `realtime.js`. The test needs `npm install -D socket.io-client`.

content.text: ok 1 - auth, private messages and notifications
The test connects without a token and is refused, connects two users, sends a private message from one to the other, checks that a third user does not receive it, and calls `notify`.
Scaling sockets

Sockets are **stateful**: a connection lives on one server process. With two copies of your app, a message emitted on copy A does not reach a user connected to copy B. The fix is an **adapter**, usually the Redis adapter for Socket.IO, which passes events between the copies. You also need a load balancer that keeps a client on the same server during the connection (*sticky sessions*) when the long-polling fallback is used. Without these, real-time features work in development and break in production.

The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.
Your task

items: Add a `typing` event that tells the other user that someone is typing.
Add a room per chat group, and let a user join only the groups that they belong to.
Limit the number of messages per second for each socket.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: A connection without a token is refused.
A private message reaches only its receiver.
You can explain why presence is removed only when the last connection closes.

steps.say: The browser opens a socket and sends its token in the handshake.
The server verifies the token once. A bad token means the connection is refused.
Each verified user joins a private room, so messages can target one person on all devices.
Other server code calls notify to push to that room without knowing about sockets.

faqs.q: WebSocket or Socket.IO?
faqs.a: WebSocket is the browser standard. Socket.IO builds on it and adds rooms, reconnection, fallbacks and acknowledgements, at the cost of using its own protocol on both sides.

faqs.q: Do I authenticate every message?
faqs.a: You authenticate the connection once, and keep the verified user on the socket. Still validate the content of every message.

faqs.q: Why does real time break when I run two servers?
faqs.a: A socket lives on one process, so events must be shared between processes, for example with the Redis adapter.

quiz.q: Where should a Socket.IO connection be authenticated?
options: In a middleware that verifies the JWT when it connects

quiz.q: What is a room used for here?
options: Sending to one user on all their devices

quiz.q: Why do sockets break across two servers without an adapter?
options: A socket lives on one process, so events must be shared

lessons.title: Payment Integration Basics: Server-Side Prices, Webhooks and Idempotency
lessons.metaTitle: Payments: Prices, Webhooks, Idempotency
lessons.description: Integrate payments safely: calculate prices on the server in cents, let the provider take card data, and mark orders paid only from a signed webhook.

content.text: Payments are where mistakes cost real money, so this is the lesson to read slowly. The good news is that the safe design is simple, and almost every provider, Razorpay, Stripe, PayPal and others, works the same way. Learn the pattern once and the provider's own documentation becomes easy to follow.
Four rules

items: **Money is a whole number of the smallest unit.** Use paise or cents, `1999`, not `19.99`. Decimals can drift.
**The server decides the price.** The browser sends *what* the user wants, such as a product code and a quantity, never *how much*. A client that sends a price can send any price.
**The provider takes the card.** Card numbers must never touch your server, which keeps you out of heavy compliance rules. You receive a payment link or token instead.
**An order becomes paid only when a verified webhook says so.** The user coming back to your site with `?success=true` proves nothing, because anyone can type that URL.

content.text: Here is the flow. The browser asks to create an order. Your server calculates the total from **your own catalogue**, saves the order as `pending`, asks the provider to create a payment for that amount, and returns a payment URL. The user pays on the provider's page. The provider then calls your **webhook** with a signed message. Your server verifies the signature, finds the order, checks that the amount matches, and only then marks it `paid`.

Notice three details in the code. The webhook route comes **before** `express.json()` and uses `express.raw`, because the signature is calculated over the exact raw bytes. Next, the signature is compared with `timingSafeEqual`, as in lesson 28. Last, `seenEvents` makes the handler **idempotent**: providers resend an event when they do not receive a quick 200, so the same event can arrive twice, and you must not process it twice. In a real system you would store event ids in the database with a unique index.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Install what the lesson needs: `npm install express`.
Save the code as `payments.js`. The test needs `npm install -D supertest`. It uses a fake payment provider, so no account is needed.

content.text: ok 1 - server computes the price and only a signed webhook marks it paid

The test creates an order whose price comes from the catalogue even though the client tries to send its own, checks that the order is `pending`, sends a webhook with a bad signature and gets 400, sends a correct one and sees `paid`, and sends the same event again to confirm that it is recognised as a duplicate.
Other things a real integration needs

items: **Refunds and failures:** handle `payment.failed` and refund events, and show a clear state to the user.
**Amounts must match.** The code compares the paid amount with the order total. Without this a cheap payment could pay for an expensive order.
**Test mode first.** Every provider has a sandbox with test card numbers. Use it until the whole flow works, including failures.
**Keep records.** Store the provider's payment id on your order so that you can match it with their dashboard.
**Legal and tax rules:** invoices, taxes and refunds are governed by the law of your country. Ask an accountant or lawyer, and read the provider's own rules.

content.text: This lesson uses a fake provider so that you can run everything. Each real provider has its own library, field names and signature header. Follow its current documentation for those details, and do not copy this code straight into a live shop.

Reject an order that asks for more than 10 of one item.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: A price sent by the client is ignored.
A webhook with a bad signature returns 400.
Sending the same webhook twice changes nothing the second time.

animation.title: The order becomes paid only by webhook

steps.say: The browser says what it wants. It never says what it costs.
The server computes the total in cents and saves a pending order.
The provider shows the payment page and takes the card. Card data never reaches your server.
The provider calls your webhook. A verified, matching, first-time event marks the order paid.

faqs.q: Why not trust the success page after payment?
faqs.a: Anyone can open that URL by hand. Only a signed message from the provider, received by your server, proves that money moved.

faqs.q: Why must the server set the price?
faqs.a: A browser can send any value. If the server accepted the price, a user could pay one rupee for any product.

faqs.q: What if the webhook arrives twice?
faqs.a: Providers retry, so keep the event ids you have seen and ignore repeats. That is idempotency.

lessons.title: Scaling Node Apps: Microservices, Load Balancing and Health Checks
lessons.metaTitle: Scaling Node: Microservices, Load Balancing
lessons.description: Learn when to split an app into microservices, how a load balancer spreads traffic and skips sick copies with health checks, and what stateless means.

content.text: A popular app gets slow. The first reaction is often *we need microservices*, and that is usually the wrong first step. This lesson explains the real options for handling more traffic, in the order that you should try them, and shows the central trick of scaling, a **load balancer** that spreads requests over several copies, in a small running example.
Scale up, scale out

**Scaling up** means a bigger machine, with more CPU and memory. It is the easiest change, and it works until the machine is the largest available or too expensive. **Scaling out** means more machines, or more copies, sharing the load. It has no hard ceiling, but your app must be ready for it. Before either, measure: many slow apps are really slow queries, a missing index or no caching, and fixing those is much cheaper than new servers.
Stateless servers

To scale out, every copy of the app must be **interchangeable**. A request can go to any copy and get the same result. That means no important data in the memory of one copy: sessions, caches, uploaded files and counters must live in a shared place such as the database, Redis or cloud storage. If a copy can be killed and replaced at any moment without losing anything, your design is **stateless**, and scaling and deployment both become easy.
The load balancer

A **load balancer** sits in front of the copies. Clients talk to it, and it forwards each request to one copy. The simplest rule is **round robin**: the first request goes to copy 1, the next to copy 2, then 3, and back to 1. A good balancer also runs **health checks**: every few seconds it asks each copy `GET /health`. A copy that does not answer with 200 is taken out of rotation until it recovers, so users never see it. nginx, HAProxy and cloud balancers all do this. The example is a miniature version in about thirty lines.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Save the code as `scale.js`. The test uses only Node.

content.text: ok 1 - round robin, and a sick copy is skipped

The test starts three small services and sends six requests, and sees that the answers rotate among the three. Then it makes one service unhealthy and sends more requests, and shows that the sick copy never answers. Finally, if every copy is unhealthy, the balancer throws an error, which a real system turns into a 503.
Microservices: when and why not

A **microservice** architecture splits one large app into several small services, each with its own code, its own database and its own deployment, talking over HTTP or a message queue. The benefits are real: teams can work and deploy independently, and each part can scale on its own. The costs are real too: network calls can fail, data is spread over several databases, debugging crosses many logs, and you need tooling for deployment and monitoring. Many successful companies run a well-organised **modular monolith**, one deployable app with clear internal boundaries, until size or team structure makes splitting worth the pain. Project 10 in this course builds a small two-service example so that you can feel both the benefit and the cost.

items: Measure first: slow queries, missing indexes and no caching are the common causes.
Make the app stateless, so any copy can serve any request.
Add a health route that checks real dependencies, such as the database.
Run at least two copies behind a load balancer, and deploy one at a time.
Split into services only when a clear need, such as team size or very different scaling, pays for the extra complexity.

Your task

A sick copy receives no traffic.
You can name two costs of microservices.

steps.say: Clients know one address. They do not know how many copies exist.
The balancer picks a copy for each request and skips any that fail the health check.
Any copy can answer, because none of them keeps important data in its own memory.
Sessions, caches and files live in shared stores that every copy can reach.

faqs.q: Should my first project use microservices?
faqs.a: No. Start with one well-organised app. Split later if team size or scaling needs justify the extra complexity.

faqs.q: What is a health check?
faqs.a: A small route, often /health, that a balancer calls to see if a copy is working, so it can stop sending traffic to a broken one.

faqs.q: What does stateless mean?
faqs.a: No copy keeps important data only in its own memory, so any copy can handle any request and can be replaced at any time.
