lessons.title: Node Performance: Memory Leaks and Blocking the Event Loop
lessons.metaTitle: Node Performance: Memory Leaks and Blocking
lessons.description: Find and fix two classic Node.js performance problems: memory that grows forever and code that blocks the event loop, with two small programs that show both.

content.text: When a Node app is slow, the cause is nearly always one of a few things: a slow database query, too many sequential calls that could run together, memory that grows until the process is killed, or code that blocks the event loop. The first two are about your design. This lesson covers the last two, which are Node-specific and which interviewers ask about often. Each has a small program that makes the problem visible.
Memory leaks

Node cleans memory with a **garbage collector**, which frees anything that nothing refers to. A **leak** is memory that you no longer need but still refer to, so it is never freed. The heap grows slowly until the process becomes slow and finally dies with an out-of-memory error, often at the worst hour. The usual causes are: a global array or object that only grows, such as a cache without a size limit; event listeners added again and again and never removed; timers that are never cleared; and closures that hold large objects.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Save the code as `memory.js` and run it with `node --expose-gc memory.js`. The flag lets the program ask for garbage collection, so the numbers are steady.

content.text:
Leaky cache grew the heap by more than 50 MB: true
Bounded cache stays small (under 20 MB more): true
Bounded size: 100

The program does the same work twice. The leaky version stores every result in a `Map` that never forgets, and the heap grows by tens of megabytes. The bounded version keeps at most 100 entries and throws away the oldest, so the heap stays flat. The fix for most leaks is exactly that: **put a limit on anything that grows**, use a cache with a maximum size and an expiry, and remove listeners and timers when you are done with them.
How to look for a leak in a real app

items: Watch the memory of the process over time, with `process.memoryUsage()` or your monitoring tool. A line that only goes up is the sign.
Start the app with `node --inspect`, open `chrome://inspect`, and take **heap snapshots** at two moments. Compare them to see which objects increased.
Look at what you store in module-level variables. A `Map` or array at the top of a file lives as long as the process.
Check that every `on` has a matching `off`, and every `setInterval` has a `clearInterval`.

content.text: Blocking the event loop

The event loop runs your JavaScript one piece at a time. A piece that runs for 300 milliseconds means that **every other request waits 300 milliseconds**. Common culprits are huge `JSON.parse` calls, heavy loops, synchronous file functions such as `readFileSync` in a handler, slow regular expressions, and password hashing with a synchronous function. The program below starts a timer that should tick every 10 milliseconds, runs a heavy loop, and measures how long the loop kept the timer waiting.
The event loop was stuck for about 300 ms: true

Your exact number will differ. The remedy depends on the cause. Use asynchronous versions of functions. Break a big job into smaller pieces that give the loop a turn between them. Move real CPU work to a worker thread, as in lesson 23, or to a background queue, as in lesson 40. Use the asynchronous `bcrypt.hash`, not a synchronous version. And measure: `perf_hooks` can report the event loop delay in production, and a rising delay is an early warning.
Other quick wins

items: Run independent calls together with `Promise.all`.
Turn on compression, for example with the `compression` package, or let nginx do it.
Add indexes and use `lean()` or limited fields in database queries.
Cache repeated answers, as in lesson 39.
Set `NODE_ENV=production`.

content.text: The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.
Your task

items: Run the memory program again with a limit of 10 and with a limit of 10,000 and compare.
Change the blocking loop to run in pieces, using `setImmediate` between them, and see the stuck time fall.
Print `process.memoryUsage().heapUsed` every second in one of your own servers for a minute.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You can explain why an unbounded Map is a leak.
You can say what blocks the event loop.
You can name two fixes for blocking.

animation.title: Two ways a Node app slows down

steps.say: A leak keeps references to data nobody needs, so the garbage collector cannot free it.
The fix is a limit: bounded caches, expiry times, removed listeners and cleared timers.
Blocking is a long synchronous task. Every other request waits behind it.
Split the work, use a worker thread or move it to a background queue.

faqs.q: How do I know if my app has a memory leak?
faqs.a: Watch memory over time. If it keeps rising and never falls back after garbage collection, there is probably a leak. Heap snapshots show which objects grow.

faqs.q: Is readFileSync always bad?
faqs.a: Not at start-up, for example reading config once. Inside a request handler it blocks every other user, so use the asynchronous version there.

faqs.q: What is event loop delay?
faqs.a: How late the loop runs a timer that should be on time. A rising delay means something is blocking it.

quiz.q: What is a memory leak in Node?
options: Memory you no longer need but still refer to, so it is never freed

quiz.q: What is a common fix for a growing cache?
options: A maximum size and an expiry

quiz.q: Why is readFileSync in a request handler a problem?
options: It blocks every other request while it runs

lessons.title: Debugging Node Apps: Breakpoints, --inspect and Reading Stack Traces
lessons.metaTitle: Debugging Node.js: Breakpoints, Traces
lessons.description: Debug Node.js properly: read stack traces, pause with breakpoints in VS Code and Chrome DevTools using --inspect, and find the bug in a practice file.

content.text: Beginners debug by adding `console.log` everywhere, running again, and reading a wall of output. It works for small problems. For anything harder, the faster tool is a **debugger**: it pauses your program at a line you choose and lets you look at every variable at that moment. Learning it early repays you for the rest of your career. This lesson shows how, with a small file that has a real, typical bug in it.
Read the error first

When Node crashes it prints a **stack trace**: the error message, then the chain of function calls that led to it, newest first. Read it in this order. First, the message and the error type, for example `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name')`. It tells you what went wrong. Second, the first line of the trace that points to *your* file, not to `node_modules` or `node:internal`. It tells you where. Then look at that line and ask what could be `undefined` or the wrong type there. Half of all bugs end here.

items: `ReferenceError`: you used a name that does not exist, often a typo or a missing import.
`TypeError`: you used a value in a way it does not allow, often because it is `undefined` or `null`.
`ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` or `Cannot find module`: a wrong path or a missing package.
`EADDRINUSE`: another process already uses that port.
`UnhandledPromiseRejection`: a promise failed and nothing handled it.

content.text: A bug to practise on
The function below should return the average of the order amounts. The result is wrong, and no error appears, which is exactly the kind of bug where a debugger helps.
node d41-bug.js
An average of three orders worth about a hundred each should be near 133, not more than three million. Do not guess. Use the debugger.
Debugging in VS Code

items: Open the folder in VS Code and open the file.
Click in the left margin next to the line `total += order.amount;`. A red dot, a **breakpoint**, appears.
Open the *Run and Debug* panel and choose *Run and Debug*, then *Node.js*. The program runs and **pauses** on your line.

Look at the **Variables** panel. `order` is `{ amount: 100 }` and `total` is `0`. Press **Continue** twice more. On the second round, `order.amount` is the **text** `'250'`, and `total` becomes the text `'100250'`.
Now you see it: adding a number and a string in JavaScript joins them as text. Fix it by converting with `Number(order.amount)`, or better, by validating the data when it enters, as in lesson 31.

content.text: The useful controls are: **Step over**, run this line and stop at the next; **Step into**, go inside the function that this line calls; **Step out**, finish the current function; and **Continue**, run until the next breakpoint. The **Watch** panel lets you type an expression such as `typeof order.amount` and see it update. A **conditional breakpoint**, set by right-clicking the red dot, pauses only when a condition is true, for example `order.amount === '250'`. That is the tool for the bug that appears only on record 8,000.
Debugging with --inspect

Node has a debugger built in. Run `node --inspect-brk d41-bug.js`; `-brk` pauses at the first line. Then open `chrome://inspect` in Chrome, click *inspect* below your process, and the same stepping tools open in Chrome DevTools. This also works for a server that runs on another machine, when you forward the port through an SSH tunnel. Never open the debug port to the internet. Anyone who connects can run any code on your server.
Habits that save hours

items: Make the bug **reproducible** before anything else. A bug that you can trigger on demand is half solved.
Change **one** thing at a time, and test after each change.
Shrink the problem: remove code until the smallest example still fails.
Read the error message slowly and completely. Most of the answer is in it.
Write a test for the bug before you fix it, so that it can never return unnoticed.
Explain the problem aloud to someone, or to a rubber duck. This habit is famous because it works.

content.text: The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.
Your task

items: Fix the bug with `Number(order.amount)` and also add a check that rejects an amount that is not a number.
Put a conditional breakpoint that stops only when `typeof order.amount === 'string'`.
Start a small Express server with `node --inspect` and attach Chrome DevTools to it.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You found the string `'250'` with a breakpoint and not by guessing.
You can say what step over and step into do.
You know why the debug port must never be public.

steps.say: The result is wrong but nothing crashed, so there is no stack trace to read.
Set a breakpoint on the suspicious line and run in the debugger.
Look at the real values. One amount is the text 250, so adding joins text instead of adding numbers.
Fix the cause, validate the input, and write a test so the bug cannot return.

faqs.q: Is console.log wrong?
faqs.a: No, it is quick and useful. A debugger is better when you need to see many values at one moment, or step through unknown code.

faqs.q: What is a breakpoint?
faqs.a: A marker on a line where the program pauses so that you can look at its variables and step forward.

faqs.q: Why is it dangerous to expose the inspect port?
faqs.a: Anyone who can connect to it can run code inside your process. Keep it on localhost and use an SSH tunnel.

quiz.q: Which part of a stack trace should you read first?
options: The error message and type, then the first line in your own file

quiz.q: What does a breakpoint do?
options: Pauses the program on that line so you can inspect variables

quiz.q: Why must the --inspect port never be public?
options: Anyone who connects can run code in your process

lessons.title: Testing Node APIs: Jest, Mocha, Chai, Supertest and Mocking
lessons.metaTitle: Testing Node: Jest, Mocha, Supertest
lessons.description: Write automated Node.js tests: unit tests with Jest, Mocha and Chai, API tests with Supertest, and mocks and stubs that replace payment and weather APIs.

content.text: You have seen tests all through this course. This lesson gathers the ideas and shows the three tools that employers ask about: **Jest**, **Mocha with Chai**, and **Supertest**. Their names differ, but the structure is the same: set up some data, run the code, and check the result. A test is a small program that fails loudly when your code stops doing what you meant, so that you find out in a second on your laptop, not a week later from a customer.
What to test

items: **Unit tests** check one small function or class with no network and no database. They are fast, so you can have thousands.
**Integration tests** check several parts together, such as a route, the service and a test database.
**API tests** send real HTTP requests to your app and check the status and the body. Supertest does this without opening a port.
A good balance is many unit tests, a fair number of API tests, and a few end-to-end tests of the most important journeys, such as sign up and checkout.

content.text: The code under test

The cart module below adds up prices in cents and charges a payment gateway. The gateway is a **dependency**, a thing the code needs from outside. In the test we do not want to charge a real card, so we pass a replacement.
Mocks and stubs

A **stub** is a fake that returns a fixed answer, such as a gateway that always says `ok: false`. A **mock** is a fake that also **records how it was used**, so you can ask afterwards: was `charge` called once, and with the amount 1000? The tools of each library create them for you. They work only because the code receives the gateway as an argument, which is why dependency injection in lesson 37 makes testing easy.
Jest

**Jest** is the most widely used test runner. It includes the test runner, the `expect` assertions and mocking, so one package does everything. A test is `test('name', fn)`, tests are grouped with `describe`, and `jest.fn()` creates a mock.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Run `npm install -D jest`, save the module as `t42-cart.cjs` and the tests next to it, and run `npx jest`.

content.text: Tests:       4 passed, 4 total
Mocha and Chai

**Mocha** is a runner that does only that job, and it pairs with an assertion library such as **Chai**, which reads like English: `expect(result.paid).to.equal(false)`. For stubs and spies you add a library such as Sinon, or write a small stub by hand, as the example does. Many older codebases use Mocha, so you will meet it often.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Run `npm install -D mocha chai`, save the file with the extension `.mjs`, and run `npx mocha t42-cart.mocha.test.mjs`.

content.text: 3 passing
Supertest and the built-in runner

**Supertest** sends requests straight into an Express app. Node 20 and later also has a **built-in test runner**, `node:test`, with `mock.fn()`, so you can write tests with no extra packages except Supertest. The test below creates an app that depends on a weather service, replaces the service with a mock that says it is 38 degrees, and checks the advice. It then changes the mock to 22 degrees and checks again.
Run it with `node --test`. It passes. Notice that the test never calls the real weather service, so it is fast and does not break when the internet does.
Writing tests that help

items: Test **behaviour**, not implementation details. A test that breaks when you rename a variable is a burden.
Name tests as sentences: `rejects an empty cart and never calls the gateway`.
Cover the **unhappy paths**: empty input, wrong types, missing permissions, and failures of the thing you depend on.
Keep tests independent. One test must not need another to run first.
Run them on every push, as lesson 50 shows. A test that is never run protects nobody.

content.text: Jest and Mocha are different runners. If you run all three styles with the plain `node --test` command, the Jest and Mocha files will fail, because their special functions such as `describe` and `jest.fn` belong to their own runners. Run each file with its own tool. The Jest file ran with 4 tests passing, the Mocha file with 3, and the Supertest file with the built-in runner.

The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.
Your task

items: Add a test that a gateway failure, a thrown error, makes `checkout` reject.
Write the same cart test in the built-in `node:test` style.
Check coverage with `npx jest --coverage` and add a test for a line that is not covered.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You can explain the difference between a stub and a mock.
A test never calls a real payment or weather service.
You can say why the gateway is a parameter.

animation.title: Replace what you do not own

steps.say: A test arranges data, runs the code and checks the result.
The code receives its dependencies as arguments, so a test can pass fakes.
The mock gateway returns a fixed answer and remembers how it was called.
The test checks both the result and that the gateway was used correctly.

faqs.q: Jest or Mocha?
faqs.a: Both are common. Jest is all-in-one and popular for new projects. Mocha with Chai is in many older codebases. The built-in node:test runner needs no packages.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a mock and a stub?
faqs.a: A stub returns fixed answers. A mock also records how it was called so a test can check that.

faqs.q: Does Supertest need the server to listen on a port?
faqs.a: No. You pass the Express app and it sends the request internally, which is faster and avoids port clashes.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a stub and a mock?
options: A mock also records how it was called

quiz.q: Why does Supertest not need the server to listen on a port?
options: It does not send real requests
It sends the request straight into the Express app

quiz.q: Why pass the payment gateway as an argument?
options: A test can replace it with a fake

lessons.title: Linux Server Basics for Node Developers: Commands, Permissions and SSH
lessons.metaTitle: Linux Server Basics for Node Developers
lessons.description: Learn the Linux commands you need before deploying Node.js: files and folders, permissions, pipes, processes, SSH and firewalls, with a safe practice script.

content.text: Almost every Node.js app in production runs on Linux. Your laptop may run Windows or macOS, but the server that you rent will most likely have Ubuntu or a similar system, and you will control it through a text terminal. It looks scary the first time, but you need only a small set of commands to be productive. This lesson teaches those commands with a harmless practice script, and the safety habits that matter on a real server.
The terminal and the file system

A **terminal** is a window where you type commands, and the program that reads them is called a **shell**, most often `bash`. Linux organises everything in a single tree of folders that starts at `/`, called *root*. Your own files live in your **home folder**, such as `/home/asha`, which is also written `~`. A **path** says where a file is. An *absolute* path starts with `/`. A *relative* path starts from where you are now. The commands you will use all the time are these.

items: `pwd` prints the folder you are in. `ls` lists files, `ls -l` adds details, and `ls -a` shows hidden files whose names start with a dot.
`cd folder` moves into a folder, `cd ..` goes up one level, and `cd ~` goes home.
`mkdir` makes a folder. `cp` copies, `mv` moves or renames, and `rm` removes. `rm -r` removes a folder and everything inside it.
`cat file` prints a file. `head -n 5` and `tail -n 5` print the first or last lines, and `tail -f` follows a log file as it grows.
`nano file` is a simple text editor in the terminal.
`grep text file` searches for text inside files, and `find` searches for files by name.

content.text: `rm` has **no recycle bin**. A removed file is gone. Check the path twice before you press Enter, never run `rm -r` with a path that you have not read, and never copy a command from the internet that you do not understand.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Save the script below as `lx-basics.sh` and run it with `bash lx-basics.sh`. It only touches a folder named `demo` that it creates and then removes.

content.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Safe practice: everything happens inside one new folder.
set -e
mkdir -p demo && cd demo
pwd
echo "hello server" > a.txt
cp a.txt b.txt
ls -l
chmod 600 a.txt              # only the owner can read and write
ls -l a.txt
grep -n "hello" a.txt        # search inside a file
cat a.txt b.txt | wc -l      # a pipe sends the output of one command into the next
echo "second line" >> a.txt  # >> appends, > replaces
head -n 1 a.txt
cd .. && rm -r demo          # remove the folder when you are done
bash lx-basics.sh

/home/asha/demo
total 8
-rw-r--r-- 1 asha asha 13 Nov 11 08:59 a.txt
-rw-r--r-- 1 asha asha 13 Nov 11 08:59 b.txt
-rw------- 1 asha asha 13 Nov 11 08:59 a.txt
1:hello server
2
hello server

Your folder name, user name and dates will differ. Notice three things. First, the **pipe** `|` sends the output of one command into the next, so `cat a.txt b.txt | wc -l` counts the lines of both files together. Second, `>` writes a command's output to a file and replaces what was there, while `>>` appends. Third, look at the left column of `ls -l`, which shows the permissions.
Permissions

Every file has an owner, a group and a set of rights for three kinds of people: the owner, the group, and everyone else. Each can have **r** (read), **w** (write) and **x** (execute). The text `-rw-r--r--` means that the owner can read and write, and the group and others can only read. `chmod 600 a.txt` changes it so that only the owner can read and write, which is right for a file with secrets, such as a `.env` file. Scripts need the `x` right to run directly. The `chown` command changes the owner. If you meet *Permission denied*, the answer is usually to fix the ownership or the rights, not to use `sudo` on everything.
sudo, users and updates

The **root** user can do anything, including destroying the system, so you work as a normal user and put `sudo` in front of the few commands that need extra rights. Servers are kept up to date with the package manager. On Ubuntu that is `sudo apt update` to refresh the list and `sudo apt upgrade` to install updates. Do not run your Node app as root: create a normal user for it, so that a bug in your code, or an attacker, cannot control the whole machine.
Processes, ports and logs

items: `ps aux | grep node` shows running Node processes, and `top` or `htop` shows CPU and memory use.
`kill PID` asks a process to stop. `kill -9 PID` forces it, and should be the last resort.
`ss -tulpn` shows which program listens on which port. It answers the `EADDRINUSE` question from lesson 10.
`df -h` shows disk space, and `free -h` shows memory. A full disk is a very common cause of strange failures.
`journalctl -u servicename` and `tail -f /var/log/...` show logs.

content.text: SSH: reaching the server

**SSH** is the secure way to open a terminal on a remote machine: `ssh asha@203.0.113.10`. Use a **key pair** instead of a password. You create it on your own computer with `ssh-keygen`, keep the private key secret, and put the public key on the server in `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`. Move files with `scp` or `rsync`, or, better, deploy with Git as lesson 50 shows. A **firewall** lets only the ports you need through. With `ufw`, allow SSH, HTTP and HTTPS, and enable it. Do this in the right order, **allow SSH first**, or you lock yourself out.

Lesson 48 uses everything from this page. You rent a server, log in with SSH, update it, create a user, open the firewall, install Node and run the app. If every command there feels familiar, the deployment will feel easy.

The practice script above was run in a Linux sandbox and its output matches. The remaining commands in this lesson, especially SSH and the firewall, need a real server and were not run here, so try them first on a cheap test machine and read the manual with `man command` when in doubt.
Your task

items: Run the practice script, then change it to make a second folder and copy `a.txt` into it.
Use `ls -l` to compare the permissions before and after `chmod 600`.
Run `ss -tulpn` while a Node server is running on your machine and find its port.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You can say what `pwd`, `ls -l`, `cd ..` and `grep` do.
You can read `-rw-r--r--`.
You know why to allow SSH in the firewall before enabling it.

animation.title: Reaching and running on a server

steps.say: You log in with an SSH key, not a password.
A small set of commands lets you move around, read files and search logs.
Permissions decide who can read, write and run each file. Secrets get 600.
A firewall closes everything except the ports that you need. Allow SSH first.

faqs.q: Do I need Linux to deploy Node.js?
faqs.a: You can deploy on other systems, but most servers and containers run Linux, so a basic knowledge of it is expected.

faqs.q: What is the difference between rm and rm -r?
faqs.a: rm removes files. rm -r removes folders and everything inside. Neither has an undo, so check the path first.

faqs.q: Why not run my app as root?
faqs.a: If the app has a bug or is attacked, root rights give the attacker control of the entire machine. A normal user limits the damage.

quiz.q: What does chmod 600 file do?
options: Only the owner can read and write it

quiz.q: Why is rm dangerous?
options: There is no recycle bin, so the file is gone

quiz.q: What must you do before you enable a firewall on a remote server?

lessons.title: Deploy Node to a VPS: nginx Reverse Proxy, PM2, DNS and Let's Encrypt
lessons.metaTitle: Deploy Node on a VPS: nginx, PM2 and HTTPS
lessons.description: Put a Node.js app on the internet: rent a VPS, run it with PM2, put nginx in front as a reverse proxy, point a domain with DNS and add a free HTTPS certificate.

content.text: An app that runs only on your laptop helps nobody. This lesson walks the classic route to production: a small rented Linux server, called a **VPS** (virtual private server), running your app behind nginx with HTTPS on your own domain. It is not the only way, and managed platforms are easier, but this route teaches how the internet actually fits together, and employers like people who have done it once.
The picture

A visitor types your domain. **DNS** turns the name into the IP address of your server. The browser connects to port 443 where **nginx** listens. nginx handles HTTPS and passes the request on to your Node app, which listens only on `127.0.0.1:3000`, a port that the outside world cannot reach. **PM2** keeps the Node app running, restarts it if it crashes and starts it after a reboot. This layout is called a **reverse proxy**, and it is standard.
Step by step

items: **Rent a server.** Pick a small Ubuntu LTS VPS from any provider. Add your SSH key during creation, because passwords are weak.
**Log in and update.** `ssh user@SERVER_IP`, then `sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade`. Create a normal user for the app, and do not run it as root.
**Install Node.** Use the NodeSource instructions or a version manager such as nvm, and install a current LTS version of Node.
**Firewall.** Allow only SSH, HTTP and HTTPS, for example with `ufw allow OpenSSH`, `ufw allow 'Nginx Full'` and `ufw enable`. Do not open port 3000.
**Get the code.** `git clone` your repository into `/var/www/app`, run `npm ci --omit=dev`, and create the `.env` file on the server with the production secrets.
**Run it with PM2.** Install it with `npm i -g pm2`, start with the config below, then run `pm2 save` and `pm2 startup` and follow what it prints, so the app starts after a reboot.
**Set up nginx.** Install nginx and use the configuration below as a site file.
**Point DNS.** In your domain provider's panel, add an **A record** for `api` (or `@`) that points to the server IP. It can take from a few minutes to a few hours to spread.
**Add HTTPS.** Install Certbot and run `sudo certbot --nginx -d api.example.com`. It gets a free certificate from **Let's Encrypt**, edits the nginx file and sets automatic renewal.

content.text: PM2: keep it alive

`instances: 'max'` with `exec_mode: 'cluster'` starts one copy per CPU core, as lesson 23 described. `max_memory_restart` restarts a copy that grows too big, which is a safety net for a leak, not a cure. `pm2 reload` restarts the copies one at a time, so users see **no downtime**, while `pm2 restart` stops them all briefly. Useful commands are `pm2 status`, `pm2 logs`, and `pm2 monit`.
nginx: the reverse proxy

The `upstream` block lists your Node copies. `proxy_pass` forwards requests to them. The `proxy_set_header` lines pass the real client address and the original protocol, and this is why the app sets `trust proxy` in lesson 24. The `Upgrade` and `Connection` lines allow WebSockets. `client_max_body_size` must match the upload limit in your app, or nginx will refuse large uploads with 413 before your code sees them.
Production checklist

items: `NODE_ENV=production`, real secrets in the environment, and a strong `JWT_SECRET`.
The database allows connections only from your server, not from the whole internet. On MongoDB Atlas, add the server IP to the access list.
HTTPS only, with a redirect from port 80. Certbot can do it.
Logs go somewhere you can read, with rotation, and `pm2 logs` is a start.
Backups run and a restore has been tested, as lesson 50 explains.
A `/health` route that you can use for monitoring.

content.text: The server commands, the PM2 configuration and the nginx configuration in this lesson were written to follow the current documentation, but they were not run on a real server when the lesson was written, because that needs a machine, a domain or an account. Run them first on a test server, read each line, and check the current documentation of every tool before you use them for something that matters.
Your task

items: Rent the cheapest server you can, or use a free trial, and follow the steps with a spare domain or a subdomain.
Check the certificate renewal with `sudo certbot renew --dry-run`.
Open `/health` from your phone and then run `pm2 reload` while refreshing the page.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The site opens over HTTPS and port 3000 is not reachable from outside.
The app survives a server reboot.
You can draw the path from the browser to your Node app.

steps.say: The browser asks DNS which IP address your domain points to.
It connects to nginx on port 443. nginx ends the HTTPS and forwards the request.
PM2 keeps several copies of your app running on a private port, and restarts them if they crash.
The app talks to the database, which accepts connections only from this server.

faqs.q: Why put nginx in front of Node?
faqs.a: It handles HTTPS, compression, static files and buffering very well, and it lets you run several copies of the app behind one address.

faqs.q: Is Let's Encrypt really free?
faqs.a: Yes, the certificates are free. They last 90 days and Certbot renews them automatically.

faqs.q: What is the difference between pm2 restart and pm2 reload?
faqs.a: Restart stops all copies and starts them again. Reload restarts them one at a time, so the app stays available.

quiz.q: What does nginx do in front of Node?
options: Handles HTTPS and forwards requests to the app

quiz.q: What is the difference between pm2 reload and pm2 restart?
options: Reload restarts copies one at a time to avoid downtime

quiz.q: What does a DNS A record do?
options: Points a domain name at a server IP address

lessons.title: Docker for Node Developers: Dockerfile, Compose and Small Images
lessons.metaTitle: Docker for Node: Dockerfile and Compose
lessons.description: Package a Node.js app in a Docker image with a multi-stage Dockerfile, run it with MongoDB and Redis using Docker Compose, and follow image safety rules.

content.text: "It works on my machine" is a classic problem. The server has a different Node version, a missing package or a different setting. **Docker** removes the problem by packaging your app together with everything it needs, into an **image**. A **container** is a running copy of an image. The same image runs the same way on your laptop, on a colleague's laptop and on a server, which is why almost every company uses containers in some form.
Words to know

items: **Image:** a read-only package: an operating system layer, Node, your code and its dependencies.
**Container:** a running instance of an image. You can start many from one image.
**Dockerfile:** a text file with the recipe to build an image.
**Registry:** a place that stores images, such as Docker Hub or the registry of your cloud.
**Volume:** storage that outlives a container, used for database files.
**Compose:** a tool that starts several containers together from one file.

content.text: A good Dockerfile

# --- build stage: install all dependencies ---
FROM node:22-alpine AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

# --- run stage: small image with only what is needed ---
FROM node:22-alpine
ENV NODE_ENV=production
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY . .
# never run as root
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s CMD wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/health || exit 1
CMD ["node", "src/server.js"]

This file uses a **multi-stage build**. The first stage installs the production dependencies. The second stage starts again from a clean small image and copies in only the result, so build tools do not end up in the final image. Several details matter. `node:22-alpine` is a small base image. `npm ci --omit=dev` installs exactly what the lock file says and leaves out the dev tools. `COPY package*.json` comes before `COPY . .`, so Docker can **reuse the cached layer** of installed packages when only your code changed, which makes rebuilds fast. `USER node` runs the app without root rights, which limits the damage if the app is attacked. The `HEALTHCHECK` lets Docker see whether the app is alive.
Also create a `.dockerignore` file so that `node_modules`, `.git` and especially `.env` are never copied into the image. A secret inside an image can be read by anyone who gets the image.

# .dockerignore
node_modules
.git
.env
*.log
coverage
Compose: app, database and cache together

services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      MONGODB_URI: mongodb://mongo:27017/app
      REDIS_HOST: redis
      JWT_SECRET: ${JWT_SECRET}       # comes from your shell or a .env file, never written here
    depends_on:
      - mongo
      - redis
    restart: unless-stopped

  mongo:
    image: mongo:7
    volumes:
      - mongo-data:/data/db           # keeps the data when the container is replaced
    restart: unless-stopped

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped

volumes:
  mongo-data:

Compose starts three containers. They can reach each other by **service name**: inside the app container, the database address is `mongo`, not `localhost`. The `volumes` entry stores the database files outside the container, so removing the container does not delete your data. The secret `JWT_SECRET` is read from your shell or a `.env` file, not written in the file.

items: Build and start everything: `docker compose up --build`. Add `-d` to run in the background.
See the logs with `docker compose logs -f api`.
Stop with `docker compose down`. Add `-v` only if you really want to delete the data volume.

content.text: Compose is excellent for development and for small single-server deployments. For many servers, teams move to a platform such as Kubernetes or a managed container service, which is a large topic of its own.

The Dockerfile and Compose file in this lesson were written to follow the current documentation, but they were not run on a real server when the lesson was written, because that needs a machine, a domain or an account. Run them first on a test server, read each line, and check the current documentation of every tool before you use them for something that matters.

items: Pin a major Node version in `FROM`, and update it on purpose.
Never put secrets in the Dockerfile or the image. Pass them at run time.
Keep one process per container, and log to the console, because Docker collects it.
Scan images with a tool such as `docker scout` or Trivy.
Do not store uploads or database files inside a container without a volume.

content.text: Your task

items: Build the image for your own project and compare its size with a version that uses the full `node:22` image.
Add a `.env.example` file that lists the variables without real values.
Change the Compose file so that it also starts an nginx container in front of the app.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The image runs as the `node` user and not as root.
Changing one source file does not reinstall every package on rebuild.
Your `.env` file is listed in `.dockerignore`.

steps.say: The Dockerfile lists the steps: base image, install packages, copy code.
The build produces an image. A multi-stage build keeps build tools out of it.
A container is one running copy of the image, with limited rights.
Compose starts the app together with its database and cache on a private network.

faqs.q: What is the difference between an image and a container?
faqs.a: An image is the packaged recipe. A container is a running instance of it. You can start many containers from one image.

faqs.q: Where should I keep database data?
faqs.a: In a volume. Anything written inside a container is lost when the container is removed.

faqs.q: Do I need Docker to deploy Node?
faqs.a: No. A VPS with PM2 works well, as in the previous lesson. Docker helps with identical environments and with larger teams.

quiz.q: What is the difference between an image and a container?
options: An image is a running process
A container is a running instance of an image

quiz.q: Why copy package.json before the rest of the code in a Dockerfile?
options: Docker can reuse the cached layer of installed packages

quiz.q: Where should database files live in Compose?

lessons.title: CI/CD with GitHub Actions, Monitoring, Backups and Zero-Downtime Releases
lessons.metaTitle: CI/CD, Monitoring and Backups for Node Apps
lessons.description: Automate tests and deploys with GitHub Actions, release without downtime using PM2 reload, watch your app with logs and health checks, and back up the database.

content.text: Deploying by hand, copying files and typing commands, works the first ten times. Then one evening you forget a step, or skip the tests, and the site is down. **CI/CD** replaces the manual steps with a script that runs the same way every time. This lesson covers that script, and the three habits that keep a live app healthy afterwards: monitoring, backups and careful releases.
CI and CD

items: **Continuous integration (CI):** every push and pull request automatically installs the project and runs the tests and checks. A failing test blocks the merge.
**Continuous delivery or deployment (CD):** when the checks pass on the main branch, the new version is automatically published to the server.
The benefit is not speed alone. It is **confidence**: nobody can ship something that fails the tests by accident.

content.text: A GitHub Actions workflow

GitHub Actions reads files in `.github/workflows`. The workflow below has two jobs. The `test` job runs on every push to `main` and on pull requests. It checks out the code, installs Node 22 with npm caching, runs `npm ci`, runs `npm audit` so that serious known vulnerabilities fail the build, and runs the tests. The `deploy` job runs only on `main` and only after `test` succeeded. It logs in to your server over SSH and runs the update commands.

# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm audit --audit-level=high      # fail on serious known vulnerabilities
      - run: npm test

  deploy:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Deploy over SSH
        uses: appleboy/ssh-action@v1.0.3
        with:
          host: ${{ secrets.SERVER_HOST }}
          username: ${{ secrets.SERVER_USER }}
          key: ${{ secrets.SERVER_SSH_KEY }}
          script: |
            cd /var/www/app
            git pull origin main
            npm ci --omit=dev
            pm2 reload ecosystem.config.cjs --env production    # reload = no downtime

The values `secrets.SERVER_HOST`, `SERVER_USER` and `SERVER_SSH_KEY` come from the repository settings, under *Secrets*. They are never written in the file. Use a dedicated deploy key that can only access this server, not your personal key. The last command is `pm2 reload`, which restarts the app copies one by one, so the release has **no downtime**.
Safer releases

items: **Roll back quickly.** Keep the previous version ready. With Git, redeploy the previous commit. With Docker, run the previous image tag.
**Database changes need care.** Make them backwards compatible, such as adding a column first and removing the old one later, so old and new code work together during a release.
**Graceful shutdown.** On `SIGTERM`, stop accepting new requests, finish the current ones, close the database and exit. PM2 and Docker both send that signal.
**Release small and often.** A small change is easy to understand and to undo.

content.text: Monitoring: know before your users tell you

items: **Health route:** `/health` answers 200 when the app and its database work. An external uptime service, such as UptimeRobot, checks it every minute and sends you a message.
**Logs:** structured logs from lesson 38, kept somewhere searchable.
**Errors:** a tool such as Sentry collects exceptions with the stack and context, and alerts you.

**Metrics:** CPU, memory, response times and error rates. Tools such as Prometheus with Grafana, or the dashboards of your cloud, show trends. Event loop delay, from lesson 44, is a good Node-specific metric.
**Alerts that people can act on.** Too many alerts teach everyone to ignore them.

content.text: Backups

Databases are lost through mistakes, bugs, attacks and broken disks. A backup is the only cure, and a backup that was never tested is a hope, not a backup. The script below dumps the MongoDB database every night, compresses it, and deletes dumps older than 14 days.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Daily database backup. Run from cron:  0 2 * * * /var/www/app/backup.sh
set -euo pipefail
STAMP=$(date +%F)
DEST=/var/backups/app
mkdir -p "$DEST"
mongodump --uri "$MONGODB_URI" --archive="$DEST/db-$STAMP.gz" --gzip
find "$DEST" -name 'db-*.gz' -mtime +14 -delete        # keep 14 days
# Copy $DEST to another machine or a storage bucket too. A backup on the same disk is not enough.
# And TEST a restore now and then:  mongorestore --uri "$TEST_URI" --archive=... --gzip

items: Follow the **3-2-1 idea**: three copies, on two kinds of storage, with one copy in another place.
Copy backups **off the server**, for example to a storage bucket. A backup on the same disk dies with the disk.
Encrypt backups that contain personal data, and restrict who can read them.
**Test the restore** on a separate machine, on a schedule. Write down how long it takes.
MongoDB Atlas and most managed databases offer automatic backups. Turn them on and read what they include.

content.text: The workflow file and the backup script in this lesson were written to follow the current documentation, but they were not run on a real server when the lesson was written, because that needs a machine, a domain or an account. Run them first on a test server, read each line, and check the current documentation of every tool before you use them for something that matters.
Your task

items: Add a CI workflow to a repository that only runs the tests, without the deploy job.
Add a `/health` route that pings the database and returns 503 on failure.
Run the backup script on a test database, then restore it into another database and compare the document counts.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: A pull request with a failing test shows a red mark.
The deploy job never runs on a failing build.
You have restored a backup at least once.

steps.say: Every push or pull request starts the workflow.
CI installs the exact locked packages, audits them and runs the tests. A failure stops everything.
Only a passing build on main is deployed, and pm2 reload replaces the copies one by one.
Health checks, logs and error alerts watch the result. Backups protect the data.

faqs.q: What is the difference between CI and CD?
faqs.a: CI runs checks on every change. CD publishes the version automatically after the checks pass.

faqs.q: What is zero-downtime deployment?
faqs.a: Replacing the running app without a period when users get errors, for example by restarting copies one at a time behind a balancer.

faqs.q: How often should I test a backup restore?
faqs.a: At least when you set it up and then on a regular schedule, such as every few months. An untested backup may not work when you need it.

quiz.q: What does CI do?
options: Runs checks and tests automatically on every change

quiz.q: Why test a backup restore?
options: An untested backup may not work when you need it

quiz.q: What does the 3-2-1 backup idea suggest?
options: Three copies, two storage types, one in another place

lessons.title: TypeScript, Prisma, Redis, PostgreSQL and AWS: The Wider Node Stack
lessons.metaTitle: TypeScript, Prisma, Redis, Postgres and AWS
lessons.description: A guide to the tools around Node.js that job listings mention: TypeScript with Express, Prisma, Redis, PostgreSQL, AWS basics, Git and API docs.

content.text: Job descriptions for Node developers list a long set of tools. Nobody learns all of them at once, and no one expects it. What they expect is that you understand what each tool is for, have used one or two properly, and can learn the rest when needed. This lesson is a map of the common ones, with one working TypeScript example, so that you know where each tool fits and what to learn next.
TypeScript

**TypeScript** is JavaScript with types. You describe the shape of data, and the compiler warns you when code does not match it, before the program runs. In a back end this catches typos in field names, missing `await`s and wrong arguments. The nice trick used below is to write the validation rule once with Zod and **derive the type from it** with `z.infer`, so the runtime check and the compile-time type can never disagree.

Install `typescript` and the type packages with `npm install -D typescript @types/express @types/node`, and compile with `npx tsc`. In development, tools such as `tsx` run TypeScript files directly. The code above compiled without errors with the TypeScript compiler. Types exist only at compile time, so they do not replace validation of requests: that is why Zod is still used.
The rest of the map

items: **Prisma and PostgreSQL:** the SQL route shown in lesson 31. Learn tables, relations, joins, indexes and migrations. This is the most common pairing in new TypeScript back ends.
**Redis:** the shared in-memory store from lessons 39 and 40 for caching, sessions, rate limits and queues. Learn strings, hashes, expiry and how to keep keys organised.

**AWS:** the largest cloud. Start with four services: **EC2** for virtual servers, **S3** for file storage, **RDS** for managed databases, and **IAM** for access control. Learn IAM carefully, because wrong permissions cause most cloud security incidents. Other clouds, Google Cloud and Azure, work along the same lines.
**Git and GitHub:** branches, pull requests and code review. Use small commits with clear messages, and never commit secrets.
**API documentation:** the OpenAPI file from lesson 26, kept in the repository.
**Docker, CI/CD and monitoring:** the last three lessons.

content.text: How to learn the rest without being overwhelmed

items: Choose **one stack** and build a real project on it from start to finish. A good choice is TypeScript, Express, PostgreSQL with Prisma, Redis for caching, Docker, and GitHub Actions.
Add each new tool only when a real need appears in your project, such as slow lists, which need a cache, or a slow email, which needs a queue.
Write down for each tool: what problem it solves, one alternative, and one limitation. This is the form interviewers ask in.
Put the project online with a README, a live link, and a short description of the decisions that you made. That page is your best answer to "tell me about a project".

content.text: Tools and versions change fast. Treat the tool names here as the current common choices at the time of writing, not as permanent truths, and check their official documentation before you start.

Your resume should show this work honestly. List the tools that you used in a real project, and be ready to explain how. A short list that you can defend is stronger than a long list of names. You can build a clean, ATS-friendly resume with our [resume templates](/templates), and check how it reads to an applicant tracking system with the [ATS checker](/features/ats-checker).

The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.
Your task

items: Compile the TypeScript example and add a `GET /tasks` route with a typed response.
Make a table of the tools in this lesson with the columns problem, alternative and limitation.
Plan a project that uses at least TypeScript, one database and one cache.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: `tsc` finishes without errors.
You can say why TypeScript types do not replace request validation.
You can name the problem that each tool in this lesson solves.

steps.say: TypeScript catches wrong field names and arguments before the app runs.
PostgreSQL with Prisma stores strongly connected data with migrations and typed queries.
Redis speeds up reads and carries queues and counters shared by all copies.
Docker and a cloud such as AWS run the copies, with IAM controlling who can do what.

faqs.q: Do I need TypeScript to get a Node job?
faqs.a: Many employers prefer it, and it is common in new projects. Good JavaScript and a real project still get you interviews, and TypeScript is easy to add afterwards.

faqs.q: Which AWS services should I learn first?
faqs.a: EC2 for servers, S3 for files, RDS for databases and IAM for permissions. IAM matters most for safety.

faqs.q: Should I list every tool on my resume?
faqs.a: No. List the tools you used in a real project and can explain. A short, honest list beats a long list of names.

quiz.q: Why is Zod still used with TypeScript?
options: Types exist only at compile time and do not check real requests

quiz.q: Which AWS service stores files?
How should you list tools on a resume?
options: Every tool you have heard of
Only those you used in a real project and can explain

lessons.title: Project 1: A CRUD REST API for Users
lessons.metaTitle: Project 1: Users CRUD REST API
lessons.description: Build your first complete Express REST API: create, read, update and delete users with validation, paging, search, unique emails and correct status codes.

content.text: Every back end developer builds a CRUD API first, and interviewers still ask to see one. CRUD stands for create, read, update and delete, the four things you do with almost any kind of data. This project is small enough to finish in an evening, and complete enough to show that you know the details that separate a tutorial from real work: validation, unique emails, paging, search, the difference between PUT and PATCH, and honest status codes. All ten projects in this part of the course follow the same pattern: a short description, the code, the rules that matter, and a test that proves them.
What you will build

items: `POST /api/users` creates a user and returns **201** with a `Location` header.
`GET /api/users` lists users with `page`, `limit` and a search word `q`.
`GET`, `PUT`, `PATCH` and `DELETE` on `/api/users/:id`.
Clean validation messages with **422**, a duplicate email with **409**, a missing user with **404**, and delete with **204**.

content.text: Design decisions before any code

A user has an id, a name, an email, an optional age and a creation time. Before writing code, decide the rules, because rules are the real content of an API. A name needs at least two letters. An email must look like an email, is trimmed and turned into lower case, and must be unique, so that `ASHA@Example.com` and `asha@example.com` cannot be two people. An age, if sent, must be a whole number between 0 and 120.

The shape of the code follows lesson 24. The `clean` function checks and cleans a body and throws an `AppError` with the right status code, and one error handler at the bottom turns errors into JSON replies. The shared file `p-kit.js` holds `AppError` and the handlers, and the later projects reuse it, so read it first.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Install what the lesson needs: `npm install express jsonwebtoken`.
Copy `p-kit.js`, `p01-users.js` and `p01.test.js` into the folder. The shared `p-kit.js` is in Project 1.
Install the test tools with `npm install -D supertest`, then run `node --test p01.test.js`.

content.text: First the shared helpers. `AppError` carries a status code, `requireAuth` and `requireRole` protect routes, and `errorHandler` makes sure that a bug never shows its stack trace to the client.
Now the project. Read `clean`, then `createApp`, and notice how short each route is, because the rules live in `clean` and in two small helpers.
The test goes through the whole life of a user and checks each rule.
Rules worth understanding

**PUT replaces, PATCH changes.** A `PUT` sends the whole new version of the user, so a field that you leave out disappears. A `PATCH` sends only what changes, so the rest stays. The test shows this with the `age` field: after a `PATCH` it is still there, and after a `PUT` it is gone. Many APIs use `PUT` for both, and that is a common source of confusion.

**Conflict is not invalid.** A malformed email is **422**: the data fails the rules. A duplicate email is **409**: the data is fine, but it clashes with something that already exists. Telling the two apart lets a front end show the right message.

**Paging and search together.** The list route clamps `limit` to 50, falls back to defaults for bad numbers, and applies the search before slicing the page, so that `total` in the reply counts the matches and not all users. Front ends use that number to draw page buttons.
**A missing user inside a helper.** The `find` helper throws a 404 `AppError`, so every route that needs a user is a single line and none of them can forget to check.
Security and honesty notes

There is no login in this first project, so anyone can call it. In a real system these routes sit behind the authentication of Project 2. The body is never copied straight into the stored user: `clean` builds a new object with only the allowed fields, which protects you from a client sending extra fields such as `isAdmin`.
The email check here is a simple pattern. The only real proof that an address works is to send a message to it, as lesson 33 does.

The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.

To keep every project runnable with no setup, the data is kept in memory and disappears when the server restarts. The first extension task of every project is to move the store to MongoDB or PostgreSQL. The rules and the tests stay the same, which is exactly why the code is split into layers.
Folder structure for the real version

The files in this course are flat, so that you can read each project in one sitting. In a real repository, split them as lesson 19 and lesson 32 showed. This is a sensible layout for this project, and the purpose of each folder is in the comments.

users-api/
├── package.json
├── .env.example          # PORT, MONGODB_URI (no real values)
└── src/
    ├── server.js         # app.listen only
    ├── app.js            # middleware, routes, 404 and error handler
    ├── routes/users.routes.js
    ├── controllers/users.controller.js   # req and res
    ├── services/users.service.js         # rules: unique email
    ├── repositories/users.repository.js  # the only file that talks to the database
    ├── validators/users.schema.js        # Zod schemas
    └── middleware/error-handler.js
tests/users.test.js
Test the API with Postman

Start the app, open Postman, and create a collection for this project. Set a collection variable `baseUrl` to `http://localhost:3000`, and use `{{baseUrl}}` in every request, so that the same collection works on a live server later. Where a route needs a login, open the *Authorization* tab, choose *Bearer Token* and paste the token. These are the requests to send, in order. The automated test above sends the same ones, so the answers must match.

items: `POST {{baseUrl}}/api/users` with `{"name":"Asha","email":"asha@example.com","age":29}` expects 201 and a Location header.
The same request again expects 409. Send `{"name":"A","email":"x"}` and expect 422.
`GET {{baseUrl}}/api/users?q=asha&page=1&limit=5` expects a list with `meta.total`.
`PATCH {{baseUrl}}/api/users/1` with `{"name":"Asha K"}` keeps the age. `PUT` with a full body replaces it.
`DELETE {{baseUrl}}/api/users/1` expects 204, and a `GET` afterwards expects 404.

content.text: Add a small test to a request in the *Scripts* tab, such as checking that the status is 201, and run the whole collection with the *Collection runner*. You can also import an OpenAPI file, as lesson 26 showed, to get all requests at once.
Deploy it

The deployment steps are the same for every project in this part of the course, and each is taught in full earlier. First run the tests and `npm audit`. Put secrets such as `JWT_SECRET` in environment variables, never in Git. Then pick one route: a VPS with PM2, nginx and a Let's Encrypt certificate (lesson 48), or Docker and Compose (lesson 49). Automate it with GitHub Actions (lesson 50). Replace the in-memory store with a real database first, because a restart on the server would otherwise erase the data, and add a `/health` route for monitoring.
Extend it
Your task

items: Move the store to MongoDB with Mongoose and add a unique index on the email.
Add sorting with an allow-list of fields.
Write the OpenAPI file for these routes, as in lesson 26, and open it in Swagger UI.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Your test passes.
A duplicate email returns 409 and a bad email returns 422.
You can explain the difference between PUT and PATCH using the age field.

content.text: **On your resume.** A line such as "Built a REST API with Express, with validation, paging, search and automated tests with Supertest" is honest and specific. Write only what you really built and can explain, and keep the repository link next to it. Our [resume templates](/templates) have a project section that suits this, and the [ATS checker](/features/ats-checker) shows how a tracking system reads it.

steps.say: A client sends a JSON body.
The clean function checks every field and throws a 422 error with a clear message.
The store checks that the email is unique, otherwise a 409 conflict.
The reply is 201 with the new user and its URL in the Location header.

faqs.q: Why is 409 used for a duplicate email?
faqs.a: The data is valid but conflicts with existing data. 422 is for data that breaks the rules.

faqs.q: Should the id be a number or a string?
faqs.a: Databases such as MongoDB use string ids. Numbers are simple for learning. Either way, treat the id as text from the URL and convert it on purpose.

faqs.q: Why return a Location header?
faqs.a: It tells the client the URL of the new item, which is the REST convention for 201 Created.

quiz.q: Which status code fits a duplicate email?
What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
options: PUT replaces the whole item, PATCH changes only the fields sent

quiz.q: What does the Location header on 201 hold?
options: The URL of the new item

lessons.title: Project 2: An Authentication System
lessons.metaTitle: Project 2: Authentication, JWT and Reset
lessons.description: Build a complete login system in Express: register, log in with bcrypt and JWT, rotate refresh tokens, reset a forgotten password and protect routes.

content.text: Login is the first feature that every real product needs, and the one where mistakes hurt most. This project puts together the ideas of lessons 32 and 33 into one working service that you could put in front of any other app: registration, login, refresh tokens that rotate, a forgot-password flow that does not reveal who has an account, and a protected route. It is a strong project for a portfolio, because many candidates only show a login form, and few show that they understand what happens behind it.
What you will build

items: `POST /auth/register` with validation and password hashing.
`POST /auth/login` that returns a short-lived access token and a refresh token.
`POST /auth/refresh` that rotates the refresh token and refuses a reused one.
`POST /auth/forgot-password` and `/auth/reset-password` with an expiring, single-use token.
`GET /me`, a route that needs a valid token.

content.text: Design decisions before any code

The service stores a user with a **password hash**, never the password. It stores refresh tokens as hashes with an expiry and a `used` flag. It stores a reset token as a hash with an expiry time. The clock is passed in as `now`, so that the test can move time forward instead of waiting fifteen minutes.

The only thing the client ever keeps is the two tokens. The access token proves who the user is for a few minutes. The refresh token can only be exchanged once for a new pair. Compare the code with lesson 32 and notice what this project adds: the full password reset.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Install what the lesson needs: `npm install express jsonwebtoken bcryptjs`.
Copy `p-kit.js`, `p02-auth.js` and `p02.test.js` into the folder. The shared `p-kit.js` is in Project 1.
Install the test tools with `npm install -D supertest`, then run `node --test p02.test.js`.

content.text: The service in one file. Read the register and login routes first, then the refresh route, and last the two password routes.
The test registers, logs in, refreshes, tries to reuse a refresh token, resets a password and checks that the old password no longer works.
Rules worth understanding

**The same answer for a wrong user and a wrong password.** Login replies `Wrong email or password` in both cases. If it said which one was wrong, an attacker could use the form to find out which emails are registered.

**Refresh tokens are single-use.** A refresh token is marked used when it is exchanged. If someone presents it again, the server answers 401 and the user has to log in again. A used token appearing a second time is a sign that it was copied.

**Reset tokens expire and work once.** The token is random, stored only as a hash, valid for a short time, and removed after use. The reply to `forgot-password` is identical whether or not the email exists.

**Hashing is slow on purpose.** `bcrypt.compare` takes a noticeable fraction of a second, so an attacker who guesses passwords pays that cost on every guess. Use the asynchronous version so the event loop is not blocked, as lesson 44 explains.
Security and honesty notes

In this project the reset token is handed to a `mailer` object, and the test passes in a fake mailer that remembers it, so that the test can read it. A real service sends it by email, as in lesson 33, and never returns it in the HTTP reply. Add rate limiting to login and forgot-password before you put anything like this online.
The secret used to sign tokens has a development default in `p-kit.js`. Production must set `JWT_SECRET` to a long random value, and the code should refuse to start without it, as lesson 36 shows.

The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.

To keep every project runnable with no setup, the data is kept in memory and disappears when the server restarts. The first extension task of every project is to move the store to MongoDB or PostgreSQL. The rules and the tests stay the same, which is exactly why the code is split into layers.
Folder structure for the real version

The files in this course are flat, so that you can read each project in one sitting. In a real repository, split them as lesson 19 and lesson 32 showed. This is a sensible layout for this project, and the purpose of each folder is in the comments.

auth-service/
├── package.json
├── .env.example          # JWT_SECRET, REFRESH_SECRET, SMTP_*
└── src/
    ├── server.js
    ├── app.js
    ├── routes/auth.routes.js
    ├── controllers/auth.controller.js
    ├── services/auth.service.js       # hashing, tokens, reset rules
    ├── repositories/users.repository.js
    ├── repositories/tokens.repository.js  # refresh and reset token hashes
    ├── middleware/require-auth.js
    ├── mail/mailer.js                 # Nodemailer in production, a fake in tests
    └── config/env.js                  # validated settings
tests/auth.test.js
Test the API with Postman

Start the app, open Postman, and create a collection for this project. Set a collection variable `baseUrl` to `http://localhost:3000`, and use `{{baseUrl}}` in every request, so that the same collection works on a live server later. Where a route needs a login, open the *Authorization* tab, choose *Bearer Token* and paste the token. These are the requests to send, in order. The automated test above sends the same ones, so the answers must match.

items: `POST {{baseUrl}}/auth/register` with name, email and an 8+ character password expects 201.
`POST {{baseUrl}}/auth/login` expects the tokens. Save the access token in a variable, and use it as the Bearer token.
`GET {{baseUrl}}/me` with the token expects your user, and without it expects 401.
`POST {{baseUrl}}/auth/refresh` with the refresh token expects a new pair. Send the old one again and expect 401.
`POST {{baseUrl}}/auth/forgot-password` expects the same message for any email, then `/auth/reset-password` with the token from the email.

The deployment steps are the same for every project in this part of the course, and each is taught in full earlier. First run the tests and `npm audit`. Put secrets such as `JWT_SECRET` in environment variables, never in Git. Then pick one route: a VPS with PM2, nginx and a Let's Encrypt certificate (lesson 48), or Docker and Compose (lesson 49). Automate it with GitHub Actions (lesson 50). Replace the in-memory store with a real database first, because a restart on the server would otherwise erase the data, and add a `/health` route for monitoring.
Extend it
Your task

items: Replace the fake mailer with Nodemailer and a test inbox service.
Add email verification before the first login.
Add a `/logout` route that removes the refresh token, and a test for it.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: A used refresh token is refused.
The reset flow works once and fails the second time.
Unknown and known emails get the same reply from forgot-password.

content.text: **On your resume.** "Implemented JWT authentication with refresh-token rotation, bcrypt password hashing and a secure password reset flow" is a precise line that interviewers can ask about. Write only what you really built and can explain, and keep the repository link next to it. Our [resume templates](/templates) have a project section that suits this, and the [ATS checker](/features/ats-checker) shows how a tracking system reads it.

steps.say: Registration stores only a hash of the password.
Login compares the hash and returns a short access token and a refresh token.
Refreshing swaps the refresh token for a new pair. Reusing the old one fails.
A forgotten password is replaced through an expiring, single-use token.

faqs.q: Why not return the user password hash?
faqs.a: Even a hash helps an attacker who steals it. Never send it to a client and never log it.

faqs.q: How long should an access token live?
faqs.a: Common choices are 5 to 15 minutes. The shorter it is, the less a stolen token is worth.

faqs.q: Do I need both bcrypt and JWT?
faqs.a: They do different jobs. bcrypt protects stored passwords. JWT carries the proof of login in requests.

quiz.q: Why does login give the same message for a wrong email and a wrong password?
options: It stops attackers learning which emails exist

quiz.q: What happens when a used refresh token is presented again?
options: It is refused and the user must log in again

quiz.q: Why is bcrypt slow on purpose?
options: Every password guess costs an attacker time

lessons.title: Project 3: A Blog API with Roles
lessons.metaTitle: Project 3: Blog API with Roles
lessons.description: Build a blog back end in Express with posts, categories, comments and three roles: readers, authors who edit only their own posts, and admins who publish.

content.text: A blog sounds simple until you ask who may do what. Anyone may read a published post. A logged-in user may comment. An author may write and edit their own posts but not those of others. Only an admin may publish. That list of permissions is what makes this project a good test of your understanding of authorization, and it is a standard portfolio piece for a reason: the data is easy to understand, so the reviewer can concentrate on how you handled the rules.
What you will build

items: Public `GET /api/posts` that lists only published posts, with paging, a category filter and search.
`GET /api/posts/:slug` that shows one published post.
Authors and admins create, edit and delete posts. Authors only their own.
`POST /api/posts/:id/publish` for admins only.
Logged-in users add comments to published posts.
`GET /api/categories` with the number of posts in each.

content.text: Design decisions before any code

Three roles are used: `reader`, `author` and `admin`. A post has a title, a body, a slug made from the title, a category, a status of `draft` or `published`, and the id of its author. New posts always start as drafts, so an author can never publish by mistake or on purpose. Publishing is a separate action with its own route and its own role check.
Drafts must not leak. The public list and the single-post route filter on `status === 'published'`. A draft asked for by slug answers 404, not 403, because 403 would confirm that the draft exists.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Install what the lesson needs: `npm install express jsonwebtoken`.
Copy `p-kit.js`, `p03-blog.js` and `p03.test.js` into the folder. The shared `p-kit.js` is in Project 1.
Install the test tools with `npm install -D supertest`, then run `node --test p03.test.js`.

content.text: The code uses the helpers from `p-kit.js`: `requireAuth` for logged-in routes and `requireRole` for role checks. Notice that the ownership check for editing and deleting is written inside the route, because it needs the post that it loads.
The test plays the three roles one after another.
Rules worth understanding

**Role check first, ownership second.** `requireRole('author', 'admin')` decides whether the kind of user may use the route at all. Then the route loads the post and checks `post.authorId === req.user.id`, unless the user is an admin. Both checks are needed. A role says *what kind of user*, ownership says *whose data*. Forgetting the second check is one of the most common real-world access control bugs, because every author could then edit every post.

**Slugs.** A slug is the readable part of a URL, such as `my-first-post`. It is made from the title in lower case, with spaces turned into hyphens and strange characters removed, and it must be unique. Good slugs help both people and search engines.
**Comments belong to published posts only.** A comment on a draft or a missing post returns 404. The text is trimmed and limited to 1000 characters.
**Counting categories.** The categories route returns each name with its number of posts. With a database this becomes a `$group` stage of an aggregation, as in lesson 30.
Security and honesty notes

Comments contain text from strangers. The API stores them as they are, and the front end must escape them when drawing the page, as lesson 35 explains. If you allow HTML in posts, clean it with a library such as DOMPurify before you save or show it.
Never take the author id from the request body. The code uses `req.user.id` from the verified token.

The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.

To keep every project runnable with no setup, the data is kept in memory and disappears when the server restarts. The first extension task of every project is to move the store to MongoDB or PostgreSQL. The rules and the tests stay the same, which is exactly why the code is split into layers.
Folder structure for the real version

The files in this course are flat, so that you can read each project in one sitting. In a real repository, split them as lesson 19 and lesson 32 showed. This is a sensible layout for this project, and the purpose of each folder is in the comments.

blog-api/
├── package.json
└── src/
    ├── server.js
    ├── app.js
    ├── routes/posts.routes.js, comments.routes.js, categories.routes.js
    ├── controllers/
    ├── services/posts.service.js     # slugs, draft and publish rules
    ├── repositories/posts.repository.js
    ├── models/Post.js, Comment.js, User.js
    └── middleware/require-auth.js, require-role.js
tests/blog.test.js
Test the API with Postman

Start the app, open Postman, and create a collection for this project. Set a collection variable `baseUrl` to `http://localhost:3000`, and use `{{baseUrl}}` in every request, so that the same collection works on a live server later. Where a route needs a login, open the *Authorization* tab, choose *Bearer Token* and paste the token. These are the requests to send, in order. The automated test above sends the same ones, so the answers must match.

items: Log in as an author, then `POST {{baseUrl}}/api/posts` with a title, body and category. It is a draft, so it is not in `GET /api/posts`.
`POST {{baseUrl}}/api/posts/1/publish` as the author expects 403. As an admin it expects 200.
`GET {{baseUrl}}/api/posts?category=tech&q=node` now shows the post, and `GET /api/posts/<slug>` shows one.
`PATCH` the post as a different author and expect 403.
`POST {{baseUrl}}/api/posts/1/comments` with `{"text":"Nice"}` as a reader expects 201.

content.text: Add a small test to a request in the *Scripts* tab, such as checking that the status is 201, and run the whole collection with the *Collection runner*. You can also import an OpenAPI file, as lesson 26 showed, to get all requests at once.
Deploy it

The deployment steps are the same for every project in this part of the course, and each is taught in full earlier. First run the tests and `npm audit`. Put secrets such as `JWT_SECRET` in environment variables, never in Git. Then pick one route: a VPS with PM2, nginx and a Let's Encrypt certificate (lesson 48), or Docker and Compose (lesson 49). Automate it with GitHub Actions (lesson 50).
