Extend it
Your task

items: Add `GET /api/posts/mine` for an author to see their drafts.
Add tags with a filter, and an index on them in MongoDB.
Add a moderation flag to comments and an admin route to hide them.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: An author cannot edit another author's post.
A draft returns 404 to the public.
Only an admin can publish.

content.text: **On your resume.** "Designed role-based access control for a blog API, with ownership checks, draft and publish workflow and automated tests of every permission" shows that you understand authorization. Write only what you really built and can explain, and keep the repository link next to it. Our [resume templates](/templates) have a project section that suits this, and the [ATS checker](/features/ats-checker) shows how a tracking system reads it.

steps.say: Anyone may read published posts. Drafts are never shown.
An author creates drafts and edits only the posts that they own.
Only an admin can publish, or change any post.
Any logged-in user may comment on a published post.

faqs.q: Why return 404 for another author's draft?
faqs.a: A 403 would confirm that the draft exists. A 404 tells a stranger nothing.

faqs.q: What is a slug?
faqs.a: A readable, unique text in the URL, made from the title, such as my-first-post. It is better for people and for search engines than a number.

faqs.q: Where should roles be stored?
faqs.a: In your database, on the user. They are copied into the token by the server, and never read from the request body.

quiz.q: Why check ownership as well as the role?
options: A role says what kind of user, ownership says whose data

quiz.q: What does the public API return for a draft?
Who can publish a post?

lessons.title: Project 4: An E-Commerce Back End
lessons.metaTitle: Project 4: E-Commerce Back End
lessons.description: Build an online shop back end in Express: products, a cart per user, checkout with server-side prices, stock control and a payment provider behind an interface.

content.text: An online shop is the classic big portfolio project, and the code behind it is more interesting than the screens. Money is involved, stock is limited, and two customers may want the last item at the same moment. This project builds the core: products, a cart for each user, and checkout. Its real lessons are all about trust: never trust the price sent by the browser, check stock again at the moment of purchase, and never reduce stock for a payment that failed.
What you will build

items: `GET /api/products` shows products that are in stock.
`POST /api/products` lets an admin add a product with a price in cents and a stock count.
`PUT /api/cart/:productId` sets the quantity of a product in your cart, and 0 removes it.
`POST /api/orders` turns the cart into an order, charges the payment provider, reduces stock and empties the cart.
`GET /api/orders` shows the orders of the logged-in user.

content.text: Design decisions before any code

Prices are integers in cents. The cart stores only a product id and a quantity. When the customer checks out, the server looks up each price in its own data and calculates the total. The browser has no say in the price. That one rule prevents the oldest trick in e-commerce, changing a price in the browser's developer tools.

The payment provider is passed into `createApp` as an object with a `charge` function, so the test can use a fake that approves or declines, and a real provider can replace it later without changes to the shop. That is the storage driver idea of lesson 27 applied to money.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Install what the lesson needs: `npm install express jsonwebtoken`.
Copy `p-kit.js`, `p04-shop.js` and `p04.test.js` into the folder. The shared `p-kit.js` is in Project 1.
Install the test tools with `npm install -D supertest`, then run `node --test p04.test.js`.

content.text: The shop in one file. Read the checkout route slowly, because the order of its steps is the whole lesson.
The test covers an admin adding products, a customer filling a cart, a successful checkout, a declined payment, and a customer who asks for more than is in stock.
Rules worth understanding

**Checkout order matters.** The route checks that the cart is not empty, looks up every product, checks the stock **again**, adds up the total from the server's prices, charges the provider, and only if the payment works does it reduce stock and create the order. If the payment fails, nothing has changed and the reply is **402**. If the steps were in a different order, a failed payment could still remove stock.

**Stock races.** In this in-memory version, JavaScript runs one request at a time between awaits, so the check and the update are safe. With a database, two requests can both see 1 item left. The fix is the conditional update of lesson 30: `findOneAndUpdate({ _id, stock: { $gte: qty } }, { $inc: { stock: -qty } })`, which checks and subtracts in one step, or a transaction when several documents are involved.
**Own data only.** The cart and the order list are found by `req.user.id`. A customer can never read another customer's orders by changing an id in the URL.
**Hide products that are out of stock.** The product list filters on `stock > 0`, so customers do not see items that they cannot buy.
Security and honesty notes
Only an admin can add products. The body of that route is checked: a name, an integer price of at least 1, and an integer stock of 0 or more. A price of `-5` or `19.99` is refused.

In a real shop, the payment goes through a redirect or a hosted page and a webhook, as lesson 42 describes, and the order stays `pending` until the webhook arrives. This project charges directly through the fake provider to keep the stock logic easy to see.

The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.

To keep every project runnable with no setup, the data is kept in memory and disappears when the server restarts. The first extension task of every project is to move the store to MongoDB or PostgreSQL. The rules and the tests stay the same, which is exactly why the code is split into layers.
Folder structure for the real version

The files in this course are flat, so that you can read each project in one sitting. In a real repository, split them as lesson 19 and lesson 32 showed. This is a sensible layout for this project, and the purpose of each folder is in the comments.

shop-api/
├── package.json
├── .env.example          # PAYMENT_KEY, MONGODB_URI
└── src/
    ├── server.js
    ├── app.js
    ├── routes/products.routes.js, cart.routes.js, orders.routes.js
    ├── controllers/
    ├── services/checkout.service.js    # price, stock and payment steps
    ├── repositories/products.repository.js, orders.repository.js
    ├── payments/gateway.js             # the interface, with a fake for tests
    └── middleware/
tests/checkout.test.js
Test the API with Postman

Start the app, open Postman, and create a collection for this project. Where a route needs a login, open the *Authorization* tab, choose *Bearer Token* and paste the token. These are the requests to send, in order. The automated test above sends the same ones, so the answers must match.

items: As an admin, `POST {{baseUrl}}/api/products` with `{"name":"Pen","priceCents":1500,"stock":5}` expects 201. Try `"priceCents":9.99` and expect 422.
As a customer, `PUT {{baseUrl}}/api/cart/1` with `{"qty":2}` expects the cart. A quantity above the stock expects 409.
`POST {{baseUrl}}/api/orders` expects 201 and the total in cents.
Make the fake gateway decline, send it again and expect 402 with the stock unchanged.
`GET {{baseUrl}}/api/orders` shows only your orders.

Deploy it

The deployment steps are the same for every project in this part of the course, and each is taught in full earlier. First run the tests and `npm audit`. Extend it

content.text: **On your resume.** "Built the back end of an online shop with server-side pricing in cents, per-user carts, stock control and a payment gateway behind an interface, tested with mock payments" is a clear, true summary. Our [resume templates](/templates) have a project section that suits this, and the [ATS checker](/features/ats-checker) shows how a tracking system reads it.

steps.say: The cart holds only product ids and quantities.
The server looks up each price and checks stock again.
It charges the provider. A decline stops here with 402 and nothing changes.
Only after success does it reduce stock, save the order and clear the cart.

faqs.q: Why recheck stock at checkout?
faqs.a: Stock may have changed since the item was added to the cart. The check at the moment of purchase is the one that counts.

faqs.q: What is HTTP status 402?
faqs.a: Payment Required. It is rarely used but is a clear fit for a declined payment.

faqs.q: How do I stop two people buying the last item?
faqs.a: With a database, use a conditional atomic update or a transaction, so that checking and subtracting happen in one step.

quiz.q: Where does the checkout price come from?
When is stock reduced?
options: When the item enters the cart

options: A test can use a fake provider

lessons.title: Project 5: An Employee Management System
lessons.metaTitle: Project 5: Employee Management System
lessons.description: Build an HR back end in Express: departments, employees, daily attendance check-in and check-out, soft delete and four roles with different data access.

content.text: Company software is where role-based access control becomes interesting, because the rules are not only about actions but about *which rows* a person may see. An HR officer sees everyone. A manager sees only their department. An employee sees only themselves. This project builds an employee system with departments and attendance, and its main lesson is the idea of **scoping**: the same URL returns different data to different users.
What you will build

items: Admins and HR create departments and employees.
`GET /api/employees` returns all employees to HR and admins, the department to a manager, and only themselves to an employee.
Soft delete: removing an employee keeps their history.
Employees check in and check out once a day.
Admins, HR and managers read attendance.

content.text: Design decisions before any code

There are four roles: `admin`, `hr`, `manager` and `employee`. Every employee belongs to a department, and managers belong to the department they manage. A route that lists data must filter by what the caller is allowed to see, and the filter belongs on the server, never in the front end. A front end that hides rows is decoration. The API must refuse to send them.

Deleting an employee changes a field, `active: false`, instead of removing the record. Attendance history, payroll history and audit trails refer to the person, so the record must stay. Deactivated employees can no longer check in.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Install what the lesson needs: `npm install express jsonwebtoken`.
Copy `p-kit.js`, `p05-employees.js` and `p05.test.js` into the folder. The shared `p-kit.js` is in Project 1.
Install the test tools with `npm install -D supertest`, then run `node --test p05.test.js`.

content.text: Read the list route first, because it contains the scoping rule. Then read the two attendance routes.
The clock is a parameter again, so the test can pretend that it is a different day without waiting.
Rules worth understanding

**Scoping by role.** The list route starts with every employee and narrows it: no change for `admin` and `hr`, only the manager's own department for a `manager`, and only the person's own record for an `employee`. Test each role on the same URL and compare the results.

**One check-in per day.** The attendance record has the employee id and the date. A second check-in on the same date answers **409**. Check-out is allowed only after a check-in, and only once. The date comes from the server clock, in one known time zone, never from the client, because a client could claim any day.
**Soft delete.** `DELETE` sets `active` to false and keeps the record. Listing, check-in and reports must then agree on how they treat inactive people, and a test should protect that decision.
**Unique department names.** Names are compared in lower case, so `Sales` and `sales` are the same department and the second one answers 409.
Security and honesty notes

Personal data about employees is sensitive, and in many countries the law controls how it is stored and who may see it. Collect only what you need, protect it with the role checks shown here, log who reads sensitive records, and ask for professional advice before you use anything like this with real people.
Time zones are a classic source of bugs. Decide on the zone of the company, and calculate the date in it, rather than using the server's local time by accident.

The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.

To keep every project runnable with no setup, the data is kept in memory and disappears when the server restarts. The first extension task of every project is to move the store to MongoDB or PostgreSQL. The rules and the tests stay the same, which is exactly why the code is split into layers.

The files in this course are flat, so that you can read each project in one sitting. In a real repository, split them as lesson 19 and lesson 32 showed. This is a sensible layout for this project, and the purpose of each folder is in the comments.

hr-api/
├── package.json
└── src/
    ├── server.js
    ├── app.js
    ├── routes/departments.routes.js, employees.routes.js, attendance.routes.js
    ├── controllers/
    ├── services/employees.service.js   # scoping rules by role
    ├── services/attendance.service.js  # one check-in a day
    ├── repositories/
    ├── models/Department.js, Employee.js, Attendance.js
    └── middleware/require-auth.js, require-role.js

lessons.title: Project 6: A Real-Time Chat Application
lessons.metaTitle: Project 6: Real-Time Chat with Socket.IO
lessons.description: Build a chat back end with Socket.IO and Express: JWT-authenticated sockets, private messages, online status, saved history and a REST route to read it.

content.text: Chat is the favourite real-time project, because you can see it work with two browser tabs. Under the screen there are three real questions. How do you know who is connecting? How do you deliver a message to exactly one person? And what happens to the messages when the person is offline? This project answers them with Socket.IO for live delivery and a normal REST route for history, which is how real chat apps are built: sockets for what is happening now, HTTP for what has already happened.
What you will build

items: Sockets that connect only with a valid JWT.
Private messages sent to one user, delivered to every device that they have open.
An online list that updates when people connect or leave.
Saved history for each pair of users.
`GET /api/messages/:other` that returns a conversation for the logged-in user.

content.text: Design decisions before any code

Each conversation has a key made from the two user ids in sorted order, so that `alice:bob` and `bob:alice` are the same thread. Messages are saved in a `Map` here and in a collection in a real system, with an index on the conversation key and the time. The sender of a message is always taken from the verified token on the socket, never from the message itself, because a message that says `from: someone-else` must not be believed.
This project builds on lesson 41. Read that first if the words *room* and *handshake* are new.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Install what the lesson needs: `npm install express socket.io jsonwebtoken`.
Copy `p-kit.js`, `p06-chat.js` and `p06.test.js` into the folder. The shared `p-kit.js` is in Project 1.
Install the test tools with `npm install -D supertest socket.io-client`, then run `node --test p06.test.js`.

content.text: The chat is created by `createChat`, which returns the HTTP server and the Socket.IO server together. Notice the connection counter: a user is offline only when the last of their sockets closes.
The test connects two real Socket.IO clients to the server on a free port, and checks delivery, history and presence.
Rules worth understanding
**Authenticate once, on connect.** The handshake middleware verifies the JWT. A bad token means the connection is refused, so no code that runs afterwards has to wonder who the user is.
**Validate every message.** A message must be a text, not empty and not too long. Anything else is ignored. Never trust the content just because it came through a trusted connection.

**Many tabs, one user.** A person may have a phone and a laptop open. Each is a socket in the same private room, so a message reaches both. The online list uses a counter per user, so closing one tab does not make a person look offline.

**History through HTTP.** When a user opens a conversation, the front end loads the saved messages with a normal request and then listens on the socket for new ones. HTTP is easy to cache, page and secure with the same middleware as the rest of your API.
Security and honesty notes

Escape message text when you draw it, because a chat is a perfect place for the cross-site scripting of lesson 35. Limit the message size and the number of messages per second for each user, or one client can flood the room.
With more than one server process, you need the Redis adapter of Socket.IO so that events pass between them, as lesson 41 explains. This project runs in one process.

The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.

To keep every project runnable with no setup, the data is kept in memory and disappears when the server restarts. The first extension task of every project is to move the store to MongoDB or PostgreSQL. The rules and the tests stay the same, which is exactly why the code is split into layers.

    ├── app.js             # REST routes
    ├── socket/index.js    # connection auth, rooms, events
    ├── socket/presence.js
    ├── routes/messages.routes.js
    ├── services/chat.service.js
    ├── repositories/messages.repository.js
    └── middleware/require-auth.js
tests/chat.test.js

The verified user joins a private room. Messages go to the room of the receiver.
Every message is saved under the conversation key.

faqs.q: Why use both sockets and REST?
faqs.a: Sockets are best for live events. REST is simple, cacheable and secure for loading the past. Real chat apps use both.

faqs.q: How do I know who sent a message?
faqs.a: From the token that was verified when the socket connected. Never from a field in the message.

faqs.q: What changes with several servers?
faqs.a: Use the Redis adapter, so events pass between server copies, and a load balancer that supports WebSockets.

From a field in the message

Why load history over REST?
options: HTTP is easy to page, cache and secure like the rest of the API

lessons.title: Project 7: A Hotel Booking System
lessons.metaTitle: Project 7: Hotel Booking System
lessons.description: Build a hotel booking API in Express: rooms, date-range availability, reservations that cannot overlap, payment and a cancellation rule with a partial refund.

content.text: Booking systems look easy and are famous for hiding hard problems. Two guests must never get the same room on the same night. Dates have edge cases. Payments fail halfway. Cancellations have rules. This project is a strong one for a portfolio because its logic is the kind that real companies struggle with, and because it is easy to test: you give it dates, and you check the answer.
What you will build

items: Admins add rooms with a number, a type and a price per night in cents.
`GET /api/availability?checkIn=...&checkOut=...` lists free rooms.
`POST /api/reservations` reserves a room, charges the payment provider and confirms.
`POST /api/reservations/:id/cancel` applies the refund rule.
Clear errors for bad dates, taken rooms and failed payments.

content.text: Design decisions before any code

Dates are plain text in the form `2026-12-24`, checked with a pattern and a real calendar check. A stay has a check-in day and a check-out day, and the number of nights is the difference. The most important rule is the overlap rule, and it is easy to get wrong, so it deserves a precise sentence: **two stays overlap when each one starts before the other one ends**. The check-out day is free, so a guest can leave in the morning and the next guest can arrive the same day, and the test checks exactly that.

Money is in cents, the total is the nights multiplied by the price, and the price comes from the server's room record. The clock is injected, so the test can make a stay start in 30 hours or in 10 days without waiting.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Install what the lesson needs: `npm install express jsonwebtoken`.
Copy `p-kit.js`, `p07-hotel.js` and `p07.test.js` into the folder. The shared `p-kit.js` is in Project 1.
Install the test tools with `npm install -D supertest`, then run `node --test p07.test.js`.

content.text: Read `overlaps` and `isFree` first. The reservation route then applies them in a clear order: validate, check room, check dates, check availability, charge, confirm.
Three tests: the overlap rule on its own, a full run of availability, booking, double booking and refunds, and a late cancellation together with a failed payment.
Rules worth understanding

**The overlap rule.** A new stay from `start` to `end` clashes with an existing one from `s` to `e` when `start < e` and `s < end`. If `end` equals `s`, the new guest leaves exactly when the other arrives, and that is allowed. Test the boundary days explicitly.

**Order of checks.** Cheap checks come first, such as dates and room. The availability check comes right before the payment. In a real database, the check and the creation of the reservation must happen together, with a unique constraint or a transaction, or two requests could both pass the check at the same instant.
**A failed payment is recorded.** If the provider declines, the reservation is marked `payment_failed` and the reply is 402. The dates are not held. The reservation does not block the room.

**Cancellation rule.** Cancelling at least 48 hours before check-in gives a full refund, and later gives 50 percent. The rule lives in one small function that is easy to read and test, because a refund rule is exactly the sort of thing that a business will change next month.
**Own reservations.** A guest can cancel only their own reservation, and an admin can cancel any. Others get 404.
Security and honesty notes
Do not let the client send the price or the total. Do not accept dates in the past. Reject stays that are unreasonably long, which an attacker could use to block a room for years.
The refund percentages and the 48-hour rule here are an example and not legal advice. Real businesses must follow the consumer laws of their country and their own published terms.

├── package.json
└── src/
    ├── server.js
    ├── app.js
    ├── routes/rooms.routes.js, reservations.routes.js
    ├── controllers/
    ├── services/availability.service.js   # the overlap rule
    ├── services/reservations.service.js   # payment and cancellation rules
    ├── repositories/
    ├── payments/gateway.js
    └── middleware/
tests/overlap.test.js, tests/booking.test.js
Test the API with Postman

Start the app, open Postman, and create a collection for this project. Set a collection variable `baseUrl` to `http://localhost:3000`, and use `{{baseUrl}}` in every request, so that the same collection works on a live server later. Where a route needs a login, open the *Authorization* tab, choose *Bearer Token* and paste the token. These are the requests to send, in order. The automated test above sends the same ones, so the answers must match.

items: As an admin, `POST {{baseUrl}}/api/rooms` with a number, a type and `pricePerNightCents`.
`GET {{baseUrl}}/api/availability?checkIn=2026-12-24&checkOut=2026-12-27` lists free rooms.
`POST {{baseUrl}}/api/reservations` with a room id and the same dates expects 201. The same room and overlapping dates expect 409.
Book a stay that starts on the earlier stay's check-out day and expect 201.
`POST {{baseUrl}}/api/reservations/1/cancel` far ahead expects a full refund, and close to check-in expects half.

Deploy it

The deployment steps are the same for every project in this part of the course, and each is taught in full earlier. First run the tests and `npm audit`. Put secrets such as `JWT_SECRET` in environment variables, never in Git. Then pick one route: a VPS with PM2, nginx and a Let's Encrypt certificate (lesson 48), or Docker and Compose (lesson 49). Automate it with GitHub Actions (lesson 50). Replace the in-memory store with a real database first, because a restart on the server would otherwise erase the data, and add a `/health` route for monitoring.
Extend it
Your task

items: Add a unique index or a transaction so that two simultaneous requests cannot book the same room.
Add a temporary hold of ten minutes while the guest pays.
Add seasonal prices, higher at weekends, calculated per night.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: A stay that starts on another stay's check-out day is accepted.
A declined payment does not block the room.
Cancelling 10 hours before check-in refunds 50 percent.

content.text: **On your resume.** "Implemented a booking engine with date-range availability, overlap detection, payments and a rule-based cancellation policy, covered by boundary-case tests" is exactly the kind of line that gets questions in an interview. Write only what you really built and can explain, and keep the repository link next to it. Our [resume templates](/templates) have a project section that suits this, and the [ATS checker](/features/ats-checker) shows how a tracking system reads it.

steps.say: The dates are validated: real calendar days, in the future, check-out after check-in.
The overlap rule decides if the room is free. A check-out day does not clash.
The payment is charged. A decline marks the reservation payment_failed and frees the room.
The reservation is confirmed. Later, a cancellation applies the 48-hour refund rule.

faqs.q: How do I stop double bookings under load?
faqs.a: Make the check and the insert one atomic step: a unique constraint, a conditional write or a transaction in the database.

faqs.q: Why is the check-out day free?
faqs.a: The guest leaves in the morning, so the next guest may arrive the same day. The overlap rule uses strict comparisons for this.

faqs.q: Should the refund rule be in the route?
faqs.a: Keep it in its own small function so that it is easy to read, test and change.

quiz.q: When do two stays overlap?
options: They have the same room number
Each one starts before the other ends

quiz.q: Can a guest arrive on another guest’s check-out day?
options: Yes, the check-out day is free

quiz.q: What does a failed payment do to the reservation?
options: Marks it payment_failed so the room is not blocked

lessons.title: Project 8: A File Upload and Storage API
lessons.metaTitle: Project 8: File Upload and Storage API
lessons.description: Build a personal file storage API in Express: uploads checked by real file type, per-user quotas, private downloads and a driver for local disk or ImageKit.

content.text: Almost every product stores files: profile pictures, invoices, resumes, attachments. This project is a small version of a cloud drive: users upload files, list them, download them and delete them, and every file belongs to its owner. It combines three earlier lessons, the safe uploads of lesson 27, the roles and tokens of lesson 32 and the interface idea of dependency injection, so that the bytes can live on a disk today and in the cloud tomorrow.
What you will build

items: `POST /api/files` uploads a file in the field `file`, for logged-in users.
Allowed types: PNG, JPEG, PDF and plain text, from an allow-list.
A storage quota for each user.
`GET /api/files` lists your files, and `GET /api/files/:id` downloads one.
`DELETE /api/files/:id` removes the bytes and the record.
A driver with three functions, `put`, `get` and `remove`, so that storage is replaceable.

content.text: Design decisions before any code

Two things are stored for each upload: the **bytes**, which go to the driver under a random key, and a **record**, with the owner, the original name, the real type, the size and the key. The user's original file name is kept only as a label. It is never used to build a path. The record is what the API lists and checks. A file belongs to a person if and only if `record.ownerId` equals the user from the token.

Because the driver is a small interface, the tests run with a folder in the operating system's temporary directory, and production can use a cloud driver. The second file below shows the same three functions on ImageKit, which is how the main server of this site stores its images. It was **not run**, because it needs an account and keys, so read it as a pattern and follow the current documentation of the service.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Install what the lesson needs: `npm install express multer jsonwebtoken`.
Copy `p-kit.js`, `p08-files.js` and `p08.test.js` into the folder. The shared `p-kit.js` is in Project 1.
Install the test tools with `npm install -D supertest`, then run `node --test p08.test.js`.

content.text: The API and the local-folder driver. Read the upload route to see the order of checks: type, then quota, then save.
The same driver interface for ImageKit. For cloud storage, you normally serve files by URL, so `get` explains that.
The test uploads allowed files, an `.exe` file, a file that is too large and uploads that pass the quota, and then tests downloads and deletes by the owner and by someone else.
Rules worth understanding

**An allow-list of types.** Only four types are accepted, and anything else is refused with **415**. This project trusts the type that the upload declares. That is a weakness, because a client can lie about it, and lesson 27 shows the stronger check of reading the first bytes. Adding that check is the first extension task.

**A quota per user.** Before saving, the code adds the new size to what the user already stores. If the total goes above the quota, the reply is **413**. Without a quota, one account can fill your disk or your cloud bill.
**404 instead of 403.** If the file exists but belongs to someone else, the reply is `File not found`. A 403 would reveal that a file with that id exists, and ids can be guessed.
**Clean up both sides.** Deleting removes the bytes from the driver and the record from the list. If the first step fails, the record must stay, so you can try again.
**Download headers.** Send the stored type, and for types that a browser could run, such as HTML, force a download with `Content-Disposition: attachment`. This project does not allow HTML at all.
Security and honesty notes

The names given by the user are never part of a path, and the key is a random UUID with an extension that the server chose. Files are stored outside the folders that Express serves as static content. Ask whether uploaded files could contain malware, and if the files are shared with others, add a virus scan.
Edge cases are where upload bugs live, so test a file that is too large, a type that is not allowed, and a user who is exactly at the limit of the quota.

The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.

To keep every project runnable with no setup, the data is kept in memory and disappears when the server restarts. The first extension task of every project is to move the store to MongoDB or PostgreSQL. The rules and the tests stay the same, which is exactly why the code is split into layers.

└── src/
    ├── server.js

    ├── routes/files.routes.js
    ├── controllers/files.controller.js
    ├── services/files.service.js       # type check and quota
    ├── storage/local-driver.js, imagekit-driver.js
    ├── repositories/files.repository.js
    └── middleware/upload.js            # Multer settings
tests/files.test.js
Test the API with Postman

Start the app, open Postman, and create a collection for this project. Set a collection variable `baseUrl` to `http://localhost:3000`, and use `{{baseUrl}}` in every request, so that the same collection works on a live server later. Where a route needs a login, open the *Authorization* tab, choose *Bearer Token* and paste the token. These are the requests to send, in order. The automated test above sends the same ones, so the answers must match.

items: `POST {{baseUrl}}/api/files` with the body type *form-data*, a key `file` of type *File*, and choose a PNG. Expect 201.
Upload an `.exe` file and expect 415. Upload a file above the limit and expect 413.
`GET {{baseUrl}}/api/files` lists your files. `GET /api/files/1` downloads one (use *Send and Download*).

Extend it
Your task

content.text: **On your resume.** "Built a file storage API with an allow-list of types, per-user quotas, owner-only access and a swappable storage driver for local disk and ImageKit" describes it well. Do not claim the cloud driver works in production unless you have run it. Write only what you really built and can explain, and keep the repository link next to it. Our [resume templates](/templates) have a project section that suits this, and the [ATS checker](/features/ats-checker) shows how a tracking system reads it.

steps.say: A logged-in user uploads one file.
The server checks the real type from the first bytes and the user quota.
The driver saves the bytes under a random key. It could be disk or cloud.
A record links the key to the owner. Only the owner can list, download or delete.

faqs.q: Why does the driver have only three functions?
faqs.a: A small interface is easy to implement for any storage and easy to replace without changing the API.

faqs.q: Why hide that a file exists?
faqs.a: Ids can be guessed. Answering 404 for someone else's file tells a stranger nothing.

faqs.q: Disk or cloud storage?
faqs.a: Disk is fine for one server and small apps. Cloud storage suits several servers, large files and public delivery.

quiz.q: Why return 404 for another user’s file?
options: A 403 would reveal that the file exists

quiz.q: What does the storage quota prevent?
options: One account filling your disk or cloud bill

quiz.q: What is a weakness of trusting the declared file type?
options: A client can lie about it

lessons.title: Project 9: A SaaS Subscription Back End
lessons.metaTitle: Project 9: SaaS Subscription Back End
lessons.description: Build a subscription back end in Express: plans, checkout, entitlement limits per plan, and billing events from a signed, idempotent webhook with past-due.

content.text: A SaaS product earns money from subscriptions, and behind every pricing page there is a back end that answers one question on every request: *what is this account allowed to do right now?* This project builds that core. It has plans with limits, a way to start a subscription, a webhook that activates the plan only when the provider confirms payment, and a limit check on the feature that is being sold. It combines the payment rules of lesson 42 with the access control of Project 3.
What you will build

items: `GET /api/plans` shows the plans and their limits.
`POST /api/subscribe` starts a checkout for a paid plan. It does **not** activate it.
`POST /webhooks/billing` receives signed events that activate, renew or mark an account past due.
`GET /api/account` shows the plan, its limits and the current usage.
`POST /api/projects` creates a project only if the plan allows more of them.

content.text: Design decisions before any code

There are three plans, `free`, `pro` and `team`, each with a price in cents and a limit for the number of projects. The prices in the code are only an example, and your own product will have its own. The account of each user has a plan, a status and a renewal date. The rule that makes billing safe is: **the plan changes only because of a verified webhook, never because the client says so, and never because the browser came back from the payment page**.

The limit check is called an **entitlement check**. It runs on the server on every request that uses a limited feature, and it reads the current plan from your own data. A front end can show a locked button to be polite, but the real lock is the check in the route.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Install what the lesson needs: `npm install express jsonwebtoken`.
Copy `p-kit.js`, `p09-saas.js` and `p09.test.js` into the folder. The shared `p-kit.js` is in Project 1.
Install the test tools with `npm install -D supertest`, then run `node --test p09.test.js`.

content.text: Read the webhook first: signature, duplicate check, then the state change. Then read the entitlement check in the projects route.
The test subscribes, shows that the plan is still free, sends a signed webhook, and then shows that the limit has risen. It also tests a duplicate event and a payment failure.
Rules worth understanding

**Subscribe starts, the webhook finishes.** `/api/subscribe` asks the billing provider for a checkout link and returns it. The account stays on its old plan. Only a verified `subscription.paid` event changes the plan, and the test proves that the plan does not change before the webhook.
**Signed and raw.** The webhook route is registered before `express.json()` and uses the raw body for the HMAC check, as in lesson 42, with a constant-time comparison.
**Idempotent events.** The id of every event is remembered, and a repeated event is acknowledged without being applied twice. A renewal that was counted twice would extend an account for free.

**Past due.** When a payment fails, the status becomes `past_due`, and the projects route answers **402** with a clear message. You decide the policy: many products give a grace period before they limit a feature.

**Limits on every request.** The number of projects is compared with the limit of the current plan at the moment of creation. A free account that tries to create a second project gets **403**, and the same request works after the paid webhook. A downgrade or a failed payment takes effect immediately.
Security and honesty notes

Never trust a plan name from the client in the webhook either. The provider event should contain an id that you created during checkout, which you map back to your own record. Prices, taxes and invoices follow the laws of your country, and a real provider handles much of that for you. This project is a learning model, not an accounting system.
A real provider has its own library, event names and signature header, so follow its current documentation. This lesson uses a fake provider, so that the logic can be run and tested.

The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.

To keep every project runnable with no setup, the data is kept in memory and disappears when the server restarts. The first extension task of every project is to move the store to MongoDB or PostgreSQL. The rules and the tests stay the same, which is exactly why the code is split into layers.
Folder structure for the real version

The files in this course are flat, so that you can read each project in one sitting. In a real repository, split them as lesson 19 and lesson 32 showed. This is a sensible layout for this project, and the purpose of each folder is in the comments.

saas-api/
├── package.json
├── .env.example          # BILLING_WEBHOOK_SECRET, BILLING_API_KEY
└── src/
    ├── server.js
    ├── app.js
    ├── routes/plans.routes.js, account.routes.js, projects.routes.js
    ├── routes/webhooks.routes.js      # raw body, before express.json()
    ├── services/billing.service.js    # webhook events to plan changes
    ├── services/entitlements.service.js
    ├── repositories/accounts.repository.js, events.repository.js
    └── billing/provider.js            # real provider or a fake
tests/saas.test.js
Test the API with Postman

Start the app, open Postman, and create a collection for this project. Set a collection variable `baseUrl` to `http://localhost:3000`, and use `{{baseUrl}}` in every request, so that the same collection works on a live server later. Where a route needs a login, open the *Authorization* tab, choose *Bearer Token* and paste the token. These are the requests to send, in order. The automated test above sends the same ones, so the answers must match.

items: `GET {{baseUrl}}/api/plans` lists the plans and limits.
`POST {{baseUrl}}/api/projects` twice on a free account. The second one expects 403.
`POST {{baseUrl}}/api/subscribe` with `{"plan":"pro"}` expects a checkout URL, and `GET /api/account` still shows `free`.
Send the signed `subscription.paid` webhook (the test shows how to calculate the `x-signature` header, or use a Postman script) and then the account shows `pro`.
Send the same webhook again and expect `duplicate: true`. Send `subscription.payment_failed` and expect 402 on creating a project.

content.text: Add a small test to a request in the *Scripts* tab, such as checking that the status is 201, and run the whole collection with the *Collection runner*. You can also import an OpenAPI file, as lesson 26 showed, to get all requests at once.
Deploy it

The deployment steps are the same for every project in this part of the course, and each is taught in full earlier. First run the tests and `npm audit`. Put secrets such as `JWT_SECRET` in environment variables, never in Git. Then pick one route: a VPS with PM2, nginx and a Let's Encrypt certificate (lesson 48), or Docker and Compose (lesson 49). Automate it with GitHub Actions (lesson 50). Replace the in-memory store with a real database first, because a restart on the server would otherwise erase the data, and add a `/health` route for monitoring.
Extend it
Your task

items: Add a `team` seat limit and an invite route that respects it.
Add a yearly plan with a renewal date, and a job from lesson 40 that reminds people before renewal.
Add a customer portal route for cancellation that takes effect at the end of the period.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Subscribing does not change the plan by itself.
A repeated webhook is applied once.
A past-due account is refused with 402 on limited features.

content.text: **On your resume.** "Built a subscription back end with plan limits, signed idempotent billing webhooks and past-due handling" is concise and shows that you understand what a paid product needs. Write only what you really built and can explain, and keep the repository link next to it. Our [resume templates](/templates) have a project section that suits this, and the [ATS checker](/features/ats-checker) shows how a tracking system reads it.

animation.title: A plan changes only by webhook

steps.say: The client asks to subscribe. The server returns a checkout link and changes nothing.
The provider takes the payment on its own page.
The signed webhook arrives. A verified, first-time event activates the plan.
Each limited feature checks the plan, and a past-due account is refused.

faqs.q: What is an entitlement check?
faqs.a: A server-side check, on every request, that the account's current plan allows the feature or the amount that the request needs.

faqs.q: Why not activate the plan when the user returns from checkout?
faqs.a: Anyone can open the return URL. Only a signed message from the provider proves that money moved.

faqs.q: What is past due?
faqs.a: The state of an account whose latest payment failed. Products usually limit features, with or without a grace period, until it is fixed.

quiz.q: What activates a paid plan?
options: A field in the subscribe request

quiz.q: What is an entitlement check?
options: A server check that the plan allows the requested feature or amount

quiz.q: Why remember billing event ids?
options: A repeated event must not be applied twice

lessons.title: Project 10: A Microservices Application
lessons.metaTitle: Project 10: Microservices with Gateway
lessons.description: Build a small microservices system in Node.js: users, orders and notifications services, an API gateway that checks tokens, an event broker and health checks.

content.text: The last project is the one that people find hardest to picture, so it is built to be small and runnable. Instead of one app, there are three small services and a front door. Each service has one job, they talk to each other over HTTP and through an event broker, and the only way in from the outside is the gateway. It runs in one process for the test, but every part uses its own port and could be moved to its own machine, which is the whole point. Read lesson 43 first for the reasons to split, and the reasons not to.
What you will build

items: A **users service** that owns user data.
An **orders service** that creates orders, asks the users service who the customer is, and publishes an `order.created` event.
A **notifications service** that listens for events and reacts, with no HTTP call from the orders service.
An **API gateway**, the only public address. It checks the JWT and forwards requests to the right service.
`/health` on every service, a 504 for timeouts at the gateway and a clear 503 when a dependency is down.

content.text: Design decisions before any code

Each service owns its own data, and nobody reads another service's data directly. The orders service does not open the users data. It asks the users service over HTTP. That is the rule that makes the services independent, and it costs something: a network call can fail, so there must be a timeout and an error. For work that does not need an answer, such as sending a notification, the orders service **publishes an event** to a broker, and the notifications service subscribes. The orders service neither knows nor cares who listens. In this project the broker is a few lines on top of `EventEmitter`. In production it would be Redis with BullMQ, RabbitMQ or Kafka, as in lesson 40.

The gateway checks the token once and then forwards the request, so the services behind it can trust that the caller was checked. This only works if the services are not reachable from the internet, so in a real system they sit on a private network, as the Compose file below shows.

items: Make a folder and open it in a terminal. Run `npm init -y`, then open `package.json` and add `"type": "module"` so that `import` works.
Install what the lesson needs: `npm install express jsonwebtoken`.
Copy `p-kit.js`, `p10-microservices.js` and `p10.test.js` into the folder. The shared `p-kit.js` is in Project 1.
Install the test tools with `npm install -D supertest`, then run `node --test p10.test.js`.

content.text: All four parts in one file so that you can read the whole system. Each `start...` function creates one service on a free port and returns its URL.
How the same four parts would run as containers. This file was **not run**. Only the gateway publishes a port to the outside.

# The same system as separate containers. NOT run in this course.
services:
  gateway:
    build: ./gateway
    ports: ["3000:3000"]
    environment:
      USERS_URL: http://users:3001
      ORDERS_URL: http://orders:3002
      JWT_SECRET: ${JWT_SECRET}
    depends_on: [users, orders]

  users:
    build: ./users                    # no ports: only the gateway can reach it
    environment:
      MONGODB_URI: mongodb://users-db:27017/users
    depends_on: [users-db]

  orders:
    build: ./orders
    environment:
      USERS_URL: http://users:3001
      REDIS_HOST: redis
      MONGODB_URI: mongodb://orders-db:27017/orders
    depends_on: [orders-db, redis]

  notifications:
    build: ./notifications
    environment:
      REDIS_HOST: redis
    depends_on: [redis]

  users-db:
    image: mongo:7
  orders-db:
    image: mongo:7
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine

The test starts all the services, logs in through the gateway, creates an order and waits for the notification, and then stops the users service to see that the orders service answers with a clear 503.
Rules worth understanding

**Synchronous and asynchronous calls.** Use a direct HTTP call when you need the answer now, such as *who is this customer*. Use an event when you only need to say *this happened*. Events keep services loosely coupled, and they let you add new reactions without changing the sender.

**Timeouts everywhere.** Every call between services has a timeout, using `AbortSignal.timeout` as in lesson 28. When a service does not answer in time, the gateway returns **504** instead of hanging. When the orders service cannot reach the users service at all, it answers **503** with a plain message.
**A single public door.** Only the gateway is exposed. It verifies the JWT, and the services trust what comes through it. Do not let outside traffic reach a service directly.
**Health checks.** Each service has `/health`. A load balancer, Docker or an uptime tool calls it and replaces or avoids a sick service.

**Failure is normal.** The test stops one service on purpose and checks that the system fails in a controlled way. When you design for several services, think about what happens when each of them is down.
Security and honesty notes

Services should not trust each other blindly. A production system adds service-to-service authentication, and keeps private networks, logs with a shared request id, and monitoring. Distributed systems also make data consistency harder: an order may exist while its notification is still on the way. Think about retries and idempotency as in lessons 40 and 42.

Be honest about the trade. For most projects, one well-organised app is easier to build, test and run. Choose several services when you can say why, and be ready to explain that choice in an interview.

The code in this lesson was run with Node.js 22 and its tests passed when the lesson was written. Library versions move, so run npm install and the tests on your own machine, and fix any small differences you see.

To keep every project runnable with no setup, the data is kept in memory and disappears when the server restarts. The first extension task of every project is to move the store to MongoDB or PostgreSQL. The rules and the tests stay the same, which is exactly why the code is split into layers.
Folder structure for the real version

The files in this course are flat, so that you can read each project in one sitting. In a real repository, split them as lesson 19 and lesson 32 showed. This is a sensible layout for this project, and the purpose of each folder is in the comments.

microservices/
├── docker-compose.yml
├── gateway/        # the only public service, checks JWT, forwards
│   ├── package.json
│   └── src/server.js
├── users-service/
│   ├── package.json
│   └── src/server.js
├── orders-service/
│   ├── package.json
│   └── src/server.js   # calls users, publishes order.created
├── notifications-service/
│   ├── package.json
│   └── src/server.js   # subscribes to events
└── shared/             # small shared helpers, if any
tests/system.test.js
Test the API with Postman

Start the app, open Postman, and create a collection for this project. Set a collection variable `baseUrl` to `http://localhost:3000`, and use `{{baseUrl}}` in every request, so that the same collection works on a live server later. Where a route needs a login, open the *Authorization* tab, choose *Bearer Token* and paste the token. These are the requests to send, in order. The automated test above sends the same ones, so the answers must match.

items: `GET {{baseUrl}}/api/orders` without a token expects 401 from the gateway.
With a Bearer token, `GET {{baseUrl}}/api/users/me` expects your user from the users service.
`POST {{baseUrl}}/api/orders` with `{"item":"Mouse"}` expects 201, and the notifications service logs the event.
Send an order for an unknown user and expect 422.
Stop the users service, send the order again and expect a clear 503. Call `/health` on each service.

content.text: Add a small test to a request in the *Scripts* tab, such as checking that the status is 201, and run the whole collection with the *Collection runner*. You can also import an OpenAPI file, as lesson 26 showed, to get all requests at once.
Deploy it

The deployment steps are the same for every project in this part of the course, and each is taught in full earlier. First run the tests and `npm audit`. Put secrets such as `JWT_SECRET` in environment variables, never in Git. Then pick one route: a VPS with PM2, nginx and a Let's Encrypt certificate (lesson 48), or Docker and Compose (lesson 49). Automate it with GitHub Actions (lesson 50). Replace the in-memory store with a real database first, because a restart on the server would otherwise erase the data, and add a `/health` route for monitoring.
Extend it
Your task

items: Add a fourth service for products and make the orders service check stock through it.
Pass a request id from the gateway to every service and log it, as in lesson 38.
Replace the broker with BullMQ and Redis, and run everything with Docker Compose.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The only public address is the gateway.
A stopped users service gives a clear 503 and not a hang.
The notification arrives without the orders service calling it.

content.text: **On your resume.** "Built a small microservices system with an API gateway, service-to-service calls with timeouts, an event broker and health checks" is a precise line. Say clearly that it was a learning project, and what you would add for production. Write only what you really built and can explain, and keep the repository link next to it. Our [resume templates](/templates) have a project section that suits this, and the [ATS checker](/features/ats-checker) shows how a tracking system reads it.

steps.say: The gateway is the only public address. It verifies the token and forwards the request.
The orders service asks the users service who the customer is, with a timeout.
Orders saves the order and publishes order.created. It does not call anyone else.
The notifications service reacts to the event on its own.

faqs.q: Why not let services read each other's databases?
faqs.a: Shared databases couple the services together, so changing one breaks the others. Each service should own its data and share it through its API or events.

faqs.q: Why publish an event instead of calling the notification service?
faqs.a: The orders service does not need an answer, and an event lets you add or remove listeners without changing the sender.

faqs.q: Is this how real companies do it?
faqs.a: The ideas are the same. Real systems add message brokers like RabbitMQ or Kafka, service meshes, tracing and orchestration such as Kubernetes.

quiz.q: Why should services not read each other’s databases?
options: It couples them so changing one breaks the others

quiz.q: When should you publish an event instead of calling a service?
options: When you need the data now
When you do not need an answer

quiz.q: What is the gateway’s role?
options: The only public door that checks the token and forwards requests

lessons.title: Node.js and Express Interview Questions and Answers
lessons.metaTitle: Node.js and Express Interview Questions
lessons.description: Practise 40 common Node.js and Express interview questions with short answers, grouped by topic: Node, Express, REST, databases, security and deployment.

content.text: This lesson collects 40 questions that come up again and again in Node.js and Express interviews, with short answers in simple English. It is a **starter set**, not a complete list of every question that exists. Do not memorise the answers word for word. Interviewers can tell, and they often ask a follow-up such as *how would you do that in your project?* Read an answer, close the page, say it aloud in your own words, and then check yourself. Each answer points to the lesson where the topic is taught in full, so that you can run the code and speak from experience.
JavaScript and Node basics

**Q. What is Node.js?**  
A runtime that runs JavaScript outside the browser. It uses the V8 engine and adds modules for files, networks and more. It is not a language or a framework.

**Q. Why is Node.js good for I/O-heavy apps?**  
It starts slow operations, such as network and disk calls, and carries on with other work, then runs a callback when the result is ready. One thread can serve many users that mostly wait.

**Q. Explain the event loop.**  
The loop checks for finished work and runs the waiting callbacks one at a time on the single JavaScript thread. If you block it with a long task, every request waits.

**Q. What is the difference between a callback, a promise and async/await?**  
A callback is a function that is called later. A promise is an object for a future value. async/await is a way to write promise code in a straight line, with try/catch for errors.

**Q. What is the difference between CommonJS and ES modules?**  
CommonJS uses require and module.exports and loads synchronously. ES modules use import and export, are the language standard and allow top-level await. See the CommonJS vs ES modules lesson.

**Q. What are streams and why use them?**  
Streams process data in small chunks, so memory stays small for big files. Use pipeline to connect them with proper error handling.

**Q. What is the difference between process.nextTick and setImmediate?**  
nextTick callbacks run right after the current operation, before the event loop continues. setImmediate runs in a later phase of the loop. Prefer promises and normal code unless you know why you need them.

**Q. How do worker threads, child processes and cluster differ?**  
Worker threads run heavy JavaScript in other threads of the same process. Child processes run other programs. Cluster runs several copies of a server that share a port.
Express and REST

**Q. What is middleware?**  
A function with req, res and next that runs between the request and the response. It can change the request, end the response or call next to continue. Order matters.

**Q. How do you handle errors in Express?**  
Use an error handler with four parameters, placed last. Throw AppError objects in code, and in Express 5 async errors reach the handler automatically. Hide the details of 500 errors from clients and log them.

**Q. What is the difference between req.params, req.query and req.body?**  
params come from the path, such as /users/:id. query comes from the part after the question mark. body is the data in the request, parsed by express.json().

**Q. What is express.Router?**  
A mini app that groups related routes, so you can mount them under a path, such as /api/users.

**Q. PUT or PATCH?**  
PUT replaces the whole item. PATCH changes only the fields sent.

**Q. Which status codes do you use most?**  
200, 201 with a Location header, 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, 429 and 500. 401 means not logged in, 403 means not allowed.

**Q. How do you design pagination?**  
Take page and limit from the query, clamp them to safe values, set a maximum limit, return the items with the total and page details. Cursor paging suits very large or changing lists.

**Q. How do you version an API?**  
Put the version in the URL, such as /api/v1. Create a new version only for breaking changes, and announce the end date of the old one.

**Q. What is CORS?**  
A browser rule that blocks pages from one origin calling an API on another unless the server allows it with headers. It protects users in browsers and is not a replacement for authentication.
Databases

**Q. SQL or NoSQL?**  
SQL suits strongly connected data and strict rules. NoSQL document databases suit flexible shapes read as a whole. It depends on the data and the queries, and many systems use both.

**Q. Embed or reference in MongoDB?**  
Embed small data that belongs to one parent and is read together. Reference data that is large, shared or grows without limit.

**Q. What does populate do?**  
It replaces a stored id with the referenced document by running another query. It is not a database join, so use it on purpose.

**Q. Why use indexes and what is their cost?**  
Indexes make queries fast by avoiding a full collection scan. They slow writes and use memory, so index only what your queries use.

**Q. What is an aggregation pipeline?**  
A list of stages such as $match, $group, $sort and $lookup that transform documents inside the database to build reports.

**Q. When do you need a transaction?**  
When several documents must change together or not at all. A change to one document is already atomic. Transactions need a replica set.
Authentication and security

**Q. How do you store passwords?**  
Never in plain text. Hash them with a slow algorithm such as bcrypt or Argon2, and compare with the library function.

**Q. Explain access and refresh tokens.**  
A short-lived access token is sent with each request. A longer refresh token, stored as a hash on the server, gets a new access token and rotates on every use, so it can be cancelled and reuse can be detected.

**Q. JWT or sessions?**  
Sessions are simple and easy to cancel, and suit websites. JWT suits services and mobile apps that cannot share a session store. Many systems use both.

**Q. Is a JWT encrypted?**  
No. It is signed, so it cannot be changed, but anyone can read it. Never put secrets in it.

**Q. What are XSS and CSRF and how do you stop them?**  
XSS runs attacker script in your page, so escape output. CSRF makes a browser send an authenticated request from another site, so use sameSite cookies and a CSRF token.

**Q. What is NoSQL injection?**  
Operators such as $ne hidden in JSON input change a query. Validate types, strip keys that start with $, and never pass raw input into queries.

**Q. What is the difference between authentication and authorization?**  
Authentication asks who you are, for example by checking a password or a token. Authorization asks what you may do, for example with roles and ownership checks. A route usually needs both.

**Q. How do you secure an Express app?**  
Use HTTPS, helmet, validated input, rate limiting, strict CORS, hashed passwords, short tokens, validated environment secrets and regular npm audit.

**Q. How do you verify a webhook?**  
Calculate an HMAC of the raw body with the shared secret, compare with timingSafeEqual, and store event ids to ignore duplicates.
Architecture, performance and deployment

**Q. What is the repository pattern?**  
A layer that is the only place that talks to the database, so the service holds business rules and can be tested with a fake repository.

**Q. What is dependency injection?**  
Passing what a piece of code needs, such as a repository or a payment gateway, as an argument, so tests can replace it.

**Q. How do you cache and what is hard about it?**  
Use cache-aside with a time to live, in memory or Redis. The hard part is invalidation: delete or refresh entries when the data changes.

**Q. How do you run slow tasks?**  
Put them on a queue, such as BullMQ with Redis, and process them with a worker with retries. Make jobs idempotent.

**Q. How do you find a memory leak?**  
Watch memory over time and take heap snapshots with --inspect. Look for caches without limits, listeners never removed and timers never cleared.

**Q. How do you scale a Node app?**  
Measure first, fix queries and caching, make servers stateless, run several copies behind a load balancer with health checks, and split into services only when there is a clear need.

**Q. How do you deploy a Node app?**  
On a VPS: Node with PM2 in cluster mode behind nginx with HTTPS from Let's Encrypt, a firewall and backups. Or in Docker with Compose. Automate tests and releases with CI/CD and use pm2 reload for no downtime.

**Q. What do you do when production is down?**  
Check health and logs first, find the last change, roll back if needed, then find the cause with the request id, and write a test so it cannot return.
How to use this lesson

items: Answer each question aloud without reading, then compare.
Add one real example from your own projects to each answer. Interviewers remember examples.
If you do not know something, say so and say how you would find out. That is a good answer.

content.text: Questions and good answers change with the job and the year. Treat these as practice, and read the job description to see which topics matter most.
Your task

items: Pick ten questions and record yourself answering them, then listen and shorten each answer to under a minute.
Write one example from Projects 1 to 10 for each of the sections above.
Ask a friend to ask you the questions in a random order.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You can answer ten questions without notes.
You can attach a project example to the security answers.
You know which lesson to reread for each weak answer.

steps.say: Listen to the whole question and think for a moment.
Give a short, clear answer in your own words.
Add an example from a project that you built.
Expect a follow-up. If you are unsure, say so and explain how you would find out.

faqs.q: Should I memorise these answers?
faqs.a: No. Understand them and say them in your own words, with an example from your projects.

faqs.q: How many questions will I be asked?
faqs.a: It varies a lot. Interviews often go deep on a few topics from your resume instead of covering many.

faqs.q: Where can I practise more?
faqs.a: Build the projects in this course, explain each design choice aloud, and ask a friend to challenge you.

quiz.q: What is the best way to use these sample answers?
options: Say them in your own words with an example from your project

quiz.q: What should you do when you do not know an answer?
options: Say so and explain how you would find out

quiz.q: Which question asks who you are versus what you may do?
